### Layer 5.6: Green's theorem for planar regions and curves

Green's theorem here means the circulation identity

\[
 \oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_D(\partial_x Q-\partial_y P)\,dx\,dy.
\]

The scope includes **both** statements linked under theorem 21 in
[Freek Wiedijk's list](https://www.cs.ru.nl/~freek/100/#21). These have different strengths;
proving the smooth-boundary specialization of 5.3 alone does not discharge this layer.

| Reference | Required specialization |
| --- | --- |
| [HOL Light, `GREEN_THEOREM_CURL`](https://www.cs.ru.nl/~freek/100/hol.html#21) | A closed absolutely continuous curve, index one on every bounded component of its complement, and a `C¹` field on a neighbourhood of the curve and those components; integrability of both sides is a conclusion. No simplicity or finite-piece assumption. |
| [Abdulaziz–Paulson, Isabelle/AFP `Green`](https://isa-afp.org/entries/Green.html) | Finite type-I and type-II divisions, compatible oriented boundary chains, and the directional hypotheses of `analytically_valid`; no full `C¹` assumption on the field. The boundary integrals use Henstock–Kurzweil integration. |

The intrinsic targets below specify the mathematics; the reference statements are also
acceptance tests. In particular, provide specializations of AFP's
[`GreenThm_typeI_typeII_divisible_region`,
`GreenThm_typeI_typeII_divisible_region_finite_holes`, and
`GreenThm_typeI_typeII_divisible_region_equivallent_boundary`](https://isa-afp.org/browser_info/current/AFP/Green/Green.html),
whose hypotheses follow from the corresponding AFP hypotheses, with no added regularity
assumptions. The intrinsic cell and boundary requirements below specify the API; AFP's
particular encodings of subdivisions are not a required carrier.
HOL Light writes the field components in the order `(Q,P)`; our convention is always
`P dx + Q dy` and curl `∂x Q − ∂y P`.

**Conventions and existing inputs.** Use `ℂ` as the oriented real plane, with coordinates
`Complex.re`, `Complex.im`, positively oriented basis `(1, Complex.I)`, and `volume` as area.
Real differentiability is `ContDiffOn ℝ 1`, never complex differentiability. On an oriented
parameter interval `a..b`, the circulation is the existing `intervalIntegral`

```
∫ t in a..b, P (γ t) * (deriv γ t).re + Q (γ t) * (deriv γ t).im
```

and its `Path` form is Mathlib's `curveIntegral` of the real continuous linear map
`v ↦ P z * v.re + Q z * v.im`. Consume
`curveIntegral_eq_intervalIntegral_deriv` for agreement of `deriv` and `derivWithin`. Use
[`AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/AbsolutelyContinuous.html#AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval),
Mathlib's absolute-continuity FTC, Fubini, change of variables, connected components,

For points off a curve, use
[`TauCeti.Contour.windingNumber`](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/main/TauCeti/Analysis/Contour/Winding/Number/Basic.lean);
no second index is defined. On the trace the area-weight function is set to zero, independently

## Statements that must not enter the library

Each is a tempting mistake with its refutation.

- **"Orientable = admits a positive-Jacobian atlas", as a definition.** `Set.Icc 0 1` is orientable
  but its two charts cannot be made positively transitioning; chart signs are the definition (2.1),
  the atlas criterion a theorem for boundaryless `M`.
- **"The sigma topology on pointwise orientations is the orientation cover."** It is discrete, so
  the projection is not a local homeomorphism.
- **"`H^•_c` is functorial for all smooth maps."** Only for proper maps and open inclusions;
  `ℝ → pt` already fails on `H^0_c`.
- **"Integral manifolds are embedded", "leaves carry the subspace topology", "`T_pS ⊆ D_p`
  suffices".** The irrational line on the torus is a dense leaf; containment defines tangent
  submanifolds, for which Frobenius is false.
- **"Global sections detect involutivity without Hausdorffness."** Glue a central `ℝ³(x,y,z)`
  to a chart `ℝ³(u,y,z)` for each rational `a`, off `x = a` and `u = 0`, by `x = a + u³`.
  This second-countable non-Hausdorff manifold carries the rank-2 distribution given by
  `ker(dz − y dx)` centrally and `ker(dz − 3u²y du)` in each added chart. Every global section
  of it is a multiple of `∂y`, so the global bracket condition holds, while the central local
  fields `X = ∂x + y∂z` and `Y = ∂y` have bracket `−∂z` outside the distribution. The displayed
  annihilator glues to a global smooth `α` with `dα(X,Y) = 1` in the central chart.
  This refutes using only global smooth sections as the definition without
  the hypotheses for local bump extension. It does not refute the canonical
  local involutivity predicate, which is the definition used in layer 4.
  The global annihilating-form characterization retains its Hausdorff
  hypothesis.
- **"The boundary of a manifold with corners is a manifold."** False at a corner of `[0, ∞)²`; the
  abstract boundary of *Boundary and corners* is what Stokes needs.
- **"[Lee]'s boundary-orientation signs transfer verbatim."** Mathlib's half-space constrains the
  first coordinate, [Lee]'s the last.
- **"Δ = −div ∘ grad."** This repository pins `Δ = div ∘ grad` (12.5's flat gate).
- **"Degree is defined for noncompact domains, or at critical values without care."** The inclusion
  `(0, ∞) ↪ ℝ` has sign sum `1` over `y > 0` and `0` over `y < 0`.
- **"The de Rham comparison holds for every `IsManifold`."** The line with two origins has
  `H¹_dR = 0` and singular `H¹ ≅ ℝ`; `[T2Space M] [SigmaCompactSpace M]` are load-bearing throughout
  6–9.
- **"Smooth and continuous chains are homotopy equivalent on every charted space."** On the real
  line with preferred charts `φ_a(y) = cuberoot(y − a)`, smooth paths are constant: differentiating
  `g(s) = g(t) + (φ_{g(t)}(g(s)))³` at `t` gives `g'(t) = 0`. Smooth `H₀` therefore distinguishes
  every point, while ordinary singular `H₀` is `ℝ`. The smoothing equivalence needs smooth chart
  compatibility and the relative-approximation hypotheses in 8.3.
- **"`mpullback (g ∘ f) = mpullback f ∘ mpullback g` unconditionally."** `mfderiv` is junk-valued;
  the chain rule needs differentiability (0.3).
- **"A smooth simplex extends smoothly to a neighbourhood of the whole simplex."** Local extensions
  into a manifold cannot be patched in the target; local extendability is the definition (8.4).
- **"The smooth structure of a covering space is an instance on the total space."** It depends on
  the map (2.3).
- **"Every integral manifold is weakly embedded."** Only the injectively immersed ones with a
  second-countable carrier: the double cover `z ↦ z²` of the circle and the discrete real line fail.
- **"A closed form with values in a normed space is locally exact."** A smooth `c₀₀`-valued
  `1`-form on `ℝ` has no local primitive; the coefficients must be complete.
- **"Extension by zero exists on every manifold."** On the line with two origins it does not.
- **"The Poincaré pairing is defined on manifolds with boundary."** On `[0, 1]`, `[dx] = 0` in
  `H¹_dR`, yet `∫₀¹ dx = 1`.
- **"`Prop`-typed placeholders are acceptable in `Suggested.lean`."** A condition that cannot yet be
  stated is prose in the README, never `def _ : Prop := sorry`.

## Rectifiable curves and geometric measure theory

[GeometricMeasureTheory](../GeometricMeasureTheory/README.md), G1–G2, owns rectifiability,
arclength, variation–speed identities, and Hausdorff length. Consume those results in
planar curve calculus rather than building another metric length theory. The flat planar
Green targets of [layer 5.6](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/826)
own winding numbers, curve integration, and the actual area identity; layers 5.3–5.5
retain manifold integration and Stokes. In 5.6.1, AC trace-nullity and variation–speed
are specializations consumed from G1, whose general metric statements are the single
owned targets; this layer builds their integral and index compatibility.

For continuous BV curves, construct the geometric line integral of a continuous real
1-form along the trace with its traversal multiplicity, using G1's AC arclength
factorization. Prove independence of that factorization, invariance under increasing
continuous onto reparametrizations, and sign reversal under decreasing ones. Prove
agreement with the existing derivative-based `curveIntegral` when the parameter is AC.
The original non-AC parameter cannot in general be differentiated to recover the geometric
line integral. The metric and arclength part of G1 precedes this construction; Green's
theorem for the AC factorization then supplies its rectifiable-curve area specialization.

GMT G6 owns the finite-perimeter and boundary-normal comparison for rectifiable Jordan
domains, consuming that AC boundary-integral identity. [Isoperimetry](../Isoperimetry/README.md),
I3 and I6, owns the sharp curve inequality and circle equality. Neither Green's theorem
nor the metric length foundations depend on the sharp isoperimetric theorem.

## Relation to sibling roadmaps

One owner per shared construction, stated identically on both sides.

- **Universal covers** owns π₁, deck groups, the classification and πₙ; 2.4, 6.3 and 10.5 consume
  them.
- **Geometric topology** consumes the orientation interface (2), the canonical
  Tau Ceti distribution and foliation APIs and their integral-manifold/leaf
  extensions (4), densities and form integration (5.5, 12.4), and the abstract
  boundary of manifolds with corners (5.5). The half-space boundary manifold
  is Tau Ceti's and consumed by both. Geometric topology owns the Riemannian
  volume measure, already `TauCeti.riemannianVolume` and consumed by 12.4,
  curvature, hyperbolic structures, tubular and collar neighbourhoods,
  gluing, tautness, the Euler class, and the 3-manifold-specific applications.
  Layer 4 supplies the missing common Frobenius and leaf theory on the
  existing APIs, not a replacement distribution or foliation carrier.
- **Algebraic topology** owns singular chains and cochains, relative theory, subdivision, small
  chains, excision and Mayer–Vietoris (its Stages 2–3), and universal coefficients, cup and cap
  products and singular Poincaré duality (Stage 6); layer 8 consumes them and builds only smooth
  chains, integration over them and the de Rham comparison. It consumes this roadmap's orientation
  and degree API (layers 2 and 10).
- **Hopf–Rinow** owns the Levi-Civita connection, covariant differentiation along curves, geodesics
  and their flow, the exponential map, Hopf–Rinow, and the manifold inverse function theorem;
  layer 12 builds on the connection, 10.1 consumes the inverse function theorem, and 3.2 consumes
  its maximal integral curves and finite-dimensional maximal flow, whose extension to Banach models
  is this roadmap's.
- **Lie groups** owns `lieExp`, one-parameter subgroups, `Ad`, the closed-subgroup and Lie-specific
  theorems, consuming layer 3's flows (reconciled in 3.3), layer 4's Frobenius and leaves, and 2.3's
  covers.
- **PDE** owns everything analytic about `Δ` beyond 12.5. **DG and `A∞`** owns the generic DGA
  packaging; the wedge product on de Rham cohomology is built here, the cup product by algebraic
  topology. **Heegaard Floer (analytic)** consumes orientations and degree; layer 0.4 owns migration
  of its existing 2-form API and consumers to the generic carrier, and 6.1 supplies the integration
  interface. **Contour integration** owns contour integrals; 5.3 only reconciles with
  `curveIntegral`. **One-parameter semigroups** owns the operator-semigroup analogue of flows.
  **Modular forms** may refactor its region-Stokes onto layer 5 at its own choice.

## Ordering

Layers 0–1 first. Layers 2, 3 (except the form half of 3.4) and 12.1–12.3 are independent of them; 4
needs 3 and 1.4; 12.4–12.5 need 0, 2 and 5. The manifold integration track is
5.1–5.5 → {6, 7} → 8 → 9; 5.6 runs in parallel from Mathlib's flat calculus and integration
and compares with 5.2–5.5. Layers 6 and
most of 7 are available once 0–1 land (6.3 needs only 5.4's homotopy identity); 10 needs 2, 5, 7 and
9.2; 11 needs 10. Start 3.1 and 8.3 early. Claim single numbered items or smaller; the headline
theorems (5.3, 8.5, 9.3, 10.4, 11.1) are staged claims whose intermediate lemmas land as reusable

# Roadmap: diophantine approximation and transcendence

**Summary.** Build heights, approximation exponents and auxiliary polynomials to prove Roth and absolute quantitative Subspace theorems. Develop exponential transcendence and logarithmic bounds, then effective equations, arithmetic power series, Mahler systems and Ax–Schanuel. Schanuel’s conjectural consequences retain their hypotheses. The foundations are Mathlib’s number fields, heights, polynomials, analysis and differential algebra, with Tau Ceti’s product formula and dimension theory.

## Scope and ownership

Own the field comparisons of relative and absolute heights, absolute tuple heights, Euclidean and Plücker subspace heights with their duality and Northcott properties, the fixed-field Siegel lemma, primitive minimal-polynomial and algebraic-element size adapters, approximation exponents, multivariate divided derivatives, weighted indices, auxiliary-polynomial nonvanishing, Roth and absolute Subspace theorems, finite-rank unit equations, recurrences, exponential transcendence, logarithmic bounds, effective Diophantine equations, E-/G-/Mahler functions, the Picard–Vessiot and differential-Galois comparisons needed by E-function specialization, and exponential Ax–Schanuel with its contraction and Lie-derivative calculus on supplied ordinary algebraic forms, its generated-subgroup and additive/torus separation argument, and its arbitrary-constant-field descent.

The height, Mahler-measure, coefficient-height, subspace-height, Northcott and
Siegel foundation has one owner here: §§0.2–0.3,1.3,2.5,2.8. All consumers in
this roadmap use those sections, and this foundation supplies the same interfaces
to other roadmaps. Relative sup coefficient, matrix and Plücker heights use
`Height.AdmissibleAbsValues` over an arbitrary field; their coordinate types are
finite, and polynomial coefficients use the native Finsupp carrier. Number-field
hypotheses enter for Euclidean factors, field-degree roots, fixed-field
finiteness and Siegel's theorem. Absolute tuple heights also cover algebraic
elements in any characteristic-zero ambient field. Relative heights are primary
over a fixed field; absolute heights are their degree roots. The Euclidean vector
zero extension and the projective zero convention have explicit comparison
maps. Siegel's interfaces include bases and restriction through a finite field
extension; their counting and selection core is stated for arbitrary field towers,
without number-field or characteristic-zero hypotheses (§2.8). The foundation
uses one native Plücker point and its dual annihilator;
the dot-product perpendicular and the absolute Euclidean subspace height are
consumer adapters on that theory. Real minima and Gram bounds are supplied by
GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic; number-field kernel lattices and their
covolume/height conversion belong here. Suggested library home:
`TauCeti/NumberTheory/Height/`.

Mathlib owns places, relative and absolute heights, number-field house, polynomial Mahler measure, univariate Hasse derivatives, power series and differential modules. The variants here concern arbitrary algebraic elements, coefficient vectors and auxiliary constructions. Fixed-field Northcott and Dirichlet’s unit rank, torsion/basis decomposition and infinitude criterion are supplied by Mathlib; bounded-degree finiteness in the algebraic closure, Kronecker’s theorem and the Mahler/absolute-height dictionary belong here (§§0.2–0.3). Mathlib’s `Orientation.abs_volumeForm_apply_le` and `Orientation.volumeForm_robust'` supply the real determinant form of Hadamard’s inequality, including the empty family. GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic §0.1 supplies the Gram-determinant upper bound for real and complex inner-product spaces and families in arbitrary ambient dimension.

GlobalNumberFields Layer 0 owns places, completions, extension multiplicities and product formula. The geometric estimates in §0.0 use Mathlib’s discrete lattice and covolume carriers. [IntegralLattices](../IntegralLattices/README.md), Layer 0A and Layer 2, owns integral quadratic lattices and their bounded-norm finiteness; [EffectiveBounds](../EffectiveBounds/README.md), Layer 0, owns the measure-free lattice counting and doubling interface. [AlgebraicCurves](../AlgebraicCurves/README.md), Layer 9, owns the Kähler/Weil differential comparison for function fields; the arbitrary finite-type differential rank and algebraic Cartan calculus are §5.4 and §5.6 here. [DerivedDeRhamCohomology](../DerivedDeRhamCohomology/README.md), §§2.1–2.11, supplies ordinary algebraic forms and their differential on Mathlib’s Kähler/exterior-power carriers; §5.6 specializes that construction to characteristic-zero fields. [DifferentialGeometry](../DifferentialGeometry/README.md), the differential-forms and de Rham layers, owns smooth forms, distinct from Ax’s algebraic forms.

## Conventions

Algebraic-number fields have characteristic zero. F_x is the primitive integer minimal polynomial with positive leading coefficient a₀ and degree d; its transcendental junk value is 1. H_naive is its largest coefficient modulus, M its Mahler measure, and house the largest conjugate modulus (junk value 0). Integrality and denominator claims assume algebraicity. Absolute scalar heights are `NumberField.absMulHeight₁`, `absLogHeight₁`; relative heights are `Height.mulHeight`, `mulHeight₁`, `logHeight`, `logHeight₁`. Thus M=H_abs^d and H_K=H_abs^[K:ℚ]. Coefficient heights are projective; constants have logarithmic height zero. Relative sup heights of coefficients, entries and Plücker points use Height.AdmissibleAbsValues; their logarithms are the logarithms of the multiplicative heights. The subspace’s relative Euclidean height and subspaceHeight differ by the [K:ℚ]-th root, including the zero subspace. Plücker coordinates use Set.powersetCard and the standard exterior-power basis; changing the coordinate order only permutes and signs them.

Real-lattice minima use the supplier’s ConvexBody carrier, with zero in its interior and central symmetry for Minkowski’s bounds. The index i : Fin d means the (i+1)-st minimum. The supplier uses canonical Euclidean Haar volume, including volume 1 in dimension zero; transporting to another normed model or Haar measure transports body volume and covolume by the same factor. No second minima carrier is introduced.

Coordinate norms are sup norms. Infinite-place values are |σ_v(x)|^(mult(v)/[K:ℚ]), with mult 1 or 2; finite values are ideal-normalized moduli to power 1/[K:ℚ]. The product on K× is 1. Extension weights multiply by [L_w:K_v]/[L:K]. Absolute twisted heights on ℚ̄ give zero at zero; their Euclidean variant satisfies N^(−1/2)H₂≤H≤H₂ on nonzero N-tuples. `rationalSuccessiveInfimum` and `rationalInfimumSpace` use K-points; their absolute analogues are separate targets.

Divided derivatives use binomial coefficients; ordinary order k contributes k!. Wronskian rows are derivative orders, columns functions, starting at zero; the empty determinant is 1. Weighted index is the infimum of nonzero Taylor-coefficient weights, ∞ at zero. Zero weights use extended nonnegative division; finiteness needs positive weights. Native binary homogenization uses coordinate 0 affine, 1 homogenizing. Logarithms carry chosen branches, principal only when specified. ord_p(p)=1; ramification and residue degree remain separate. E-series use a_n/n!, G-series a_n. Conjectures are hypotheses.

irrelevant ideals. Prove chart and projective-coordinate independence,
Z_0=(ℙ¹)^m, and that membership is weightedIndex≥t.

Work over a commutative ring R with finite block set B, affine variable set S, a block map b:S→B, and degrees d:B→ℕ. Write t_h(e)=Σ_{b(j)=h}e_j and A_d(e)=(d_h−t_h(e))_h⊕e. in its real mixed-embedding span of dimension Dm. The ambient space is `PiLp 2 (fun _ : Fin V ↦ NumberField.mixedEmbedding.euclidean.mixedSpace K)`,

`mixedSpace` is not an inner-product space and does not fix this measure.

has a larger covolume and does not satisfy this identity. Prove the formula
from the archimedean Gram minors and the finite-place determinant ideal;

## Layer 5: special functions and functional transcendence

### 5.1 D-finite series and minimal equations

For k⊂ℂ define `IsDFinite k f` for f∈ℂ[[z]] by the existence of p₀,…,p_n∈k[z] with p_n≠0 and Σpᵢf^(i)=0. Equivalently its derivatives span a finite-dimensional k(z)-space; for coefficients in k this is equivalent to a polynomial recurrence Σqᵢ(n)c_(n+i)=0 with q_r≠0. (B08, §3.1, Prop. 3.2.1, pp. 11-12; Fischler–Rivoal, Def. 1, p. 1.)

Its API includes `IsDFinite.add`: Sums of D-finite series are D-finite; `IsDFinite.mul`: Products of D-finite series are D-finite; `IsDFinite.derivative`: The derivative of a D-finite series is D-finite; `IsDFinite.mono`: k≤k′ and IsDFinite k f imply IsDFinite k′ f; `isDFinite_polynomial`: A polynomial with coefficients in k is D-finite over k; `isDFinite_iff_pRecursive`: For f with coefficients in k: D-finite over k iff the coefficient sequence is P-recursive with polynomial coefficients in k[X].

**Checks.**

- PowerSeries.exp ℂ is D-finite over ℚ (f′ − f=0).
- Every polynomial p with coefficients in Q̄ is D-finite over Q̄: if p≠0, p f′−p′f=0 has nonzero leading coefficient p; if p=0, the order-zero equation 1·f=0 is a witness.
- Σ zⁿ is D-finite over ℚ ((1 − z) f′ − f=0).
- Σ z^{2^n} is not D-finite even over ℂ; a definition allowing the coefficients p_i to be arbitrary power series (rather than polynomials) would accept it.

Define `dfiniteOrder k f` as the least order of such an equation. Minimal equations p,p′ satisfy p′_n pᵢ=p_n p′ᵢ, so their monic rational operator is unique. Define `IsMinimalSingularPoint` by vanishing of the leading coefficient of every minimal equation; `IsApparentSingularity` means the operator has a full holomorphic solution basis there. (B06, §1, p. 1; B08, §3.4, Thm. 3.4.1, p. 14.)

Its API includes `exists_minimal_equation`: There is an equation of order dfiniteOrder; `dfiniteOrder_le`: Every equation has order≥dfiniteOrder; `minimal_equation_unique`: For minimal-order equations p,p′ over k with nonzero leading coefficients, p′_n p_i=p_n p′_i for all i; `dfiniteOrder_eq_zero_iff`: dfiniteOrder=0 iff f=0; `IsMinimalSingularPoint`: ξ is a singular point of the minimal equation: the leading coefficient of every minimal equation vanishes at ξ.

**Checks.**

- exp has minimal order 1.
- (z − 1)eᶻ has order 1 and 1 is a singular point of its minimal equation (an apparent one).
- The zero series has order 0.
- exp has no finite singular point; a definition of 'singular point' using an arbitrary (non-minimal) equation such as (z − 1)(f′ − f)=0 would wrongly report z=1.

For a scalar equation of order r≥1 over k(z), define `IsApparentSingularity` at ξ to require that ξ is a singular point of its normalized operator and that the space of holomorphic solution germs at ξ has dimension r. This is a property of the operator, independent of multiplication of its equation by a nonzero rational function. Its API proves invariance under equation normalization, constructs a full holomorphic solution basis, and relates this basis to the minimal equation’s solution germs; it does not assert that evaluation at ξ is invertible. (B06, §2, Thm. 2.1, pp. 3–4; B08, §3.4, Thm. 3.4.1, p. 14.)

**Checks.**

- The equation (z−1)y′−zy=0 has its one-dimensional holomorphic basis (z−1)e^z at 1, although every solution vanishes there.
- The equation y′−y=0 has no singular point at 1; multiplying it by z−1 does not make its normalized operator singular.
- The Euler equation zy′−y/2=0 has no nonzero holomorphic solution germ at 0, so 0 is a genuine singularity.

For a holomorphic matrix A on a disc D of radius r>0, every initial vector y₀ admits a holomorphic solution y′=Ay on D with y(z₀)=y₀. Two such solutions agree on D. (B08, §2.2, Thm. 2.2.1, p. 9.)

Under §5.1’s positive-radius holomorphic-system hypotheses, evaluation at the centre is a linear isomorphism from the space of solutions restricted to the disc to ℂⁿ. Its dimension is n. (B08, §2.2, Thm. 2.2.1, p.9.)

For a scalar equation Σi=0..m pᵢy^(i)=0 with m≥1, holomorphic coefficients on a positive-radius disc and nowhere-zero p_m, every initial jet c₀,…,c_(m−1) admits a unique solution on that disc. The restricted solution space has dimension m. (B08, §2.1, p.8, §2.2, Thm. 2.2.1, p.9.)

Its analytic sum `eFun a` is entire. This uses geometric coefficient growth. (Fischler–Rivoal, Def. 1, p. 1; B08, §3.1, p. 11.)

Its API includes `ePowerSeries`: The power series Σ a_n zⁿ/n!; `eFun`: The entire function z ↦ Σ a_n zⁿ/n!; `hurwitzMul`: The binomial convolution, so that ePowerSeries (hurwitzMul a b)=ePowerSeries a · ePowerSeries b; `ePowerSeries_hurwitzMul`: ePowerSeries (hurwitzMul a b)=ePowerSeries a * ePowerSeries b; `IsEFunction.add`: Sums of E-functions are E-functions; `IsEFunction.hurwitzMul`: Products of E-functions are E-functions; `IsEFunction.shift`: The derivative (shifted coefficients) of an E-function is an E-function; `IsEFunction.map_ringEquiv`: Applying a ring automorphism σ of ℂ to the coefficients gives an E-function (the Galois conjugate f^σ); `IsEFunction.differentiable`: eFun a is entire; `IsEFunction.hasSum`: The series Σ a_n zⁿ/n! converges to eFun a z for every z; `IsEFunction.exists_numberField`: All coefficients lie in one number field.

- a_n=n − 1 ((z − 1)eᶻ) is an E-function.

*Needs:* §5.1.

### 5.5 Mahler systems and their values

Define `IsMahlerFunction` as follows. For integer q≥2 define `IsMahlerFunction q f` for a series with algebraic coefficients by Σi=0..n pᵢ(z)f(z^(qⁱ))=0 for nonzero polynomial data over ℚ̄. Equivalently f is a coordinate of F(z)=A(z)F(z^q), A∈GL_m(ℚ̄(z)). Use Mathlib’s `PowerSeries.expand r hr` for f(z^r), with hr:r≠0; its `expand_apply` identifies it with formal substitution by X^r. (AF17, §1, equation (1.1), p. 2; AF17, §1, p. 2.)

Its API includes `IsMahlerFunction.add`: Sums of q-Mahler functions are q-Mahler; `IsMahlerFunction.mul`: Products of q-Mahler functions are q-Mahler; `IsMahlerFunction.expand`: f(z^q) is q-Mahler if f is; `isMahlerFunction_of_polynomial`: Polynomials with algebraic coefficients are q-Mahler; `isMahlerFunction_iff_system`: f is q-Mahler iff it is the first coordinate of a solution of F(z)=A(z)F(z^q) with A invertible over ℂ(z) (and algebraic entries).

**Checks.**

- Σ z^{2^n} is 2-Mahler.
- A series with f=(1 − z)f(z²) and algebraic coefficients is 2-Mahler.
- For q≥2, exp is not q-Mahler: the functions exp(z^{q^i}) with distinct exponents have no nontrivial polynomial-coefficient linear relation. A predicate allowing arbitrary power-series coefficient relations would fail this test.
- z is q-Mahler (z^q·z − z·z^q=0 is trivial; use p₀=z^q, p₁=−z).
- A constant series with transcendental value c is not a Mahler function in this algebraic-coefficient convention, although it solves the one-dimensional identity system A=1. The system equivalence must retain the algebraic coefficients of F and A and q≥2.

Define `IsMahlerRegularPoint` as follows. Define `IsMahlerRegularPoint q A α` for a square matrix A over ℂ(z) by q≥2, det A≠0, 0<|α|<1 and absence of poles of entries of both A and A⁻¹ at every α^(q^ℓ), ℓ≥0. Poles use reduced rational denominators. Singularities have no accumulation in the open unit disc. (AF17, §1, p. 2.)

Its API includes `isMahlerRegularPoint_iff`: Unfolding: q≥2, det A≠0, 0 < |α| < 1 and no α^{q^ℓ} is a zero of the denominator of an entry of A or A⁻¹; `IsMahlerRegularPoint.pow`: α regular implies α^q regular; `isMahlerRegularPoint_of_polynomial`: For q≥2 and polynomial A with unit determinant every α in the punctured disc is regular.

**Checks.**

- For q≥2 and A=[[1, 0], [z, 1]] every 0 < |α| < 1 is regular.
- For A=(1 − 2z)⁻¹, α=2^{−1/2} is not regular; a definition testing only ℓ=0 would call it regular.
- For q≥2, the 0 × 0 system has determinant 1 and every point of the punctured disc is regular.
- The scalar zero matrix is not a regular system at 1/2, although all reduced entry denominators of A and its total inverse are 1. Testing denominators alone must not accept a singular matrix.
- For q=1 the identity matrix at 1/2 fails the q≥2 condition.

Every Mahler-system target below has q≥2 and an invertible matrix over ℚ̄(z).
All analytic targets start with a convergent germ: there is ρ>0 for
which each coefficient series is summable at every |z|<ρ. The formal predicate
alone does not stand for an analytic evaluation. Algebraic independence for
algebraic-coefficient germs over ℂ(z) is equivalent to absence of a nonzero
relation over ℚ̄[z], and their transcendence degrees over ℂ(z) and ℚ̄(z) agree.
(B08, Thm.3.3.1, p.13.)

from a convergent q-Mahler germ. Given a system F(z)=A(z)F(z^q), set
A_ℓ(z)=A(z)A(z^q)⋯A(z^(q^(ℓ−1))). On each compact subdisc choose ℓ with
z^(q^ℓ) inside the initial convergence disc, and continue F by
A_ℓ(z)F(z^(q^ℓ)) as a meromorphic germ. Prove `mahler_iterate_independent`:
sufficiently deep iterates give the same germ, including across removable
singularities of the product. Prove `exists_mahler_meromorphic`, `mahlerMeromorphic_spec` and
`mahlerMeromorphic_unique`: the result is independent of the system and the
initial convergence radius, agrees with the Taylor germ, and uses Mathlib's

AnalyticAt ℂ (mahlerMeromorphic q f) α, equivalently no pole in this normal
form. Prove `mahlerMeromorphic_eq_tsum` wherever the original Taylor terms
are summable and |α|<1; use Abel's theorem when α is on the Taylor circle
of convergence. Summability there excludes a meromorphic pole. Outside that
summability range the continuation, rather than tsum, defines the value.

and the analytic identity theorem.) *Needs:* Mathlib meromorphic normal
forms, analytic power series, identity and Abel theorems; the system equivalence above.

of z to reduce to a power series. Record the equivalent version over ℂ(z)
by coefficient-field descent. The polynomial numerator and nonzero
denominator have algebraic coefficients. This supplies the functional
transcendence bridge used by the Fredholm example and by function-field
regularity. (Nishioka, Theorem 5.1.7; AF17, Lemma 2.2, p.10.)

- √(1−z) is algebraic and nonrational, so it cannot satisfy a q-Mahler relation for q≥2.
- z⁻¹ is covered by the meromorphic-germ version after multiplication by z; a restriction to holomorphic field elements would not suffice for regularity.

**Regularity of the generated function field.** Prove
`mahler_function_field_regular`: for convergent algebraic-coefficient F solving

field extension. The inverse system makes L stable under z↦z^q. Hence all

and form a meromorphic Mahler germ. Algebraic Mahler rationality puts that
element in ℚ̄(z). In characteristic zero this gives geometric integrality
of the finitely generated function algebra. (AF17, Lemma 2.2, p.10.)
*Needs:* `algebraic_mahler_rational`, finite extension linear algebra, and the
finite-generation and geometric-integrality comparisons stated here.

**Checks.**

- For rational F the field L is ℚ̄(z), so the relative algebraic closure is the base field.

- ℚ̄(z)(√(1−z)) is not regular over ℚ̄(z); its relative algebraic closure has degree two and is excluded by Mahler rationality.

The E-series for exp z has a_n=1, whereas the same analytic function has G-series coefficients 1/n!, which fail the denominator bound. The scaled system recurrence T=1,M=1 gives P₂=1/2. For the Laplace transform g=1/(x−1), xg−1=g; the initial-value correction is essential. The dependent tuple (1,2) in Schanuel has transcendence degree 1, so distinctness cannot replace ℚ-independence.

Heights, auxiliary polynomials, unit equations and effective logarithmic bounds feed arithmetic geometry, integral-point calculations and computational number theory. Specialisation and Ax–Schanuel supply arithmetic differential equations and functional-transcendence applications; the conditional independence conclusions always pass their conjecture hypothesis to consumers.

TauCetiRoadmap/EffectiveBounds:
# Roadmap: effective arithmetic bounds and geometry of numbers

**Status: reopened for the existing Layer 0 and Layer 3 completion targets (2026-10-28).**
The earlier archive declaration was premature for the full approved scope. The remaining work
includes removing the redundant `box` wrapper as Layer 0 requires, and the explicit regulator
lower bounds and unit-log volume comparisons of Layer 3. The two Layer 3 implementations are
[Tau Ceti #22059](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/pull/22059) and
[#22064](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/pull/22064); the wrapper removal is a separate
implementation change. These targets remain active until their source PRs merge and are verified.
The mathematical targets below are unchanged. The long-horizon Brauer–Siegel paragraph remains
an aspiration, not an additional completion target. Historical reports are retained as dated
snapshots; re-archiving will be part of the already open archive batch once all targets are met.


Mathlib has Minkowski's convex-body theorem, the canonical embedding, the Minkowski
bound, and even the qualitative summit (Minkowski's lower bound on the discriminant
`NumberField.abs_discr_ge` and **Hermite's finiteness theorem**
`NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd`), but it stops short of the **effective, explicit
estimates** that geometry of numbers exists to produce: a discriminant bound from a basis
of integers, an explicit class number bound, the index of squares in the unit group, an
explicit ideal count, and, the summit, an **effective Hermite–Minkowski**: an explicit
upper bound on the *number* of number fields of bounded discriminant, not just their
finiteness. We build the effective bounds here, with geometry of numbers as the engine.

The spine is the chain of explicit bounds; geometry of numbers is the tool, not the goal.

Suggested homes: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/EffectiveBounds/` (the bounds) and
`TauCeti/NumberTheory/GeometryOfNumbers/` (the lattice-point engine).

Several Layer-1 bounds already exist, sorry-free, inside
[kim-em/erdos-unit-distance](https://github.com/kim-em/erdos-unit-distance) (the
formalization of Alpöge's disproof of the uniform-constant Erdős unit-distance
conjecture), stated over an arbitrary number field. The first targets here **migrate**
them; credit that source in each ported file.

Migration sources, pinned at commit `140edda5974ec5afb8beefdbb3014d93d92bdc64`:
- `ErdosUnitDistance/Discriminant.lean`: `abs_discr_le_of_basis_isIntegral` and the
  trace-form helper `trace_eq_zero_of_sq_ratCast`.
- `ErdosUnitDistance/ClassNumber.lean`: `card_ideal_absNorm_le` (the explicit ideal
  count), `classNumber_le_bound`, `index_powMonoidHom_two_le_of_closure` (the abstract
  group lemma), `units_sq_index_le`.
- `ErdosUnitDistance/GeometricCore.lean`: the measure-free packing/doubling candidates
  for Layer 0 (after the `ZLattice` reconciliation below).

## Standing hypotheses

Work over a number field `F` (`[NumberField F]`), degree `n = [F : ℚ]`. State each bound
in the generality the proof needs (a discriminant bound needs only an integral basis, the
class number bound needs Minkowski's theorem and an ideal count, the unit-square index
needs Dirichlet's unit theorem), rather than bundling a single "number field with all its
invariants" hypothesis.

## What Mathlib already has (consume)

- **The Minkowski engine:** `Mathlib/Algebra/Module/ZLattice/Basic.lean` and
  `…/Covolume.lean` (lattices, covolume), `Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Group/GeometryOfNumbers.lean`
  (Minkowski's convex-body theorem).
- **The canonical embedding and discriminant:**
  `Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/CanonicalEmbedding/*` (the Minkowski space, the
  convex-body bound), `Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/Discriminant/*` (the Minkowski
  bound on `|d_F|`, `|d_F| > 1` for `F ≠ ℚ`).
- **Ideal counting (reconcile notation, but expect to build the bound):**
  `Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/Ideal/Asymptotics.lean` gives the *asymptotic* count
  of ideals by norm, eventual and non-explicit, so the uniform explicit count Layer 1
  needs does **not** follow from it. Reconcile names and API with it; the count itself is
  a fresh elementary lemma (see Layer 1).
- **Class group and unit theorem:** `Mathlib/RingTheory/ClassGroup.lean`,
  `Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/ClassNumber.lean` (in particular
  `NumberField.exists_ideal_in_class_of_norm_le`, the Minkowski-bound input to the class
  number bound), `Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/Units/DirichletTheorem.lean` (the unit
  rank, `fundSystem`).
- **The qualitative summit (consume, do not re-prove):**
  `Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/Discriminant/Basic.lean` has Minkowski's lower bound
  `NumberField.abs_discr_ge` (`(4/9)·(3π/4)ⁿ ≤ |d_F|`), the degree bound
  `rank_le_rankOfDiscrBdd`, and **Hermite's theorem** `NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd`
  (the number fields inside a fixed extension `A/ℚ` with `|d| ≤ N` form a finite set).
  And `Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/Units/Regulator.lean` already *defines* the
  regulator as the covolume of the unit lattice.

## What is missing (build here)

The explicit, effective forms: `|d_F| ≤ |disc b|` from any `ℚ`-basis `b` of algebraic
integers (an actual integral basis, a `ℤ`-basis of `O_F`, gives equality; the upper
bound is the useful general form); the explicit ideal count
`#{I ≠ ⊥ : N(I) ≤ X} ≤ X²·2ⁿ`; `h_F ≤ |d_F|·4ⁿ`; `[O_F^× : (O_F^×)²] ≤ 2ⁿ`; a clean
measure-free lattice-point packing/doubling API (reconciled with `ZLattice`); and an
explicit bound on the number of number fields of discriminant `≤ B` (Mathlib has the
finiteness, not a count). None of these explicit bounds is upstream.

---

## The build, in layers

As each layer makes the next layer's *types* expressible in `TauCeti/`, state its
milestones in `Suggested.lean` (with `sorry`).

### Layer 0: the geometry-of-numbers engine
- Measure-free lattice-point **packing** and **doubling** bounds in boxes/polydiscs (a
  separated set in a box is small; `#(Λ ∩ 2·B) ≤ C·#(Λ ∩ B)`). The erdos
  `GeometricCore` lemmas are the migration candidate.
  ⚠ **Reconcile with `ZLattice` first.** Before porting, map every proposed definition to
  the existing `ZLattice`/covolume API and **drop any `box`/separation definition that is
  just a Mathlib wrapper**; migrate only genuinely measure-free cardinal/doubling lemmas
  not already expressible cleanly upstream.

### Layer 1: effective upper bounds (the first migration targets)
- **Discriminant from a basis of integers.** `|d_F| ≤ |disc b|` for any `ℚ`-basis `b` of
  algebraic integers (the index of `b` in a maximal order is a nonzero integer, and
  `disc b = index² · d_F`). (erdos `abs_discr_le_of_basis_isIntegral`.) The helper
  `trace_eq_zero_of_sq_ratCast` (an element with `x² ∈ ℚ`, `x ∉ ℚ` has trace zero) is not
  needed for the bound itself, but it diagonalises the trace form on square-root bases:
  it is how the `ℚ(i)` worked example below evaluates `|disc b|`.
- **Explicit ideal count.** `#{I : Ideal O_F | I ≠ ⊥, N(I) ≤ X} ≤ X²·2ⁿ` for `X ≥ 1`
  (erdos `card_ideal_absNorm_le`, a Rankin-style argument:
  `∑_{N𝔞 ≤ X} 1 ≤ X² ∑ N𝔞⁻² ≤ X²·ζ(2)ⁿ ≤ X²·2ⁿ`). ⚠ This is the genuinely new counting
  lemma; it does **not** follow from the asymptotic count in `Ideal/Asymptotics`.
- **Class number bound.** `h_F ≤ |d_F|·4ⁿ`, from two inputs: Mathlib's
  `NumberField.exists_ideal_in_class_of_norm_le` (every class contains an integral ideal
  of norm `≤ (4/π)^{r₂} · (n!/nⁿ) · √|d_F|`, the Minkowski constant; the prefactor is
  `≤ 1`, but the migrated proof simply carries it) and the explicit ideal count above
  with `X` that Minkowski norm bound. (erdos `classNumber_le_bound`.)
- **Unit-square index.** `[O_F^× : (O_F^×)²] ≤ 2ⁿ`, from Dirichlet's unit theorem and a
  squaring-map index computation. (erdos `units_sq_index_le`; the abstract group lemma
  `index_powMonoidHom_two_le_of_closure` migrates independently.)

### Layer 2: effective Hermite–Minkowski (the summit)
- ⚠ **Mathlib already has the qualitative theorems; consume them, do not re-prove.**
  Minkowski's lower bound on `|d_F|` growing with `n` is `NumberField.abs_discr_ge`, the
  bounded-degree consequence is `rank_le_rankOfDiscrBdd`, and Hermite's finiteness
  theorem is `NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd` (number fields inside a fixed `A/ℚ` with
  `|d| ≤ N` form a finite set), all in `Discriminant/Basic.lean`.
- What this layer builds is the **effective count**: an explicit upper bound on the
  number of number fields (in a fixed `A/ℚ`) of discriminant `≤ B`. Mathlib's finiteness
  proof already runs through a generator of bounded height; the work is extracting and
  counting: bound the defining polynomial's coefficients explicitly, count the
  polynomials.

### Layer 3: regulators and unit-lattice volume
- Mathlib already *defines* the regulator as the covolume of the unit lattice
  (`NumberField.Units.regulator = ZLattice.covolume (unitLattice F)`, in
  `Units/Regulator.lean`). What is missing is the effective side: explicit lower bounds
  on the regulator, and the volume computations feeding the analytic class number
  formula.

### Long horizon (aspiration)
**Brauer–Siegel**: `log(h_F · R_F) ∼ log √|d_F|`; effective bounds with explicit
constants.

## Worked examples (acceptance criteria, keeping the bounds honest)

- The class number bound is non-vacuous on a small field: for `ℚ(√−5)` (`d = −20`,
  `n = 2`, `h = 2`), `2 ≤ 20·16`.
- A concrete lattice-doubling instance for a rank-2 lattice in `ℝ²`, exercising the
  Layer-0 engine.
- The discriminant bound recovers `|d_{ℚ(i)}| = 4` from the basis `{1, i}`.

## Ordering

Layer 1 first: the explicit upper bounds are direct migrations and validate the pipeline
(within it: the discriminant bound is the most self-contained, then the abstract group
lemma and the unit-square index, then the ideal count and the class number bound that
consumes it). Layer 0 (the engine) is best done after its `ZLattice` reconciliation
spike, since that determines what is even worth porting. Layer 2 (the effective count) is
the summit; it consumes Mathlib's `abs_discr_ge` and `finite_of_discr_bdd` rather than
re-proving them.

## References

- J. Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*, Ch. I §5–6, III §2 (Minkowski theory, the
  discriminant and class number bounds, Hermite–Minkowski).
- H. Cohen, *A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory* (effective bounds).
- W. Narkiewicz, *Elementary and Analytic Theory of Algebraic Numbers* (Brauer–Siegel).

## Acknowledgements

The Layer-1 bound lemmas are migrated from
[kim-em/erdos-unit-distance](https://github.com/kim-em/erdos-unit-distance), where they
were written for the formalization of Alpöge's disproof of the uniform-constant Erdős
unit-distance conjecture. Thanks to its authors.
TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticIntegrals:
# Elliptic integrals, the AGM, and Jacobi elliptic functions

This roadmap builds the classical real theory of elliptic integrals as a library:
- Legendre's incomplete and complete integrals of the first, second and third kinds.
- Their dependence on the modulus.
- Their evaluation by the arithmetic–geometric mean (AGM) and by Landen's transformation.
- Legendre's relation and the classical special values.
- Carlson's symmetric integrals.
- The Jacobi elliptic functions of a real variable, obtained by inverting the integral of the
  first kind.

Its applications are part of the roadmap:
- The arc length of an ellipse.
- The exact motion and period of the nonlinear pendulum.
- The Gauss–Brent–Salamin formula for `π`.
- An exact AGM formula for the real period `WeierstrassCurve.realPeriod` of an elliptic curve
  over `ℝ`. That formula is how the period in the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer quotient is actually
  computed.

Suggested homes are `TauCeti/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/EllipticIntegral/` (Milestones 1–6 and 8)
and `TauCeti/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/JacobiElliptic/` (Milestone 7). Both sit beside Mathlib's
`Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/ArithmeticGeometricMean.lean` and
`Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Elliptic/Weierstrass.lean`.

## Scope and completion criterion

The roadmap is complete when Tau Ceti proves all of the following.

1. **Legendre integrals.** `F(φ, k)`, `E(φ, k)`, `Π(φ, k, α²)` and their complete values `K(k)`,
   `E(k)`, `Π(k, α²)` are defined for real arguments. Each has full basic API: integrability,
   parity, quasi-periodicity in `φ`, the algebraic substitution, monotonicity, the degenerate
   moduli `k = 0` and `k = 1`, and the elementary reductions of the third kind.
2. **The complete integrals as functions of `k`.** This covers continuity, the derivative
   formulas, Legendre's differential equations, the hypergeometric series, the logarithmic
   singularity at `k = 1`, and **Legendre's relation** `E K′ + E′ K − K K′ = π/2`.
3. **The AGM.** This covers quadratic convergence, Gauss's theorem `K(k) = π / (2 M(1, k′))`,
   Landen's transformation of `K` and `E`, the AGM evaluation of `E`, and the
   Gauss–Brent–Salamin formula for `π`.
4. **Special values.** These are `K(1/√2) = Γ(1/4)² / (4√π)`, the companion value of `E(1/√2)`,
   and the lemniscate constant `ϖ` with its three classical evaluations.
5. **Carlson's symmetric integrals** `R_F, R_D, R_J, R_C, R_G` on the complex slit plane, with
   their symmetry, homogeneity, holomorphy, duplication theorem, elementary `R_C`, and the
   dictionary with the Legendre integrals.
6. **Jacobi elliptic functions of a real variable.** These are the amplitude `am` as an order
   isomorphism of `ℝ`, and `sn`, `cn`, `dn` with derivatives, periods, the addition theorem and
   the degenerations at `k = 0` and `k → 1`. They are applied to the nonlinear pendulum: an
   explicit solution, uniqueness, and the period `4K(sin(θ₀/2))/ω`.
7. **Geometry and the Weierstrass bridge.** The perimeter of an ellipse is `4aE(e)`. A real
   cubic integral evaluates in terms of `K`. Hence `WeierstrassCurve.realPeriod` is given by
   explicit `K` and AGM formulas, in both the one-component and the two-component cases.

**What this roadmap owns:** real-variable statements about the Legendre integrals, the AGM, and
the Jacobi functions of a real argument, plus Carlson's integrals on slit-plane nodes.

**What it does not own:**
- Anything about a lattice in `ℂ`.
- Analytic continuation in the modulus.
- The complex Jacobi functions as elliptic functions.
- Theta functions and the modular `λ`.
- Cauchy principal values.

## Ownership and dependencies

- **[EllipticCurves](../EllipticCurves/README.md)** owns `WeierstrassCurve.realPeriod` (its
  definition by an explicit integral, finiteness, positivity, and behaviour under change of
  variables) and the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer quotient that uses it. Milestone 8 here proves the
  evaluation of that integral by `K` and by the AGM. It consumes the definition and changes
  nothing in it.
- **Lattice functions.** These are ℘ beyond Mathlib, the Weierstrass `ζ` and `σ` functions,
  quasi-periods, the lattice form of Legendre's relation (`η₁ω₂ − η₂ω₁ = 2πi`), and the
  uniformisation `ℂ/Λ ≅ E(ℂ)`. They belong to the lattice roadmaps:
  [GrothendieckPeriodConjecture](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/1059)
  and [ModularCurves part II](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/913).
  Nothing here uses them. Legendre's relation here is the identity between the real functions
  `K` and `E`, proved by differentiation (Milestone 3). Identifying it with the lattice relation
  is a statement about lattices and belongs there.
- **[ConformalMapping](../ConformalMapping/README.md)** owns Schwarz–Christoffel maps. The map
  of the upper half-plane onto a rectangle is an incomplete integral of the first kind, and it
  may consume Milestone 1. This roadmap constructs no conformal maps.
- **[DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence](../DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence/README.md)**
  owns transcendence statements. Values such as `K(1/√2)` and `ϖ` are computed here, and their
  transcendence is not.

**The boundary in one sentence:**
- A real-variable statement about the Legendre or Carlson integrals, the AGM, or a Jacobi
  function of a real argument is here.
- A statement about a lattice in `ℂ` or a meromorphic function on `ℂ/Λ` is in the lattice
  roadmaps.
- A statement about a Weierstrass equation over a field is in EllipticCurves.

That integral representation is
[mathlib4#34397](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/34397). It defines

```lean
noncomputable def agmIntegral (a b : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x in Set.Ioi 0, (√((x ^ 2 + a ^ 2) * (x ^ 2 + b ^ 2)))⁻¹
```

and proves `agmIntegral_eq_pi_div_two_div_agm : agmIntegral a b = π / 2 / agm a b` for
`a b : ℝ≥0`. Milestone 4 builds exactly this definition and theorem, under these names in the
`TauCeti` namespace, so that adopting Mathlib's version is a deletion plus an import.

## Prior formalization

B. Braams' [`lean-codes`](https://github.com/bjbraams/lean-codes) (Apache-2.0) formalizes
B. C. Carlson's *Special Functions of Applied Mathematics* on top of Mathlib and Tau Ceti. Its
`Carlson/Elliptic/` directory covers much of the mathematics of this roadmap: the Legendre
integrals, `R_F` and the other symmetric integrals, Landen's transformation, the duplication
theorem, Euler's addition theorem, the AGM evaluation of the complete integral of the second
kind, the pendulum and ellipse integrals, and a complex Jacobi `sn` built as a
Schwarz–Christoffel map. Its foundation is Carlson's general `R`-function, a Dirichlet average
over the standard simplex. That machinery is much larger than this roadmap needs, and it is not
part of this roadmap.

This roadmap specifies the mathematics intrinsically. It adopts that formalization's
conventions (modulus `k`; `legendreF`, `legendreE`, `legendrePi`, `legendreK`, `legendreEc`
with argument order `(φ, k)` and `(φ, k, α²)`), so the two developments stay interoperable.

The author has endorsed this roadmap on Zulip (`#Tau Ceti > Getting started: roadmaps`).
Implementers should treat `lean-codes` as the first source to port from, with attribution, before
proving anything from scratch. Its proofs rest on Carlson's general `R`-function, so a port
re-bases them on this roadmap's direct integral definitions (Milestone 6) rather than copying
that layer. The table records where each milestone already has a counterpart there (files under
`Carlson/Elliptic/`, checked at commit `2b8cba1`) and what is new.

| Milestone | Counterpart in `lean-codes` | Not covered there |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Legendre integrals | `LegendreStandard`, `LegendreThird`, `ZeroVariable` | |
| 2. Complete integrals | `CompleteK` (imaginary modulus, Landen for `K`) | derivatives in `k`, Legendre's differential equations, `₂F₁` series |
| 3. Singularity, Legendre's relation | `Asymptotic` (logarithmic asymptotics in Carlson form) | Legendre's relation |
| 4. AGM | `AGMSecondKind`, `LandenAlgorithm`, `Landen` | Gauss's `K` formula in this form (see mathlib4#34397), Brent–Salamin |
| 5. Special values | lemniscate arc-length exercises in `ArcLengthExercises` | `K(1/√2)`, `E(1/√2)`, the lemniscate constant |
| 6. Carlson integrals | `RF`, `Standard`, `Addition`, `ReductionTables` | |
| 7. Real Jacobi functions | `Inversion`; a complex `sn` via `SchwarzChristoffel` | real `am/sn/cn/dn` and the explicit pendulum solution |
| 8. Geometry, Weierstrass | `Applications` (pendulum, ellipse) | the AGM formula for `WeierstrassCurve.realPeriod` |

## Conventions (pinned)

- **Modulus, not parameter.** Every integral takes the **modulus** `k : ℝ`, as in DLMF Chapter 19
  and Carlson. The parameter `m = k²` never appears as an argument. The complementary modulus
  is `k′ = √(1 − k²)`, written out, and `K′(k)` means `legendreK √(1 − k²)`; neither gets its own
  definition.
- **Legendre integrals** (DLMF 19.2.4, 19.2.5, 19.2.7), in the namespace `TauCeti.Real`:

  ```text
  legendreF  φ k    = ∫₀^φ (1 − k² sin²θ)^(−1/2) dθ
  legendreE  φ k    = ∫₀^φ (1 − k² sin²θ)^(1/2) dθ
  legendrePi φ k α² = ∫₀^φ (1 − α² sin²θ)⁻¹ (1 − k² sin²θ)^(−1/2) dθ
  legendreK  k      = legendreF (π/2) k
  legendreEc k      = legendreE (π/2) k
  legendrePic k α²  = legendrePi (π/2) k α²
  ```

  The integrals are `intervalIntegral`s, and the powers are `Real.rpow` with exponents
  `-1/2 : ℝ` and `1/2 : ℝ`. These are total functions of real arguments. Their values are
  meaningful under the hypotheses `k ^ 2 < 1` and `α2 < 1`, which every theorem states
  explicitly. The one exception is the `k = 1` statements of Milestone 1, which carry
  `|φ| < π/2` instead. Positivity and integrability theorems come first, so that a junk value
  is never mistaken for a result.
- **Third kind.** `α2` is a real number, written `α²` in prose and allowed to be negative. Only
  `α2 < 1` is in scope: for `α2 > 1` the integral is a Cauchy principal value, which this roadmap
  does not treat.
- **Carlson integrals** (DLMF 19.16.1, 19.16.2, 19.16.3, 19.16.5, 19.2.17), in the namespace
  `TauCeti.Complex`, with principal powers `(t + x) ^ (-(1/2) : ℂ)` of each factor:

  ```text
  carlsonRF x y z   = ½ ∫₀^∞ (t+x)^(−½) (t+y)^(−½) (t+z)^(−½) dt
  carlsonRJ x y z p = (3/2) ∫₀^∞ (t+x)^(−½) (t+y)^(−½) (t+z)^(−½) (t+p)⁻¹ dt
  carlsonRD x y z   = carlsonRJ x y z z
  carlsonRC x y     = carlsonRF x y y
  carlsonRG x y z   = ¼ ∫₀^∞ (t+x)^(−½) (t+y)^(−½) (t+z)^(−½)
                          · (x/(t+x) + y/(t+y) + z/(t+z)) · t dt
  ```

  The domain is: `x, y, z ∈ slitPlane ∪ {0}` with at most one of them `0`, and
  `p ∈ slitPlane`. For `carlsonRD` the repeated argument `z` lies in `slitPlane`. These
  definitions are the specification. An implementation may define the functions differently,
  for instance through Carlson's `R`-function, provided it proves these integral formulas on
  this domain.
- **AGM.** Mathlib's `NNReal.agm` is the AGM. Statements about real numbers coerce through
  `Real.toNNReal` or `NNReal` literals rather than introducing a real-valued copy.
- **Jacobi functions.** In the namespace `TauCeti.Real`, `jacobiAm k`, `jacobiSn k`, `jacobiCn k`
  and `jacobiDn k` are functions `ℝ → ℝ`, with the modulus first, so that
  `Function.Periodic (jacobiSn k) (4 * legendreK k)` reads directly. They are defined for
  `k ^ 2 < 1`:
  - `jacobiAm k` is the inverse of `fun φ ↦ legendreF φ k`;
  - `jacobiSn k = sin ∘ jacobiAm k` and `jacobiCn k = cos ∘ jacobiAm k`;
  - `jacobiDn k u = √(1 − k² (jacobiSn k u)²)`.

  Complex-variable versions belong to the `TauCeti.Complex` namespace and to a later roadmap
  (see the last section).
- **Lemniscate constant.** `TauCeti.Real.lemniscateConstant = 2 ∫₀¹ (1 − t⁴)^(−1/2) dt`
  (`ϖ ≈ 2.62206`).
- **Real cubic.** In Milestone 8 the roots of `Ψ₂Sq` are given as explicit real or complex
  numbers together with a factorization hypothesis `∀ x, W.Ψ₂Sq.eval x = …`. No root-selection
  function is introduced.

## Milestone 1: the Legendre integrals

1. **Integrands.**
   - For `k ^ 2 < 1` and `α2 < 1`, the three integrands are continuous and positive on `ℝ`, and
     bounded above and below by explicit constants. All three integrals are interval-integrable
     on every bounded interval.
   - `legendreF φ k` and `legendreE φ k` are positive for `φ > 0`. `legendreK k` and
     `legendreEc k` are positive.
2. **Algebraic form** (DLMF 19.2.4, second forms). For `|φ| ≤ π/2`:
   - `legendreF φ k = ∫₀^{sin φ} ((1 − t²)(1 − k²t²))^(−1/2) dt`;
   - the analogous formulas hold for `legendreE` and `legendrePi`.

   At `φ = π/2` the integral is improper at `t = 1`, and integrability there is part of the
   statement.
3. **Symmetries and periodicity.**
   - `F`, `E` and `Π` are odd in `φ` and even in `k`.
   - `legendreF (φ + π) k = legendreF φ k + 2 * legendreK k`, and likewise for `E` with
     `legendreEc` and for `Π` with `legendrePic`. Hence also `legendreF (n * π) k = 2 * n * legendreK k`.
4. **Derivatives and monotonicity in `φ`.**
   - `HasDerivAt (legendreF · k) ((1 − k² sin²φ)^(−1/2)) φ`, and likewise for `E` and `Π`.
   - `legendreF · k` and `legendreE · k` are strictly increasing.
   - `legendreF · k` is an order isomorphism `ℝ ≃o ℝ` (unbounded by step 3). This is the input
     to Milestone 7.
5. **Degenerate moduli.**
   - `legendreF φ 0 = φ` and `legendreE φ 0 = φ`.
   - `legendreK 0 = legendreEc 0 = π/2`.
   - For `|φ| < π/2`: `legendreF φ 1 = artanh (sin φ)` and `legendreE φ 1 = sin φ`.
   - `legendreEc 1 = 1`.
   - `legendreK` tends to `+∞` as `k → 1⁻`. The statement is a `Tendsto` to `atTop`, not a
     value at `1`.
6. **Elementary third-kind reductions** (DLMF 19.6.11, 19.6.13):
   - `legendrePi φ k 0 = legendreF φ k`.
   - For `α2 < 1` and `|φ| < π/2`,
     `legendrePi φ 0 α2 = arctan (√(1 − α2) tan φ) / √(1 − α2)`.
   - For `k ^ 2 < 1`,
     `legendrePi φ k (k²) = (legendreE φ k − k² sin φ cos φ / √(1 − k² sin² φ)) / (1 − k²)`.
7. **Monotonicity in `k`.**
   - On `[0, 1)`, `legendreK` is strictly increasing and `legendreEc` strictly decreasing.
   - `legendreEc k ≤ π/2 ≤ legendreK k`, with equality only at `k = 0`.
   - `legendreF φ k` is increasing in `k ∈ [0, 1)` for `φ ≥ 0`.
8. **Imaginary modulus** (DLMF 19.7.5, complete case). For real `c`,
   `∫₀^{π/2} (1 + c² sin²θ)^(−1/2) dθ = legendreK (c / √(1 + c²)) / √(1 + c²)`.

## Milestone 2: the complete integrals as functions of the modulus

1. `legendreK`, `legendreEc` and `legendrePic · α2` are continuous on `{k | k ^ 2 < 1}`.
   `legendreEc` is also continuous at `±1`.
2. **Derivatives** (DLMF 19.4.1). For `0 < k < 1`:
   - `HasDerivAt legendreK ((legendreEc k − (1 − k²) legendreK k) / (k (1 − k²))) k`;
   - `HasDerivAt legendreEc ((legendreEc k − legendreK k) / k) k`.

   At `k = 0` both derivatives are `0`. The proof route is differentiation under the integral
   sign, followed by one integration by parts.
3. **Legendre's differential equations.** For `0 < k < 1`:
   - `k(1 − k²) K″ + (1 − 3k²) K′ − k K = 0`;
   - `k(1 − k²) E″ + (1 − k²) E′ + k E = 0`.

   They are stated with `deriv` and `deriv^[2]`, together with the twice-differentiability
   of `K` and `E`.
4. **Hypergeometric series** (DLMF 19.5.1, 19.5.2). For `k ^ 2 < 1`:
   - `legendreK k = π/2 * ₂F₁ (1/2) (1/2) 1 (k ^ 2)`;
   - `legendreEc k = π/2 * ₂F₁ (-1/2) (1/2) 1 (k ^ 2)`.

   Both use Mathlib's `ordinaryHypergeometric` over `ℝ`. The proof expands the integrand
   binomially and integrates term by term with the Wallis integrals.
5. **Analyticity.** `legendreK` and `legendreEc` are `AnalyticOnNhd ℝ` on `Set.Ioo (-1) 1`, a
   consequence of step 4.

## Milestone 3: the logarithmic singularity and Legendre's relation

1. **Behaviour at `k = 1`** (DLMF 19.12.1). As `k → 1⁻`:
   - `legendreK k − log (4 / √(1 − k²)) → 0`;
   - `legendreEc k → 1`;
   - `(1 − k²) * legendreK k → 0`.
2. **Legendre's relation** (DLMF 19.7.1). For `0 < k < 1`, with `k′ = √(1 − k²)`:

   `legendreEc k * legendreK k′ + legendreEc k′ * legendreK k − legendreK k * legendreK k′ = π/2`.

   Proof route: by Milestone 2 the left side has derivative `0` on `(0, 1)`. Evaluate its limit
   as `k → 0⁺` using step 1 applied at `k′ → 1⁻` and the series of Milestone 2.

## Milestone 4: the arithmetic–geometric mean

1. **Quadratic convergence.** For `0 < y ≤ x`, one AGM step shrinks the gap quadratically:
   `(x + y)/2 − √(xy) ≤ (x − y)² / (8y)`. Since the geometric means increase, it follows that
   `(agmSequences x y n).2 − (agmSequences x y n).1 ≤ 8y · ((x − y) / (8y)) ^ 2 ^ (n + 1)` for
   all `n`. Mathlib's `agmSequences x y 0` is already one step in. This complements Mathlib's
   halving bound.
2. **The AGM integral.** Build `TauCeti.agmIntegral` and
   `TauCeti.agmIntegral_eq_pi_div_two_div_agm` exactly as specified in the inventory, together
   with the integrability, symmetry and invariance `agmIntegral a b = agmIntegral √(ab) ((a+b)/2)`
   on which the proof rests.
3. **Trigonometric form.** For `a, b > 0`,
   `∫₀^{π/2} (a² cos²θ + b² sin²θ)^(−1/2) dθ = agmIntegral a b`.
4. **Gauss's theorem.** For `k ^ 2 < 1`, `legendreK k = π / (2 * agm 1 √(1 − k²))`.
5. **Landen's transformation** (DLMF 19.8.12, descending form). For `0 ≤ k < 1`, with
   `k′ = √(1 − k²)` and `k₁ = (1 − k′)/(1 + k′)`:
   - `legendreK k = (1 + k₁) * legendreK k₁`;
   - `legendreEc k = (1 + k′) * legendreEc k₁ − k′ * legendreK k`.

   Also prove the ascending forms obtained by solving for `k₁`.
6. **The AGM evaluation of `E`** (DLMF 19.8.6). Run the AGM from `a₀ = 1`, `g₀ = k′`, with
   `c₀ = k` and `cₙ₊₁ = (aₙ − gₙ)/2`. Then `∑ 2^(n−1) cₙ²` is summable and
   `legendreEc k = legendreK k * (1 − ∑' n, 2^(n−1) cₙ²)`.
7. **The Gauss–Brent–Salamin formula.** Run the AGM from `a₀ = 1`, `g₀ = 1/√2`, with
   `cₙ² = aₙ² − gₙ²`. Then `π = 4 agm(1, 1/√2)² / (1 − ∑'_{n ≥ 1} 2^(n+1) cₙ²)`. The proof
   combines step 6 at `k = 1/√2` with Legendre's relation.

## Milestone 5: special values

1. `legendreK (1/√2) = Γ(1/4)² / (4 √π)`. The route is the algebraic form, the substitution
   `t ↦ t⁴`, a Beta integral, and the reflection formula.
2. `legendreEc (1/√2) = legendreK (1/√2) / 2 + π / (4 legendreK (1/√2))`, from Legendre's
   relation with `k = k′`.
3. **The lemniscate constant** `ϖ = lemniscateConstant`:
   - `ϖ = √2 · legendreK (1/√2)`;
   - `ϖ = Γ(1/4)² / (2 √(2π))`;
   - **Gauss's identity** `ϖ = π / agm 1 √2`, which combines step 1 with Milestone 4.

## Milestone 6: Carlson's symmetric integrals

1. **Convergence and holomorphy.** On the domain fixed in the conventions:
   - each defining integral converges absolutely;
   - each function is holomorphic in each variable separately on `slitPlane`, the others being
     fixed;
   - each takes positive real values at positive real arguments.
2. **Symmetry and homogeneity.**
   - `carlsonRF` and `carlsonRG` are symmetric in `x, y, z`. `carlsonRJ` is symmetric in its
     first three arguments.
   - For real `λ > 0`: `carlsonRF (λx) (λy) (λz) = λ^(−1/2) carlsonRF x y z`, and
     correspondingly with exponent `−3/2` for `carlsonRJ` and `carlsonRD`, and `1/2` for
     `carlsonRG`.
3. **Diagonal values.**
   - `carlsonRF x x x = x^(−1/2)`, `carlsonRC x x = x^(−1/2)`, and
     `carlsonRJ x x x x = carlsonRD x x x = x^(−3/2)`, for `x ∈ slitPlane`.
4. **Elementary `R_C`** (DLMF 19.2.19, 19.2.20). For real `0 ≤ x < y`:
   - `carlsonRC x y = arccos (√(x/y)) / √(y − x)`.

   For real `0 < y < x`:
   - `carlsonRC x y = arcosh (√(x/y)) / √(x − y)`.
5. **Duplication theorem** (DLMF 19.26.18). For `x, y, z` in the domain, with
   `λ = √x√y + √y√z + √z√x` (principal roots):
   - `carlsonRF x y z = carlsonRF ((x+λ)/4) ((y+λ)/4) ((z+λ)/4)`.

   State it first for nonnegative reals, then on the whole domain.
6. **The Legendre dictionary** (DLMF 19.25.5, 19.25.7, 19.25.14). For `k ^ 2 < 1`, `α2 < 1` and
   `|φ| ≤ π/2`, write `c = cos²φ`, `Δ = 1 − k² sin²φ` and `s = sin φ`. Then:
   - `legendreF φ k = s · R_F(c, Δ, 1)`;
   - `legendreE φ k = s · R_F(c, Δ, 1) − (k²/3) s³ · R_D(c, Δ, 1)`;
   - `legendrePi φ k α2 = s · R_F(c, Δ, 1) + (α2/3) s³ · R_J(c, Δ, 1, 1 − α2 s²)`;
   - in particular `legendreK k = R_F(0, 1 − k², 1)` and `legendreEc k = 2 R_G(0, 1 − k², 1)`.

   Each Carlson value is taken at real arguments coerced to `ℂ`, and the identity holds for its
   real part, the imaginary part being `0`.

## Milestone 7: Jacobi elliptic functions of a real variable

Fix `k ^ 2 < 1` and write `K = legendreK k`.

1. **Amplitude.** `jacobiAm k : ℝ ≃o ℝ` is the inverse of the order isomorphism of
   Milestone 1.4. It satisfies:
   - it is odd, with `jacobiAm k (u + 2K) = jacobiAm k u + π` and `jacobiAm k K = π/2`;
   - `HasDerivAt (jacobiAm k) (jacobiDn k u) u`;
   - `jacobiAm 0 = id`.
2. **Identities.**
   - `sn² + cn² = 1` and `dn² + k² sn² = 1`.
   - `dn` is positive.
   - `sn` is odd; `cn` and `dn` are even.
3. **Derivatives.** `sn′ = cn · dn`, `cn′ = −sn · dn` and `dn′ = −k² sn · cn`, as `HasDerivAt`
   statements. The first-order equation `(sn′)² = (1 − sn²)(1 − k² sn²)` follows.
4. **Periods and values.**
   - `sn` and `cn` are `4K`-periodic, and `dn` is `2K`-periodic.
   - `sn (u + 2K) = −sn u`, `sn K = 1`, `cn K = 0`, `dn K = √(1 − k²)`.
   - `4K` is the least positive period of `sn`. At `k = 0` this is `2π`.
5. **Addition theorem** (DLMF 22.8.1):
   - `sn (u + v) = (sn u · cn v · dn v + sn v · cn u · dn u) / (1 − k² sn²u · sn²v)`.

   The companion formulas for `cn` and `dn` are part of this item. The denominator is positive.
6. **Degenerations.**
   - `jacobiSn 0 = sin`, `jacobiCn 0 = cos`, `jacobiDn 0 = 1`.
   - As `k → 1⁻`, pointwise in `u`: `jacobiSn k u → tanh u`, `jacobiCn k u → 1/cosh u` and
     `jacobiDn k u → 1/cosh u`.
7. **The nonlinear pendulum.** Let `ω > 0` and `0 < θ₀ < π`, and set `k = sin (θ₀/2)` and
   `θ(t) = 2 arcsin (k · jacobiSn k (ω t + legendreK k))`. Then:
   - `θ` is `C²`, `θ″ = −ω² sin θ`, `θ 0 = θ₀` and `θ′ 0 = 0`;
   - every `C¹` solution of the first-order system for `(θ, θ′)` with these initial values
     equals `θ` (Mathlib's `ODE_solution_unique_univ`);
   - `θ` is periodic with least positive period `4 legendreK (sin (θ₀/2)) / ω`;
   - that period tends to `2π/ω` as `θ₀ → 0⁺` and to `+∞` as `θ₀ → π⁻`.

## Milestone 8: geometry and the Weierstrass bridge

1. **Perimeter of an ellipse.** For `0 < b ≤ a`, with `γ t = a cos t + (b sin t) · I` in `ℂ`
   and `e = √(1 − b²/a²)`:

   `eVariationOn γ (Set.Icc 0 (2π)) = ENNReal.ofReal (4 a · legendreEc e)`.

   The route is `TauCeti.eVariationOn_eq_lintegral_enorm_derivWithin` and a change of variables.
   The case `b > a` follows by symmetry.
2. **Cubic integrals, three real roots.** For real `e₃ < e₂ < e₁`, with
   `k = √((e₂ − e₃)/(e₁ − e₃))`, `D(x) = 4(x − e₁)(x − e₂)(x − e₃)` and `κ = legendreK k`:
   - `∫_{(e₁, ∞)} D(x)^(−1/2) dx = κ / √(e₁ − e₃)`;
   - `∫_{(e₃, e₂)} D(x)^(−1/2) dx = κ / √(e₁ − e₃)`.

   Both are stated as `lintegral`s of `ENNReal.ofReal`, equal to `ENNReal.ofReal` of the right
   side.
3. **Cubic integrals, one real root.** For real `e₁, a, b` with `b ≠ 0`, set
   `A = √((e₁ − a)² + b²)`, `k = √((A + a − e₁) / (2A))` and `D(x) = 4(x − e₁)((x − a)² + b²)`.
   Then `∫_{(e₁, ∞)} D(x)^(−1/2) dx = legendreK k / √A`.
4. **The real period** (`W : WeierstrassCurve ℝ`).
   - If `∀ x, W.Ψ₂Sq.eval x = 4 (x − e₁)(x − e₂)(x − e₃)` with `e₃ < e₂ < e₁`, then:
     - `W.realPeriod = 4 legendreK k / √(e₁ − e₃)`;
     - `W.realPeriod = 2π / agm √(e₁ − e₃) √(e₁ − e₂)`.
   - If `∀ x, W.Ψ₂Sq.eval x = 4 (x − e₁)((x − a)² + b²)` with `b ≠ 0`, then, with `A` and `k` as
     in step 3:
     - `W.realPeriod = 2 legendreK k / √A`;
     - `W.realPeriod = 2π / agm (2√A) √(2A + 2(e₁ − a))`.

   These pin the period of the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer quotient to an AGM that converges
   quadratically (Milestone 4.1). The suggested form:

   ```lean
   open TauCeti.Real in
   theorem WeierstrassCurve.realPeriod_eq_of_three_real_roots (W : WeierstrassCurve ℝ)
       {e₁ e₂ e₃ : ℝ} (h₃₂ : e₃ < e₂) (h₂₁ : e₂ < e₁)
       (hW : ∀ x, W.Ψ₂Sq.eval x = 4 * (x - e₁) * (x - e₂) * (x - e₃)) :
       W.realPeriod = 4 * legendreK √((e₂ - e₃) / (e₁ - e₃)) / √(e₁ - e₃) := sorry

   open TauCeti.Real in
   theorem WeierstrassCurve.realPeriod_eq_of_one_real_root (W : WeierstrassCurve ℝ)
       {e₁ a b : ℝ} (hb : b ≠ 0)
       (hW : ∀ x, W.Ψ₂Sq.eval x = 4 * (x - e₁) * ((x - a) ^ 2 + b ^ 2)) :
       W.realPeriod = 2 * legendreK √((√((e₁ - a) ^ 2 + b ^ 2) + a - e₁) /
         (2 * √((e₁ - a) ^ 2 + b ^ 2))) / √(√((e₁ - a) ^ 2 + b ^ 2)) := sorry
   ```

   They are given here rather than in `Suggested.lean` because the Tau Ceti dependency pinned
   by this repository predates `RealPeriod.lean`.

## Beyond this roadmap (a roadmap for a roadmap; do not implement)

The following material is the natural continuation. It is recorded only to fix the boundary.
Contributors should not attempt it under this roadmap.
- The Jacobi functions of a complex variable as elliptic functions with periods `4K` and `2iK′`.
- Their identification with ℘ for the rectangular lattice, `℘(z) = e₃ + (e₁ − e₃) / sn²(√(e₁ − e₃) z)`.
- The analytic continuation of `K` and `E` in `k²` to `ℂ ∖ [1, ∞)`.
- The nome `q = exp(−πK′/K)` and the theta-function expressions.
- The modular function `λ`.
- Principal-value third-kind integrals.
- Incomplete integrals of complex amplitude.

All of these need the lattice roadmaps listed under ownership.

A second, independent continuation is Carlson's general theory. It would build the
`R`-function `R_t(b; z)` as a Dirichlet average over the standard simplex, together with the
measure theory on the simplex and the multivariable holomorphy it needs. It would then identify
this roadmap's integral definitions as special cases, for example
`carlsonRF x y z = R_{−1/2}(1/2, 1/2, 1/2; x, y, z)`, and transport the reduction tables and
contiguous relations to them. `lean-codes` contains a full formalization of this theory (see
Prior formalization), so it would be a port. That makes it a natural roadmap of its own. Parts
of the simplex measure theory may go to Mathlib first; check there before starting.

# Roadmap: enhanced derived categories of sheaves

**Summary.** An ordinary derived category remembers cohomology, shifts and distinguished triangles, but not the homotopies between maps or the coherences among them. Descent along hypercovers, inverse limits of complexes, Kan extensions along diagrams of topoi, adjoints of colimit-preserving functors and the reconstruction of adic coefficient systems all need that higher structure. This roadmap gives unbounded derived categories of sheaves of modules a concrete enhancement, the dg nerve of a K-injective model inside Mathlib's quasicategories, proves that its homotopy category is Mathlib's `DerivedCategory`, and builds in it the operations later roadmaps use: derived tensor products and internal Hom on ringed sites with point-site and affine comparisons, pullback and pushforward, perfect pushforward with proper support and arbitrary base change for algebraic spaces, Koszul complexes, coherent inverse limits and Postnikov completion on replete topoi, hypercover descent, coherent Kan extensions and adjoints, accessible localizations, derived completion and the reconstruction of complete complexes from their reductions modulo powers of a regular ideal, together with the commutative algebra of regular rings and perfect `𝔽_p`-algebras that descent on perfect schemes needs (global dimension, Kunz's theorem, Tor independence). Using the generic categorical and monoidal foundations of BordismFormalGroups F6.5, it supplies the higher-algebra extensions: operadic algebras and extension of scalars, idempotent completion, Barr–Beck–Lurie, descendable algebras and module descent (with h-descent for perfect schemes as the main application), compact-object and ordinary Ind comparisons, presentable, dualizable and rigid categories, the ∞-category of spectra, animated commutative rings, Frobenius on animated `𝔽_p`-algebras, and the cotangent complex. Every comparison with an ordinary category is a theorem about mapping spaces, never a definition by passage to the homotopy category. The main sources are Lurie's *Higher Topos Theory* and *Higher Algebra*, Bhatt–Scholze's *The pro-étale topology for schemes* (§3) and *Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian* (§§3, 6 and 11), Liu–Zheng's *Enhanced six operations*, Nikolaus–Scholze's *On topological cyclic homology* (Appendix A and §I.3), Mathew's *The Galois group of a stable homotopy theory* (§3), and the Stacks Project.

## Conventions

**Higher categories.** "Quasicategory" and "∞-category" both mean a quasicategory in Mathlib's sense (`SSet.Quasicategory`); "space" means a Kan complex. Mapping spaces are right mapping spaces (Section E0.1). An equivalence of quasicategories is a categorical equivalence (Section E0.2), never just an equivalence of homotopy categories.

**Grading and signs.** Complexes are cochain complexes, with differentials raising degree. For an object A of the heart, `A[1]` is concentrated in cohomological degree `−1`. Lurie's dg nerve uses homological grading; the cohomological Hom complexes of Mathlib, Tau Ceti and `DGAInfinity` are reindexed by `m ↦ −m` and their composition order is converted with the Koszul braiding of `DGAInfinity` Layer 0. Good truncation puts cycles in degree zero, so `π_i` of a mapping space is `H^{−i}` of the derived Hom complex for `i ≥ 0`: negative cohomology appears as positive homotopy. Suspension, cofibres and the rotation of triangles agree with Mathlib's cochain shift and mapping cone; this is the theorem `dgNerve_shift_cone_comparison`, not a choice made to suit the enhancement.

**Universes and cardinals.** Each small site or diagram lives in a fixed universe u, its presheaves of spaces in `u + 1`, and large-universe Ind of a presentable category in a further enlargement; raising a cardinal cutoff comes with explicit comparison functors (`cutoffRightAdjoint_compat`). Local smallness means small Kan models of mapping homotopy types, not small simplex sets. Presentable means accessible for some regular cardinal with all small colimits; it never means `ω`-compactly generated. Compact means `ω`-compact unless a cardinal is named.

**Replacements.** Functorial K-injective and K-flat replacements, bounded by one regular cardinal, are what the enhancement uses; objectwise existence is weaker. K-injective complexes need not be closed under tensor products, so the derived tensor product uses K-flat replacements.

**Inverse limits and completeness.** A replete topos is one satisfying `IsReplete` of `TauCetiRoadmap.SchemeAndStackFoundations` §2.17 (BS-proet Definition 3.1.1). Repleteness concerns sequences only; it does not make all cofiltered limits exact. Pro-zero (every stage killed by a later transition) is stronger than vanishing limit: multiplication by p on `ℤ` has `lim = 0` and `lim¹ = ℤ_p/ℤ`. For coherent towers of complexes, a cohomological pro-isomorphism asks every cohomology tower of the cone to be pro-zero, with no uniform stage across degrees. Descendability uses the stronger `IsStableProZero` condition on the fibre tower: each stage receives a null-homotopic transition from a later stage in the stable category itself. Hypercompleteness (descent along all hypercovers) and Postnikov completeness (convergence and effectivity of Postnikov towers) are different. Derived completeness is tested on every slice and every local section of the ideal. Recovery of a unit by an infinite totalization is weaker than descendability, which asks for a finite index.

**Stable subcategories.** Stable, thick and localizing closures are kept apart: a stable subcategory need not be closed under retracts, and the kernel of a Verdier quotient is the retract closure of the subcategory.

**Animated rings.** Homotopy groups of animated rings are indexed homologically, so `π_n` sits in cohomological degree `−n`. Ordinary polynomial algebras are Mathlib's `MvPolynomial`, ordinary rings `CommRingCat`, Witt vectors `WittVector`, perfect rings `PerfectRing`. The perfection of an `𝔽_p`-algebra is the colimit along Frobenius, not Mathlib's inverse-limit `Perfection`.

These inputs and the ringed-site constructions of Sections 0.1–0.4 precede the corresponding enhanced comparisons in E1, E4 and E5:cotangent-export.
