### Layer 7: masses, local densities, and the archimedean factor

Every statement in this layer is about positive definite genera, and the Conway–Sloane mass
formula paper is the source for the normalization.

⚠ **The mass formula itself is not a milestone of this roadmap.** Assembling the local factors
into `m(f)` runs through the adelic volume of `SO(V)`, which needs a Tamagawa normalization and
the volume theorem; #246 exports neither, and #255 states explicitly that only
`OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass` may export the orthogonal volume theorem. Milestones **7B,
7D, 7F, 7H and 7I are therefore that successor's**, and are stated here only as the boundary it
must meet. What this roadmap owns is everything the successor consumes from the lattice side:
the two masses and their comparison (7A), the local density with its stabilization and its
odd-`p` values (7C), the archimedean factor (7E), and the low-rank values (7G), together with
the dyadic Jordan data and density exponents of 3I. Those are lattice arithmetic and use no
adelic volume and no group scheme.

⚠ 7D is the successor's for a different reason from 7B, 7F, 7H and 7I. Those need a Tamagawa
measure; 7D needs a smooth affine group scheme over `ℤ₂` — its smoothening, its special fibre,
the unipotent radical of that fibre and the point count of the reductive quotient. No roadmap
in the portfolio supplies any of the four, and §*Scope* records why building the most delicate
integral model of the orthogonal group inside a lattice roadmap, while declaring all
algebraic-group measure infrastructure out of scope, is not a coherent boundary.

⚠ Do not conflate the two orthogonal inputs the successor needs. Strong approximation is an
*indefinite* statement, the volume theorem is what a *positive definite* mass needs, and neither
implies the other.

**7A. Proper mass and full mass.** The two sums are defined, and both are finite by 2C and
2G. For `rank L ≥ 1` the relation between them is proved, and not assumed. A class either
stays one proper class, in which case `|O(M)| = 2|SO(M)|`, or splits into two proper classes,
in which case `O(M) = SO(M)`. In both cases `m⁺ = 2m`. In rank 0 the relation fails, and 7G
gives the values there.

There is no product formula for the mass of a direct sum, and that non-statement is
recorded. The mass of a twist `L(a)` is stated for `a > 0` only.

**7B. The adelic decomposition.** *Owner:* `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`. The inputs are
`TamagawaMeasures`' quotient and Tamagawa-measure substrate, that successor's own orthogonal
volume theorem, and the dictionary of 4B, which is ours. The quotient
`SO(V)(ℚ) \ SO(V)(𝔸)` is decomposed into measurable pieces, indexed by the proper classes.
The piece of the class of `M` has volume

    vol(K_∞) / |SO(M)| · ∏_p vol(K_p⁺(M)).

Every quotient and stabilizer in that formula is named.

**7C. The local density: definition, stabilization, and the values at odd primes.** The
definition and the stabilization theorem below are for every prime, `p = 2` included; the
closed evaluation is proved here at odd `p`, and at `p = 2` it is the successor's 7D. Let `L`
be a nondegenerate `ℤ_p`-lattice of rank `n`
with Gram matrix `A` in a basis. The local automorphism density is

    α_p(L) = lim_{r→∞} p^{−r·n(n−1)/2} · #{X ∈ Mₙ(ℤ/p^r) : Xᵀ A X ≡ A (mod p^r)}.

This milestone asks for:

- stabilization: the counting function equals `p^{r·n(n−1)/2}·α_p(L)` for every `r ≥ r₀`,
  with `r₀` given explicitly in terms of `n` and `v_p(2 det A)`, so the limit exists and is
  a positive rational number;
- independence of the basis, and dependence only on the isometry class of `L_p`;
- `[K_p(L) : K_p⁺(L)] = 2` exactly when `K_p(L)` contains an element of determinant `−1`.
  ⚠ The companion identity `vol(K_p(L)) = α_p(L)`, for the measure attached to the gauge form of
  the equation `Xᵀ A X = A`, is **not** a milestone here: that measure is the local factor of the
  Tamagawa measure, which no current supplier defines. It is `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`'s
  first obligation, and `α_p` as defined above is exactly what it must be shown equal to;
- the unramified value: for `p ∤ 2 det L`, so that `L_p` is unimodular,

      α_p(L) = 2 ∏_{i=1}^{m} (1 − p^{−2i})                      if n = 2m + 1,
      α_p(L) = 2 (1 − ε p^{−m}) ∏_{i=1}^{m−1} (1 − p^{−2i})     if n = 2m,

  where `ε = ±1` is the **type** of the reduction of `L_p`, which is the split/nonsplit
  invariant of the orthogonal group and not the square class of the determinant. It is
  fixed by the signed determinant:

      ε = ((−1)^m · det L_p | p),

  the Legendre symbol. The value comes from `α_p(L) = #O(L_p ⊗ 𝔽_p)/p^{n(n−1)/2}` together
  with `#O^ε_{2m}(𝔽_p) = 2 p^{m(m−1)}(p^m − ε)∏_{i=1}^{m−1}(p^{2i} − 1)`, and `O^ε_{2m}` is
  split exactly when `(−1)^m det` is a square. The genus symbol of 3G records the Legendre
  symbol of the determinant itself, in the Conway–Sloane convention, so the translation
  between the two carries the factor `(−1 | p)^m` and the milestone states it that way;
- the mandatory test that separates the two conventions: the hyperbolic plane over `p = 3`
  has `m = 1` and `det = −1`, a nonsquare mod 3, yet it is split, `#O_2^+(𝔽_3) = 4`, and
  `α_3 = 4/3 = 2(1 − 3^{−1})`. Reading `ε` off the raw determinant would give `8/3`;
- the normalization dictionary for the product over `p`. ⚠ The raw product `∏_p α_p(L)⁻¹` is
  **not** a convergent Euler product and is not what any mass formula consumes: the displays
  give `α_p(L) → 2` as `p → ∞`, so its factors tend to `½` and its partial products tend to
  `0`, and no finite set of corrections at `p ∣ 2 det L` can repair a factor of two at every
  good prime. The factor that enters a mass is the **normalized** good-prime density
  `α_p(L)/2`, and

      ∏_{p ∤ 2 det L} (α_p(L)/2)⁻¹ = ∏_{i=1}^{m} ζ^{(S)}(2i)                       if n = 2m + 1,
      ∏_{p ∤ 2 det L} (α_p(L)/2)⁻¹ = ∏_{i=1}^{m−1} ζ^{(S)}(2i) · L^{(S)}(m, χ_L)   if n = 2m,

  with `S` the primes dividing `2 det L`, the superscript removing the Euler factors at `S`, and
  `χ_L(p) = ((−1)^m det L | p)` the character of the signed determinant. This is Conway–Sloane's
  `std_p(f) = α_p(L)⁻¹` in equation (6) of their paper, and the `2` in front of `m_p(f)` in
  their formula `∏_p 2 m_p(f)`, which the successor's 7H quotes, is exactly the `2/α_p(L)`
  above; Gan–Yu's and Cho's `β_{L_p} = α_p(L)/2` is the same normalization, as 7D records. The
  convergence and nonvanishing statements are proved in the regimes in which they hold and in
  no others:
  - `n ≥ 3`: every factor is a `ζ(2i)` with `2i ≥ 2` or an `L(m, χ_L)` with `m ≥ 2`, so the
    product converges absolutely to a nonzero value. The correction at `p = 2` is the number
    `α_2(L)` that the stabilization above defines and 7D evaluates, a single finite factor that
    convergence does not wait for;
  - `n = 2`: the good-prime product is `∏ (1 − χ_L(p) p⁻¹)⁻¹`. When `−det L` is not a square,
    which is every positive definite binary lattice and every indefinite one with nonsquare
    `Δ`, `χ_L` is a nontrivial quadratic character and the product converges conditionally, in
    the order of increasing `p`, to `L^{(S)}(1, χ_L) ≠ 0`; this is the value that B8's `h⁺/w`
    meets through the class number formula. When `−det L` is a square, `χ_L = 1` and the
    product `∏ (1 − p⁻¹)⁻¹` diverges, so there is no nonzero Euler product at all; this is the
    split branch of B7 seen from the local side, and `U` is its test;
  - `n = 1`: `m = 0` and `α_p(L) = 2` at every good prime, so the normalized product is empty
    and equal to `1`;
  - `n = 0`: `α_p(L) = 1` at every `p` and there is no factor of two to remove, the same rank-0
    exception that 7A and 7G record for the mass;
- the dictionary to the Conway–Sloane local mass `m_p` at odd `p`, in their section 12,
  including every factor of 2.

The values at odd `p` are computed from the Jordan decomposition of 3C.

**7D. The local density at 2, from Cho's smooth model.** *Owner:*
`OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`. The closed evaluation of `α_2(L)` is read off a smooth
affine group scheme over `ℤ_2`, so it needs smoothening, special fibres, unipotent radicals and
reductive quotients of integral group schemes, together with point counts of each. That is a
programme in the algebraic-group theory the successors own, and not a lattice calculation. The
theorem is Cho, Theorem 5.2, and the successor must state it in the generality Cho proves and
in his normalization, because the exponent below is generally nonzero and dropping it changes
the answer by a power of 2. It is set out here as the boundary the successor must meet, and
because the lattice-side inputs are milestones of this roadmap.

Let `R` be an unramified finite extension of `ℤ_2`, with fraction field `F` and residue
field `κ` of cardinality `f`. Let
`(L, q)` be a quadratic `R`-lattice of rank `n` with `⟨x, y⟩ = ½(q(x+y) − q(x) − q(y))`
integral and `V = L ⊗_R F` nondegenerate; in this roadmap's vocabulary `⟨·,·⟩` is `β` and
`q` is the norm form `N_L`, since `⟨x, x⟩ = q(x)`. Take the Jordan splitting, the type and
bound/free classification, and the exponents `N_M`, `N_Q` and `N` from 3I, which is ours. Let
`𝒢_L` be the smooth affine group scheme
over `R` with generic fiber `O(V, q)` and `𝒢_L(R) = O(L)`, let `𝒢̃_L` be its special fiber
and `U_L` the unipotent radical of `𝒢̃_L`. Then Cho's local density of `(L, q)`, which he
writes `β_L` and which is not the bilinear form `β` of Layer 0, is

    β_L = [O(V, q) : SO(V, q)]⁻¹ · f^N · f^{−dim O(V,q)} · #𝒢̃_L(κ),      dim O(V,q) = n(n−1)/2,

and `#𝒢̃_L(κ) = #U_L(κ)·#(𝒢̃_L/U_L)(κ)` with `#U_L(κ) = f^{dim U_L}`, the reductive quotient
`𝒢̃_L/U_L` being `∏_i O(V̄_i, q̄_i)_red` times an elementary abelian 2-group whose rank is
the `α + β` of Cho's Lemma 4.2, by his Theorem 4.12.

The successor's milestone is:

- the construction of `𝒢_L` from the Jordan data of 3D and 3I, with the convention in rank 0;
- the proof that `𝒢_L` is smooth of relative dimension `n(n−1)/2`;
- the special fibre, its unipotent radical, the reductive quotient, and the point count of
  each;
- the displayed formula, over a general unramified `R`, with `R = ℤ_2` and `f = 2`
  specialized only afterwards, using 3I's exponents unchanged;
- the factor `[O(V, q) : SO(V, q)]⁻¹`: the index is 2 for `n ≥ 1` in characteristic zero,
  so the factor is `½`, and it is the reason `β_L` is a density for `SO` and not for `O`;
- the comparison with the limit definition of 7C, which is where `α_2` is fixed. That limit
  and its stabilization are ours, so what the successor proves is an evaluation of a number
  this roadmap has already constructed, not a second definition of it. The odd-prime case
  pins the expected constant: Gan–Yu give
  `β_{L_p} = ½·p^{−n(n−1)/2}·#O(L_p ⊗ 𝔽_p)`, which is half the `α_p` of 7C, so the target
  is `α_2(L) = 2·β_L = 2^{N − n(n−1)/2}·#𝒢̃_L(𝔽_2)`, and it is proved rather than assumed;
- the proof that the resulting factor is the Conway–Sloane dyadic factor, oddity and type
  included.

The Conway–Sloane dyadic tables are data, and not a proof.

**7E. The archimedean factor.** With the measure from the standard Euclidean structure,
`SO(n)/SO(n−1) ≅ S^{n−1}` and `vol(S^{n−1}) = 2π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2)`, so

    vol(SO(n)) = ∏_{j=2}^{n} 2π^{j/2} / Γ(j/2),      vol(O(n)) = 2·vol(SO(n)).

The milestone proves the fibration, the sphere volume, the product, and then the identity
that connects it with the mass formula:

    2 π^{−n(n+1)/4} ∏_{j=1}^{n} Γ(j/2) = 2^{n+1} / vol(O(n)).

That this real volume is the archimedean factor of the Tamagawa measure of 7B is **not**
proved here: that measure is `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`'s, and the comparison is its
obligation, stated on its side against the Euclidean volume computed here. Nothing in this
milestone names that measure, so the dependency stays one-way.

**7F. The volume theorem.** *Owner:* `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`.
`vol(SO(V)(ℚ) \ SO(V)(𝔸)) = 2`, with its dimension hypotheses and normalization, and with the
low-dimensional exceptions recorded. ⚠ This roadmap's low-rank branch 7G states the rank `0`,
`1` and `2` mass values directly and does not derive them from this theorem, so the two
documents must agree on the exceptions rather than one deducing them from the other.

**7G. Low rank.** Three cases are proved directly, and none of them is a specialization of
the general derivation:

- rank 0: `O(L) = SO(L) = 1` and the genus has one class, so `m⁺ = m = 1`;
- rank 1: the genus of `⟨a⟩` with `a > 0` has one class, with `O(L) = {±1}` and `SO(L) = 1`,
  so `m = 1/2` and `m⁺ = 1`;
- rank 2: B8 gives `m⁺(gen L) = h⁺(gen L)/#𝒪(L)ˣ` and `m(gen L) = h⁺(gen L)/(2·#𝒪(L)ˣ)`,
  through the norm-one torus of B6 and its measures in B7. Both denominators count
  **proper** classes; the full class number `h(gen L)` is not what divides here, because
  `|O(M)|` is not constant on the genus.

The derivation of 7B to 7F is stated for rank at least 3, and 7H packages all ranks with
explicit branches. 7G is proved here, without any of them.

**7H. The Conway–Sloane formula and its checks.** *Owner:*
`OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`. The formula

    m(f) = 2 π^{−n(n+1)/4} ∏_{j=1}^{n} Γ(j/2) ∏_p 2 m_p(f)

with the dimension guard, together with the dictionary to Siegel's local density notation
`α_p`. Then the checks:

- the rank-8 even unimodular genus has mass `1/696729600`, class number 1, and
  `|O(E₈)| = |W(E₈)| = 696729600`;
- the genus of `A₂` has class number 1;
- in rank 16, `1/|O(E₈²)| + 1/|O(D₁₆⁺)| = m₁₆`, where `m₁₆` is the mass of the genus of 6D.

The third check is the input to 7I.

**7I. The rank-16 genus has two classes.** *Owner:* `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`; the two
automorphism orders it needs are computed here, in 6D and 6G. Both automorphism orders are
computed first. `E₈²`
has two indecomposable summands, both isometric to `E₈`, so `|O(E₈²)| = 2·|O(E₈)|²`, with
`|O(E₈)|` from 6G. The order `|O(D₁₆⁺)|` is computed from its root system `D₁₆` together
with the stabilizer of the glue vector. With `m₁₆` from 7H, the
equality `1/|O(E₈²)| + 1/|O(D₁₆⁺)| = m₁₆` and the finiteness of the class set prove that

### Layer 9: what the LMFDB lattice columns assert

**9A. The stored columns.** A record of the LMFDB lattice section is a Gram matrix `G`, a
label `dim.det.level.class_number.index`, a list of Gram matrices called the genus
representatives, and the numerical columns. This milestone defines
`StoredGenusCertificate`, whose fields are the statements the record asserts about the stored
matrices themselves:

- `G` is integral, symmetric and positive definite, so 0A to 0E apply to the lattice `L` it
  defines;
- the dimension is the rank of 0A, the determinant is that of 0C, and the level is that of
  0D;
- the minimum and the kissing number are those of 2B, the automorphism group order is that
  of 2C, and the stored `theta_series` column is the sequence of representation numbers
  `r_L(k) = #S_k(L)` of 2B, asserted as shell **counts**;
- every listed Gram matrix defines a lattice in `gen L`, by 3F;
- the listed lattices are pairwise non-isometric, which is a decidable check for positive
  definite lattices by 2G.

Every one of these is a **semantic** assertion: it says what a stored column means, and each is
proved for a given record by a finite computation with the milestones named beside it. The fifth
label component has no mathematical content in this roadmap.

⚠ `StoredGenusCertificate` deliberately has **no completeness field and no `class_number`
field**. A list of pairwise non-isometric lattices in one genus is not thereby the whole genus,
and nothing in Layers 0 to 7 proves that it is: 2G gives finiteness of the class set, which is
not the same as identifying it. Putting `class_number` beside the semantic fields would make
every certificate assert exhaustiveness, which is the one thing this roadmap cannot prove.
Completeness is 9B.

**9B. The completeness certificate, and the import it names.** `StoredClassNumberCertificate`
extends 9A's record with the class number, and it is where exhaustiveness lives. Exactly two
routes reach it, and both leave this roadmap:

- an exact mass: the mass `m(gen L)` of 7A is defined here as a sum over the classes in the
  genus, but no milestone here evaluates it. The evaluation is the Conway–Sloane formula, which
  is `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`'s 7H;
- a proved neighbour-graph connectivity theorem in the exact regime. 4G defines `p`-neighbours
  and proves the edge relation, and it explicitly claims nothing about connectivity; the
  theorem that the neighbour graph of a genus is connected is not a milestone of this roadmap
  either.

So 9B takes the mass as a **hypothesis field**, named as such: a rational number `mass`, the
assumption `mass_isGenusMass` that it is the mass of the genus in the sense of 7A, and the check
`reps_exhaust_mass` that the reciprocal automorphism orders of the listed representatives already
sum to it. Completeness is then a **theorem** of 9B and not a field of it: the listed lattices
are distinct classes in the genus, `1/|O(M)|` is an isometry invariant and positive, so a proper
sublist would sum to strictly less than the mass. The class number is the length of the list,
and it is only in 9B that it means what the LMFDB column means. A contributor who has the
connectivity theorem instead builds the analogous record with that theorem in place of
`mass_isGenusMass`; the shape is the same, and what may not happen is a certificate with neither.

This split is what keeps a certificate honest. A consumer that has not imported an exact mass or
a connectivity theorem can build a `StoredGenusCertificate` and gets every semantic column from
it; it cannot build a `StoredClassNumberCertificate` at all, because it has nothing to put in
the hypothesis field.

`Suggested.lean` carries both structures, because every condition in them is expressible at the
current Mathlib: isometry is integral congruence of Gram matrices, and genus membership is
congruence over every `ℤ_p` together with the real signature, which is 3F written out. Nothing
in either certificate waits for the genus symbols of 3E.

## Basic API for each new object

A definition without lemmas is not a contribution. For each object below the roadmap asks
for the eight items listed. The layer that introduces the object owns them.

### The lattice form (0A)

- **Constructors.** From a symmetric bilinear form; from a Gram matrix over `ℤ`; from a
  quadratic form, when the lattice is even; by restriction to a full submodule in the same
  ambient space; from an arbitrary finite-free submodule in its rational span
  `ℚ ⊗[ℤ] M`.
- **Examples.** `⟨a⟩`, `Iₙ`, `U`, the root lattices, `Λ_{K3}` (0G).
- **Morphisms.** Isometries, isometric embeddings, and primitive embeddings (5F).
- **Functoriality.** Direct sums, twists, full sublattices of finite index, and orthogonal
  complements; arbitrary finite-free submodules are compared in their rational spans.
- **Comparison lemmas.** The Gram matrix in a basis; the real form; the rational form; the
  `ℤ_p`-form.
- **Naturality.** An isometry induces equality of determinant, signature, level, scale and
  norm ideal.
- **Edge cases.** Rank 0; degenerate forms; the zero form.
- **Downstream.** Every later layer.

### The dual lattice (1B)

- **Constructors.** `B.dualSubmodule L` in `V = ℚ ⊗ L`; the dual basis of a basis.
- **Examples.** `L^⋆ = L` for unimodular `L`; `(Aₙ)^⋆/Aₙ ≅ ℤ/(n+1)`.
- **Morphisms.** An isometry of `L` induces an isometry of `L^⋆`.
- **Functoriality.** `(L ⊕ M)^⋆ = L^⋆ ⊕ M^⋆`;
  `dual_{aB}(L) = (a : ℚ)⁻¹ • dual_B(L)` for nonzero integral `a`, with scalar
  dilation on the right; inclusion reversal.
- **Comparison lemmas.** The Gram matrix of the dual basis is `G⁻¹`;
  `det L^⋆ = (det L)⁻¹`. That the dual of the real model is the image of this submodule is
  Theta Series' bridge theorem, and lives there.
- **Naturality.** Biduality `L^{⋆⋆} = L`, and its compatibility with sums and twists.
- **Edge cases.** Degenerate `β`, where the dual is not a lattice; rank 0.
- **Downstream.** 1C, 1D, 5G; and Theta Series, through 8S.

### The discriminant group and its forms (1C, 1D)

- **Constructors.** `A_L = L^⋆/L`; `b_L` from `B`; `q_L` from `B` when `L` is even.
- **Examples.** `A_{E₈} = 0`; `A_{A₂} ≅ ℤ/3` with half-norm `q = 1/3`; `A_U = 0`.
- **Morphisms.** `O(L) → O(q_L)`, whose surjectivity is 5E.
- **Functoriality.** Sums and the sign twist `L(−1)`, as canonical isometries and not
  equalities (1D); nonunit twists instead use the induced inclusion/quotient comparison.
- **Comparison lemmas.** `#A_L = |det L|`; `l(A_L) ≤ rank L`; the polarization of `q_L` is
  `b_L`; the invariant-factor description.
- **Naturality.** An isometry of lattices induces an isometry of discriminant forms, and
  this assignment respects composition.
- **Edge cases.** Unimodular `L`, where `A_L = 0`; odd `L`, which has no `q_L`; rank 0.
- **Downstream.** 1E, 1F, 5A to 5J, 6A.

### Finite quadratic forms (1G)

- **Constructors.** From `(A, q)` with the two axioms; the generators `q_θ^{(p)}(p^k)`,
  `u^{(2)}(2^k)`, `v^{(2)}(2^k)`; the discriminant form of an even lattice.
- **Examples.** The forms listed for the standard lattices above.
- **Morphisms.** Isometries, and the group `O(q)`.
- **Functoriality.** Orthogonal sums; the `p`-primary decomposition; restriction to a
  subgroup; the quotient `H^⊥/H` for isotropic `H`.
- **Comparison lemmas.** For nondegenerate modules, the relations among generators
  (Nikulin 1.8.2), the Gauss-sum invariant of each generator (1H), and its vanishing on
  metabolic modules (1H).
- **Naturality.** `sign` is additive over sums and invariant under isometry.
- **Edge cases.** The trivial group; degenerate restrictions, which remain objects of the
  carrier but are excluded explicitly from the generator and Gauss-sum classifications.
- **Downstream.** 1H, 3E, 5A to 5J.

### Lattices over `ℤ_p` and their Jordan data (3A, 3B)

- **Constructors.** `L.integralForm`; `L_p = ℤ_p ⊗[ℤ] L.carrier` with its localized
  integral form; `V_p = ℚ_p ⊗[ℚ] V` with its completed rational form; the embedding
  `L_p → V_p`; a Jordan splitting; a Gram matrix over `ℤ_p`.
- **Examples.** Unimodular `ℤ_p`-lattices at odd `p`; `U` over `ℤ_2`.
- **Morphisms.** Isometries over `ℤ_p`, and base change from `ℤ`.
- **Functoriality.** Sums, twists, and scaling by `p^i`.
- **Comparison lemmas.** `L.integralForm` casts to `L.form`; the canonical `L_p → V_p` is
  injective and full after scalar extension; its integral form is the restriction of the
  completed rational form. The Jordan invariants at odd `p` are unique (3C); at `p = 2`
  the splitting is not unique and the symbols of 3E replace it.
- **Naturality.** Localization commutes with sums, form twists, carrier dilations, duality,
  and isometries.
- **Edge cases.** `p = 2`; rank 0; a scale-zero constituent.
- **Downstream.** 3C to 3I, 4C, 7C; and the successor's 7D.

### Genus symbols (3E, 3G)

- **Constructors.** From a Jordan splitting; from a Gram matrix by an algorithm.
- **Examples.** The symbols of `A₂`, `U`, `E₈`, and one rank-4 lattice with a nontrivial
  2-adic part.
- **Morphisms.** The moves: sign walking and oddity fusion.
- **Functoriality.** The symbol of a direct sum, and of a twist.
- **Comparison lemmas.** Two symbols describe isometric lattices exactly when the moves
  relate them; the symbol determines the genus; the translation to `(t₊, t₋, q)` (5A).
- **Naturality.** The symbol depends only on the isometry class of `L_p`.
- **Edge cases.** `p = 2`; determinant `±1`, where the symbol is empty; rank 0.
- **Downstream.** 3F, 3G, 3I, 5A, 7C, 9A; and the successor's 7D.

### Class, genus and spinor genus (4A, 4C)

- **Constructors.** `cls L`, `cls⁺ L`, `gen L`, `spn L`, `spn⁺ L`.
- **Examples.** Genera of class number 1; the rank-16 genus with two classes (6D — that they
  are the *only* two is the successor's 7I).
- **Morphisms.** The inclusions between the five sets, and the double-coset description
  (4B).
- **Functoriality.** Behavior under twists, and under orthogonal sums where it is defined.
- **Comparison lemmas.** The count of proper spinor genera (4C). Eichler's theorem (4D) is the
  successor's, and this API is what it consumes.
- **Naturality.** The double-coset description is compatible with a change of the base
  lattice inside a genus.
- **Edge cases.** Rank 0, 1 and 2; definite and indefinite.
- **Downstream.** 4E to 4G, 7A, 9A, 9B; and the successor's 7B.

### The quadratic order of a binary lattice (B1)

- **Constructors.** From a binary Gram matrix through the primitive part of the norm form;
  from a discriminant `Δ ≡ 0` or `1 (mod 4)`.
- **Examples.** `A₂` gives content 2, `Δ = −3` and `𝒪 = ℤ[ζ₃]`; `U` gives content 2,
  `Δ = 1` and the split algebra `ℤ × ℤ`; `⟨1,−2⟩` gives content 1, `Δ = 8` and `ℤ[√2]`;
  `!![4,1;1,6]` gives content 2 and `Δ = −23`.
- **Morphisms.** Isometries of binary lattices induce isomorphisms of the associated
  orders, and proper isometries act trivially on `Pic`. An improper isometry acts by the
  conjugation of B4, which is inversion on `Pic`.
- **Functoriality.** A basis matrix `P` sends `G` to `PᵀGP`; a finite-index sublattice
  satisfies `det M = [L:M]² det L`, `𝔰(M) ⊆ 𝔰(L)`, and `𝔫(M) ⊆ 𝔫(L)`. Content
  has no formula determined solely by the index. The distinct form twist `L(a)` multiplies
  content by `|a|`.
- **Comparison lemmas.** `Δ(L) = disc f` with `disc N_L = −4 det L`; forms and invertible
  proper ideal classes (B2); composition and multiplication (B3); `SO(L)` and the norm-one
  units (B4).
- **Naturality.** The correspondence of B2 commutes with the maps induced by isometries.
- **Edge cases.** Imprimitive norm forms; square discriminants, which use the separate
  product-order branch and never `NumberFieldOrder`, `Pic`, `NarrowPic`, or ring class fields;
  the two orders with extra units, `Δ = −3` and `Δ = −4`, and non-ambiguous classes, where
  `O(L) = SO(L)`.
- **Downstream.** 2C, 4E, 4F, 7G.

### The mass (7A)

- **Constructors.** `m(gen L)` and `m⁺(gen L)`.
- **Examples.** Rank 0 gives 1 and rank 1 gives 1/2, both from 7G. The rank-8 even unimodular
  value `1/696729600` follows from the successor's 7H and is not proved here; what is proved
  here is `|O(E₈)| = 696729600` (6G), the number that value inverts.
- **Morphisms.** None: the mass is a rational number attached to a genus.
- **Functoriality.** Behavior under a positive twist. There is no formula for a direct sum,
  and that non-statement is recorded.
- **Comparison lemmas.** `m⁺ = 2m` for `rank L ≥ 1`, and `m⁺ = m = 1` in rank 0; the local
  factor 7C, whose dyadic evaluation is the successor's 7D. The dictionary to Siegel's `α_p` is
  stated with the successor's 7H.
- **Naturality.** The mass depends only on the genus.
- **Edge cases.** Ranks 0, 1 and 2 (7G).
- **Downstream.** 6D, 9B, where it is the named hypothesis that discharges completeness.

### Shells and representation numbers (2B)

- **Constructors.** `S_k(L) = {x ∈ L | β x x = k}` for every rank, and `r_L(k) = #S_k(L)`,
  finite by 2A for positive definite `L`. `min L` and the kissing number `#S_{min L}(L)` for
  `rank L ≥ 1`.
- **Examples.** `r_{E₈}(2) = 240`; `r_L(0) = 1`; for even `L` every odd shell is empty.
- **Morphisms.** None on `r_L` itself. An isometry carries shells to shells, so `r_L` is an
  isometry invariant.
- **Functoriality.** `S_k(L ⊕ M)` is the disjoint union over `i + j = k` of
  `S_i(L) × S_j(M)`, and `S_k(L(a)) = S_{k/a}(L)` for `a > 0`, empty unless `a ∣ k`.
- **Comparison lemmas.** These are the numbers Theta Series identifies with the
  `q`-expansion coefficients of `Θ_L` through its bridge. That identification is **its**
  theorem, and this roadmap states no theta series to compare against.
- **Naturality.** `r_L` depends only on the isometry class.
- **Edge cases.** Rank 0, where `S_0 = {0}` and every other shell is empty; negative definite
  and indefinite lattices, where the shells of nonpositive `k` are infinite and 2A fails.
- **Downstream.** 2C, 2E, 2G, 6D, 6E, 6F, 9A; and Theta Series, through 8S.

## Worked examples

Each example is discharged with the milestone that owns it. Each one catches a wrong
factor of 2, a wrong sign, or a vacuous definition.

- `⟨1⟩ = ℤ`: odd, unimodular, with the odd integers as its characteristic vectors and
  `w² ≡ 1 (mod 8)`, the odd case of van der Blij (0G, 1L). Its genus is one class and one
  proper spinor genus, while `J/(ℚˣ J_L) = 𝔸ˣ/ℚˣ𝔸^{×2}` is infinite, the rank-one rejection
  test of 4C; its good-prime densities are `α_p = 2`, with an empty normalized product (4C, 7C).
- `U`: even, `det = −1`, signature `(1,0,1)`, level 1, `A_U = 0`, and not diagonalizable over
  `ℤ_2`; its primitive binary discriminant is `1`, so its algebra/order branch is explicitly
  `ℚ × ℚ`/`ℤ × ℤ`, with one split proper class and `|O(U)| = 4` (0G, 3D, B1--B5). Over `ℤ_2`
  it is a single free type II constituent with `t = b = 0` and `c = 2`, so Cho's exponent is
  `N = 2` and `α_2(U) = 4` in 7C's count (3I). Its norm-one torus is the split `𝔾_m`, whose
  adelic quotient `𝔸ˣ/ℚˣ` has infinite volume, and `−det U = 1` is a square, so its good-prime
  product `∏ (1 − p⁻¹)⁻¹` diverges: it is the test of B7's split branch and of the rank-2
  exception in 7C (B7, 7C).
- The index-two sublattice `⟨2e₁,e₂⟩ ≤ ℤ²` restricts `x²+y²` to `4x²+y²`; its content
  remains 1 although the determinant is multiplied by 4 (0C, B1).
- `⟨-2⟩` is negative definite of signature `(0,0,1)`; the zero rank-one form is
  degenerate of signature `(0,1,0)` and has zero radical quotient (0G, 1K).
- `⟨2⟩`: every value of the form is even, so every vector is characteristic, and the
  congruence of 1L fails at every one of them — the witness that 1L requires
  unimodularity (1L). Over `ℤ_2` it is a type I constituent of scale 2 with `𝔫 = 2ℤ_2`, the
  test that the parity type is read on the unimodular rescaling, and it has `N = 2` and
  `α_2 = 8` (3I). Together with `⟨10⟩` it is one of the two minimal 2-adic realizations of
  `q_1^{(2)}(2) = q_5^{(2)}(2)`, of determinants differing by 5, so `discr K(q₂)` is not
  determined by `q₂` there (5B).
- `⟨1, −3⟩`, the form `x² − 3y²`: `Δ = 12`, `𝒪_{12} = ℤ[√3]`, fundamental unit `2 + √3` of norm
  `+1`, so `Pic` is trivial and `NarrowPic` has order 2. The forms `x² − 3y²` and `−x² + 3y²`
  are not properly equivalent, share the unoriented ideal `𝒪_{12}`, and are separated only by
  the sign clause of B2, which sends the second to the class of `√3·𝒪_{12}` (B2, B3).
- `⟨1⟩ ⊕ ⟨1⟩`: `Δ = −4`, `w = 4`, one class and one proper spinor genus, while `J/(ℚˣ J_L)`
  has order 2 because `θ_2(SO(L_2))` is the norm group of `ℚ_2(i)`; the rank-2 count is
  `[C_L : C_L²] = 1` through the torus (4C). Its good-prime factors are `α_p/2 = 1 − (−1|p)p⁻¹`,
  whose product over odd `p` is `L(1, χ_{−4})⁻¹ = 4/π` (7C).
- The discriminant form of `A₁ ⊕ A₁`: the glue class `h` satisfies `b(h,h) = 0` and
  `H = H^⊥` while `q(h) = ½` and `sign = 2` — the witness that Lagrangian means isotropic
  for `q` itself (1F, 1G, 1H).
- Affine `Ã₁` with Gram `!![2,-2;-2,2]` is even and positive-semidefinite of signature
  `(1,1,0)`, and its radical quotient is `A₁=⟨2⟩` (0E, 0G).
- `A₂`: even, `det = 3`, level 3, and `A_{A₂} ≅ ℤ/3` with half-norm
  `q = 1/3` in `ℚ/ℤ`. Its 3-adic
  Jordan splitting has two rank-one constituents, of scales 1 and 3. Equality holds in
  Hermite's bound, and the class number is 1 (0G, 1D, 2E, 3B, 4A). Its order is `ℤ[ζ₃]`,
  with `Δ = −3` and six units, and its class is ambiguous, so `|SO(A₂)| = 6`,
  `|O(A₂)| = 12` and the mass of its genus is `1/12` (B1, B4, B8).
- `!![4,1;1,6]`: content 2, `Δ = −23`, and `O(L) = SO(L) = {±I}`, so it has no improper
  automorphism. Its genus has three proper classes and two classes, `!![2,1;1,12]` with
  `|O| = 4` and `!![4,1;1,6]` with `|O| = 2`, and mass `3/4`. The lattice `!![3,1;1,4]`, of
  determinant 11 and `Δ = −44`, is the same phenomenon at the smallest determinant
  (B4, B8).
- The family `Aₙ`: `det(Aₙ) = n+1` and `A_{Aₙ} ≅ ℤ/(n+1)` (0G, 1C).
- `D₈⁺`: the preimage of the spinor subgroup in `A_{D₈}` is proved even and unimodular
  by the general isotropic-subgroup correspondence and Lagrangian criterion, then identified
  with `E₈` by an explicit isometry; its trivial discriminant group is also computed as
  `H^⊥/H` (1K).
- `E₈`: even, unimodular, positive definite, `min = 2`, 240 minimal vectors, signature
  `(8,0)`, `sign q_{E₈} = 0`, unique in rank 8, and `|O(E₈)| = 696729600` (0G, 2B, 2C, 6C, 6G).
  Its mass `1/696729600` is the successor's 7H.
- Even unimodular lattices have `8 ∣ t₊ − t₋`, so no even unimodular positive definite
  lattice has rank 1 to 7 (1I, 6B).
- Rank 16: `E₈²` and `D₁₆⁺` lie in one genus and are not isometric (6D). That they *exhaust* the
  genus is 7I, and is the successor's.
- `Λ_{K3} = U³ ⊕ E₈(−1)²`: even, unimodular, signature `(3,19)`, `det = −1`, and unique
  with that signature. For `d > 0` the lattice `⟨2d⟩` embeds primitively, and uniquely up
  to `O(Λ_{K3})`. Every even lattice of signature `(1, ρ−1)` with `ρ ≤ 10` embeds
  primitively (5G, 5H, 6A).
- One LMFDB record checked end to end: `A₂`, and one rank-4 lattice with a nontrivial
  2-adic symbol (9A). The `A₂` completeness certificate of 9B is built only from an imported
  mass, and the roadmap records that it cannot be built here.
- Mass conventions: rank 0 gives 1, and the genus of `⟨a⟩` gives 1/2 (7G).

## Ordering and parallelism

Layer 0 comes first. After it, three groups of milestones are independent of each other:

- Layer 2, which needs no dual lattice;
- Layer 1;
- milestones 3A to 3E.

The rest of the order follows the prerequisite tables:

- milestones 3F to 3H need Layer 1 and the two suppliers named in their table; 3I needs only
  3B, 3D and 3E, so it can be built in parallel with 3F to 3H;
- Layer B needs Layers 0 to 3; its nonsquare branch also needs the order and Picard carriers
  of Global Number Fields and, for negative discriminant, Class Field Theory's
  ring-class-field milestone. The square branch is elementary. Layers 4 and 7 use both
  rank-2 branches;
- Layer 4 needs Layers 2, 3 and B, and the Orthogonal and Spin Groups roadmap;
- Layer 5 needs Layers 1 and 3;
- Layer 6 needs Layers 1, 2 and 5, and milestone 6C also needs Root Systems;
- Layer 7's own milestones — 7A, 7C, 7E and 7G — need Layers 2, 3, 4 and B, and nothing
  adelic; 7B, 7F, 7H and 7I are `OrthogonalTamagawaAndLatticeMass`'s and are ordered after the
  generic `TamagawaMeasures`, and its 7D after the group-scheme material of the successors
  #246 names;
- Layer 8 is a contract and orders nothing here: it imports nothing, no milestone of Layers 0
  to 7, B or 9 has a theta series among its prerequisites, and nothing here waits on Theta
  Series. What that roadmap waits on from here is 8S — Layers 0 and 1, together with 2B, 2D,
  6D and 6E;
- Layer 9 comes last. 9A needs nothing outside this roadmap; 9B has no discharged instance
  until an exact mass or a connectivity theorem is imported from outside it.

The shortest route to the K3 results is `0 → 1 → 5`, together with the comparison 5A. That
route uses no milestone of Layers 2, 4, 6 or 7.

TauCetiRoadmap/Isoperimetry:
# Euclidean isoperimetry, sharp inequalities, and rigidity

Build Euclidean isoperimetric theory on Mathlib and Tau Ceti, including the sharp inequality
for all finite-volume finite-perimeter sets in every dimension `n ≥ 2`, equality exactly
for balls up to null sets, and the classical theorem for every rectifiable planar Jordan
curve, with equality exactly for circles. Develop the supporting convex and functional
inequalities as reusable mathematics: Prékopa–Leindler, Brunn–Minkowski, symmetrization,
sharp BV Sobolev, and the periodic curve inequality with its equality analysis.

Develop the theory independently on canonical Mathlib and Tau Ceti APIs. Every milestone
is required. Quantitative stability, anisotropic perimeter, and
isoperimetric inequalities on curved ambient manifolds are outside this roadmap.
[Suggested.lean](Suggested.lean) illustrates interfaces; this README is definitive.

## Constants, statements, and scope

Work in `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` and transport to arbitrary finite-dimensional real
inner-product spaces by linear isometries. Let `ω_n = volume (ball 0 1)`. Use normalized
Euclidean Hausdorff measure `μHE[k]`, written `Hᵏ`, and the perimeter measure defined by
[GeometricMeasureTheory](../GeometricMeasureTheory/README.md), G3–G5. In dimension two,
`ω_2 = π` and the oriented real plane is `ℂ`.
Set measurability in the general statements is Lebesgue measurability
(`NullMeasurableSet E volume`), with Borel-representative versions and a.e. transport;
`MeasurableSet` is used where the result explicitly concerns Borel sets.

For a measurable set `E` with finite volume and finite perimeter, establish

```
P(E)^n ≥ n^n ω_n |E|^(n−1),                         n ≥ 2.
```

For `0 < |E| < ∞`, equality holds **if and only if** there are `c` and `r > 0` such that
`χ_E = χ_(ball c r)` a.e. with respect to `volume`. No boundedness, connectedness, convexity,
or boundary regularity is imposed on `E`. For zero volume, prove perimeter zero and the
corresponding degenerate inequality separately. Provide extended nonnegative statements,
and real-valued versions carrying the required finiteness hypotheses. Never turn an
infinite perimeter into zero by using `ENNReal.toReal` without those hypotheses.

For a rectifiable Jordan curve `C` let `Ω = TauCeti.filledHull C \ C`, let
`A = volume Ω`, and let `L = H¹(C)`. Establish

```
4π A ≤ L²,       4π A = L² ↔ ∃ c r, 0 < r ∧ C = sphere c r.
```

Include the raw-curve formulation for every continuous `γ : ℝ → ℂ` on `[a,b]`, `a < b`,
with `γ(a)=γ(b)`, injective on `[a,b)`, and `BoundedVariationOn γ [a,b]`. In that formulation
`C = γ '' [a,b]` and `L = eVariationOn γ [a,b]`; show agreement with the geometric formulation.
Do not require the supplied parametrization to be AC, Lipschitz, differentiable, or
piecewise smooth. The curve equality is literal equality of traces with a circle; the
set equality above is equality a.e. These are different assertions with a required bridge.

## Dependencies and ownership

- [GeometricMeasureTheory](../GeometricMeasureTheory/README.md), G1–G2, supplies arclength,
  normalized Hausdorff length and surface measure, area/coarea, and sphere normalization.
  G3–G5 supplies BV, finite perimeter, strict approximation, reduced boundary, and
  `P(E) ≤ Hⁿ⁻¹(frontier E)`. G6 supplies Gauss–Green and
  `P(filledHull C \ C) = H¹(C)` for rectifiable Jordan curves.
- [DifferentialGeometry](../DifferentialGeometry/README.md), 5.6.1–5.6.3, supplies AC
  winding-number calculus and Green's genuine planar area identity. It retains ownership
  of curve integration and Green's theorem. I3 below owns the sharp periodic inequalities
  and their equality cases. The area and length bridge uses the existing curve APIs.
  The [Green layer 5.6 specification](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/826)
  supplies these flat planar targets.
- [ConformalMapping](../ConformalMapping/README.md), L5, owns the Jordan-separation and
  filled-hull targets: exactly two complementary components, one bounded and one unbounded,
  with inside `filledHull C \ C` and frontier `C`. Use the implemented
  `TauCeti.IsJordanCurve` and `TauCeti.filledHull`;
  no private predicate for a Jordan curve or surrogate for its inside.
- [PDE](../PDE/README.md), Lane A, owns weak Sobolev spaces, density, domain Poincaré and
  trace theory. This roadmap owns sharp Euclidean BV Sobolev and the periodic sharp
  Wirtinger equality theorem, with comparisons to that canonical weak derivative.
  PDE's nonsharp estimates do not depend on this roadmap.

The geometric foundation has no dependency on the sharp inequality. I1–I2 can be developed
alongside it. I3's analytic inequalities use the existing AC calculus and the Green/length
inputs; their identification with actual Jordan area also consumes GMT G6's Jordan index
theorem. I4 consumes GMT G2–G5, I1, and I2's set symmetrization and convex geometry.
I5 consumes I1, I2, I4, GMT G2–G5, and PDE's weak-derivative API; I6 consumes I3–I4,
GMT G6, and Jordan topology.
No optimal-transport theorem is an assumed input. Any analytic, geometric, or equality
lemma needed to complete these milestones and absent from their stated inputs is a target
here, including the proof machinery enumerated in I2 and I4.

## Existing floor and design evidence

Consume Mathlib's `Convex`, `ConvexBody`, pointwise set addition and scalar multiplication,
`volume`, Brunn–Minkowski-compatible set operations, Fourier series and Hilbert bases,
and the interval AC FTC. Keep a.e. function arguments on the existing measure-theory API.
For compact convex sets use [`ConvexBody`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/Convex/Body.html)
where its hypotheses match; positive volume and nonempty interior are separate hypotheses,
not silently added to its definition. Do not model Minkowski addition as an additive group.

Follow the [Brunn–Minkowski/Prékopa–Leindler discussion](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/116395-maths/topic/Brunn-Minkowski%20Inequality%20%2B%20Theory)
and [convex-body API discussion](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/116395-maths/topic/Convex%20bodies).
[Mathlib4#44802](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/44802) develops
one-dimensional Brunn–Minkowski, including `Real.volume_add_volume_le` and the compact-set
version. Adopt Mathlib's resulting signatures and naming; build missing versions in Tau
Ceti in that shape without waiting for upstream. Consume imported results whenever they
express a target. These design references do not discharge the higher-dimensional,
measurability, or equality targets below.

## I1 — Prékopa–Leindler and Brunn–Minkowski

Prove Prékopa–Leindler in every finite dimension for nonnegative measurable functions,
in its weighted extended-integral form: for `0 < θ < 1`,

```
h((1−θ)x + θy) ≥ f(x)^(1−θ) g(y)^θ
⇒ ∫ h ≥ (∫ f)^(1−θ) (∫ g)^θ.
```

State the pointwise hypothesis on measurable representatives. Include integrable real
versions, zero-integral and infinite-integral cases with explicit conventions, linear
isometric transport, product/tensorization, approximation, and the one-dimensional
monotone-transport or equivalent integral argument. The induction, parameter measurability,
and Tonelli steps are part of the target. Do not assume equality characterization for
arbitrary Prékopa–Leindler functions.

Derive Brunn–Minkowski for nonempty compact sets, then nonempty bounded Borel sets and
nonempty arbitrary measurable finite-volume sets, with outer-measure formulations when
their sum is not measurable:

```
|A + B|^(1/n) ≥ |A|^(1/n) + |B|^(1/n),              n ≥ 1.
```

Retain nonemptiness even in zero-volume cases; the unweighted inequality is false when
one summand is empty and the other has positive volume. Supply the weighted Minkowski
version for `0 ≤ θ ≤ 1`,
`|(1−θ) • A + θ • B|^(1/n) ≥ (1−θ)|A|^(1/n) + θ|B|^(1/n)`
and the elementary translation/dilation laws,
monotonicity, continuity for decreasing compact sets and the neighborhood approximation
needed for passing to measurable sets. Address measurability explicitly: the sum of two
Lebesgue measurable sets is not an automatically measurable input. Include positive-volume
**compact convex** equality: for `0 < θ < 1`, equality in the weighted inequality holds
exactly when `B = c + λ • A` for some translation `c` and `λ > 0`. Prove the convex equality argument and the
bridge between positive volume and nonempty interior. A measure inequality alone does
not provide this rigidity theorem. Derive the same homothety characterization for equality
in the unweighted inequality by applying the weighted form at `θ = 1/2` to `2 • A`
and `2 • B` and using dilation laws.

## I2 — Symmetrization, rearrangements, and convex geometry

Build Steiner symmetrization along a unit direction for measurable finite-volume sets:
replace a.e. line section by the centered interval of the same one-dimensional volume.
Provide representative independence, measurability, preservation of volume, monotonicity,
translation conventions, dilation, orthogonal transport, and preservation of convexity.
Prove perimeter nonincrease for finite-perimeter sets using GMT's slicing/coarea theory,
including the nonsmooth approximation and limit argument. Prove `L¹` contraction for
indicators under Steiner symmetrization. For every measurable positive finite-volume set,
construct a sequence of unit directions whose
successive Steiner symmetrizations converge in `L¹` of their indicators to the centered
volume-matched ball. Prove convergence first for bounded finite-perimeter sets using
compactness and limit identification, then extend to arbitrary finite-volume sets by
approximation and contraction, including the control at infinity. Single-step equality is not
assumed to imply that arbitrary sets are balls.

Define Schwarz rearrangement from the distribution function for nonnegative measurable
functions with `|{f > t}| < ∞` for every `t > 0`. Include the `Lᵖ` classes, `1 ≤ p < ∞`,
as specializations and make the a.e. representative conventions explicit. Establish
equimeasurability, layer cake, all `Lᵖ` norm comparisons that reduce
to equimeasurability, order preservation, `Lᵖ` contraction for `1 ≤ p < ∞`, and the
Hardy–Littlewood inequality. I5 adds the BV and `W¹,¹` gradient comparisons after I4.

For positive-volume convex bodies construct surface area from GMT's perimeter and show
agreement with Hausdorff boundary area. Relate outer parallel volume
`(K + r • closedBall 0 1)` to that surface area by the right derivative at zero. Prove the
needed boundary charts and volume limit. For a lower-dimensional nonempty compact convex
set, ambient volume and perimeter are zero. Prove separately that the outer-parallel right
derivative is `2 Hⁿ⁻¹(K)` when its affine dimension is `n−1`, and zero when its affine
dimension is smaller. In particular it need not equal perimeter or topological boundary
area for a degenerate body. Derive the isoperimetric inequality for positive-volume convex
bodies from Brunn–Minkowski. Prove the sharp
isodiametric inequality `|E| ≤ ω_n (diam E / 2)^n` for measurable bounded sets using their
closed convex hull and the difference-body argument. The volume-maximizing convex-body
case has ball rigidity; supply the equality proof. For measurable sets, equality implies
agreement a.e. with a ball of radius `diam E / 2`. A converse also requires the diameter
bound: arbitrary null modifications can increase diameter.

## I3 — Sharp periodic inequalities and curve energy

Prove the sharp periodic Wirtinger inequality for real- and finite-dimensional
inner-product-valued AC functions on `[0,T]`, `T > 0`, with equal endpoint values,
mean zero, and square-integrable derivative:

```
∫₀ᵀ ‖f‖² ≤ (T / (2π))² ∫₀ᵀ ‖f'‖².
```

Equality holds exactly for `f(t) = a cos(2πt/T) + b sin(2πt/T)` on the interval. Include
the canonical periodic `W¹,²` formulation and its AC representative, translation of
the mean, rescaling to any parameter interval, and complex-valued specialization.
Build the Fourier/weak-derivative integration-by-parts and Parseval comparison or the
equivalent variational argument, rather than assuming the smooth inequality extends
automatically to AC functions or that its equality cases survive density.

For any closed AC plane curve with square-integrable derivative, define signed area by
the real boundary integral `½∫ (x y' − y x')`. Prove

```
4π |signedArea γ| ≤ T ∫₀ᵀ ‖γ'‖².
```

Give the complete equality analysis: equality means a constant curve, or a translated
circle traversed once at constant angular speed with one of the two orientations.
Prove the derivative relation a.e. and solve it using the AC FTC. The mean-zero
Wirtinger equality alone also permits ellipses, so the area/energy equality needs its
own argument. Compare this signed integral with DifferentialGeometry 5.6's winding-weighted
area. Use GMT G6's Jordan index theorem to prove that for a simple curve it is `σ` times
the actual volume of the inside, where `σ ∈ {−1,1}` is its orientation sign.

For a rectifiable curve use GMT G1's arclength parametrization. Prove the constant-speed
energy identity. Prove invariance of trace, length, and inside under increasing continuous
onto reparametrizations. Define geometric signed area for a continuous BV parameter via
DifferentialGeometry's rectifiable line integral and the AC arclength factorization;
prove independence of the factorization, agreement with the derivative integral for AC
parameters, and sign reversal under decreasing continuous onto reparametrizations.
Do not use a derivative integral of the original non-AC parameter. The resulting length inequality uses actual total variation;
it is not an inequality involving the energy of an arbitrarily supplied parametrization.

## I4 — Sharp Euclidean perimeter inequality and ball rigidity

Establish the full finite-volume finite-perimeter inequality stated above, including
unbounded sets. Supply the smooth/bounded case, the volume-and-perimeter approximation
passage using GMT G4, and the exact constants from ball volume and surface measure. Give
equivalent normalized forms, scaling laws, and explicit formulas for balls. State versions
with relative perimeter only when their domain terms and hypotheses are separately proved;
the headline is whole-space Euclidean perimeter.

Prove **rigidity at finite-perimeter regularity**. For every positive finite-volume set
of finite perimeter, equality holds iff it agrees a.e. with a ball. This includes
nonsmooth, disconnected, and unbounded measurable representatives. Supply the following
structural targets and their deduction of rigidity:

- For a Lebesgue-measurable `E` with `0 < |E| < ∞` and `P(E) < ∞`, and every unit
  direction `e`, write `S_e E` for I2's Steiner symmetral. If `P(S_e E) = P(E)`,
  prove that for almost every `y ∈ e⊥` the section
  `{t : ℝ | y + t • e ∈ E}` agrees a.e. in one-dimensional Lebesgue measure with a
  possibly empty interval (an `OrdConnected` subset of `ℝ`). Use `volume` on the
  orthogonal subspace `e⊥ = (ℝ ∙ e)ᗮ` and prove that `(y,t) ↦ y + t • e` is a
  measure-preserving linear equivalence from `e⊥ × ℝ`, with its product volume, to the
  ambient Euclidean space, with `‖y + t • e‖² = ‖y‖² + t²`.
  Prove the section measurability and Fubini transport from Borel representatives:
  replacing `E` by a volume-a.e. equal set preserves this conclusion for each fixed
  direction. The exceptional set of `y` may depend on `e`. Build the finite-perimeter
  slicing theorem and its reduced-boundary/normal comparison on almost every line from
  GMT G2–G5. Prove the localized perimeter comparison with Steiner symmetrization,
  including the equality implication that the set of slices with more than two essential
  boundary points has zero transverse measure. These are I4 targets; perimeter
  nonincrease obtained solely by approximation does not supply them.
- Prove the essential-convexity theorem: if a Lebesgue-measurable set of positive finite
  volume has the preceding interval-section property in every unit direction, it agrees
  a.e. with a convex set. Take the set of volume-density-one points as the representative.
  For any two distinct such points, use the direction of the segment joining them:
  density at the endpoints makes almost all nearby parallel sections meet `E` near both
  ends, and the interval property then gives density one along the segment. Prove the
  quantitative tube estimates needed for this argument; it uses only the exceptional set
  for that direction. Obtain a compact convex representative `K` with
  nonempty interior, proving boundedness from convexity and positive finite volume and
  proving that closure changes it only on a null boundary. Transport volume and perimeter
  along this a.e. equality using GMT G5.
- Isoperimetric equality for `E` forces `P(S_e E) = P(E)` for every `e`: combine I2's
  volume preservation and perimeter nonincrease with the already established inequality
  for `S_e E`. Thus the structural targets reduce the equality case to `K`. For
  `B = closedBall 0 1`, prove concavity of `f(t) = |K + t • B|^(1/n)` on `t ≥ 0`
  from I1, proving the Minkowski-sum identity
  `(1−θ) • (K + s • B) + θ • (K + t • B) = K + ((1−θ)s + θt) • B`
  for `0 ≤ θ ≤ 1` and `s,t ≥ 0` using convexity. I2's outer-parallel derivative gives
  `f'(0+) = P(K) / (n |K|^((n−1)/n))`. Isoperimetric equality makes this derivative
  `ω_n^(1/n)`. The concave tangent bound and the Brunn–Minkowski lower bound then force
  `f(t) = f(0) + t ω_n^(1/n)` for every `t ≥ 0`. Apply I1's compact convex equality
  theorem at `t > 0` to deduce that `K` is a translate and positive dilation of `B`.
  Use the nullity of the sphere to obtain the stated a.e. equality with an open ball;
  prove the converse from ball formulas and a.e. invariance.

Smooth equality plus approximation, or convergence of successive symmetrizations to a
ball without perimeter loss, does not supply these structural conclusions. The necessary
interval-section equality condition is stated in Cagnetti–Colombo–De Philippis–Maggi,
§1.2 and Theorem A, cited below. Equality in a single Steiner step does not in general
imply that `E` is a translate of `S_e E`. Every further object introduced in the rigidity
proof must receive its basic restriction, invariance, and comparison API.

Give the topological-frontier corollary for every bounded set, and the more
general finite-volume version, with `Hⁿ⁻¹(frontier E)` on the right. An infinite frontier
measure makes the extended inequality immediate; the finite case uses GMT G5's boundary
criterion and `P(E) ≤ Hⁿ⁻¹(frontier E)`. In the finite case prove that the frontier is
Lebesgue-null and hence `E` is `NullMeasurableSet` by comparison with its open interior;
the corollary therefore requires no separate measurability hypothesis. Supply its sharp-constant equality consequences:
for positive finite volume and finite frontier measure, equality implies agreement a.e.
with a ball. Do not assert literal ball equality for arbitrary representatives or a
converse for every null modification: topological frontier is sensitive to null sets.
Give exact ball rigidity for bounded regular open sets when equality holds, proving the
passage from a.e. equality to point-set equality under that hypothesis.

Specialize to bounded Lipschitz and `C¹` domains with actual Hausdorff surface area and
their classical outward normals. The surface-area/perimeter identification is GMT G6's
comparison, not a new definition chosen to make this inequality immediate.

## I5 — Sharp BV Sobolev and its equality cases

Prove BV Pólya–Szegő from GMT's scalar coarea and I4's set inequality: Schwarz rearrangement
does not increase total variation. For every nonnegative `u ∈ W¹,¹(ℝⁿ)`, `n ≥ 2`, prove
that its Schwarz rearrangement `u*` has an `L¹` weak gradient `g`, with

```
D(u*) = g · volume,       ∫ ‖g‖ ≤ ∫ ‖∇u‖.
```

Supply an approximation argument that excludes singular concentration, with the following
targets owned by I5:

- For nonnegative integrable Lipschitz functions `h`, prove that `h*` has a Lipschitz
  representative, using I1's Brunn–Minkowski inequality and the inclusions between
  neighborhoods of superlevel sets. Identify the a.e. Rademacher gradients with the
  canonical weak gradients, supplying the required integration-by-parts comparison.
  Prove the convex-integrand Pólya–Szegő estimate
  `∫ Φ(‖∇h*‖) ≤ ∫ Φ(‖∇h‖)` for finite-valued convex nondecreasing
  `Φ : [0,∞) → [0,∞)` with `Φ(0) = 0`, whenever the right side is finite. Supply the
  distribution-function and critical-level comparisons needed to derive this estimate
  from GMT G2's Lipschitz coarea, GMT G5's comparison of superlevel perimeter with level
  surface measure, Jensen's inequality, and I4.
  Explicitly, for `μ_h(t) = |{h > t}|` and
  `m_h(t) = ∫_{{h=t} ∩ {∇h≠0}} ‖∇h‖⁻¹ dHⁿ⁻¹`, prove
  `m_h(t) ≤ −μ_h'(t)` for a.e. `t > 0`, and prove that the critical part of the level
  surface has zero `Hⁿ⁻¹` measure for a.e. `t`. For `h*`, prove equality
  `m_h*(t) = −μ_h'(t)` using the nullity of critical values for its one-dimensional
  Lipschitz radial profile. Prove that `s ↦ s Φ(P/s)` is nonincreasing for `s > 0`
  and `P ≥ 0`, so Jensen and the level-perimeter inequality combine in the required
  direction. Treat empty levels and zero denominators separately.
- For nonnegative `u ∈ W¹,¹`, construct nonnegative smooth Lipschitz approximants
  `u_j = u * ρ_j` using nonnegative compactly supported smooth probability kernels.
  Prove convergence in `W¹,¹`, the convolution identity for weak gradients, and Jensen's
  bound `∫ Φ(‖∇u_j‖) ≤ ∫ Φ(‖∇u‖)`. Use a de la Vallée Poussin integrability lemma
  to choose such a `Φ` with `Φ(t)/t → ∞` and `∫ Φ(‖∇u‖) < ∞`.
- Apply the Lipschitz convex-integrand estimate both to this superlinear `Φ` and to
  `Φ(t) = t`. Prove the resulting uniform-integrability estimate: for every `ε > 0`
  there is a finite `T > 0` such that
  `∫_A ‖∇u_j*‖ ≤ T |A| + ε` for every measurable `A` and every `j`.
  I2's `L¹` contraction gives `u_j* → u*` in `L¹`. GMT G4's local lower semicontinuity
  therefore gives `|D(u*)|(U) ≤ T |U| + ε` for every open `U`. Use outer regularity of
  volume to cover volume-null sets by open sets of arbitrarily small volume and deduce
  `|D(u*)| ≪ volume`. GMT G3's measure-valued derivative and Radon–Nikodym comparison
  then supply `D(u*) = g · volume`. The identity `|D(u*)| = ‖g‖ · volume` and the
  global BV comparison prove `∫ ‖g‖ ≤ ∫ ‖∇u‖`. This explicitly excludes singular
  concentration in the limit.

The convex-integrand estimates and uniform-integrability lemmas are supporting theory
for the `p = 1` result; a general Orlicz-space development is outside this roadmap. I2's
equimeasurability supplies `u* ∈ L¹`; GMT G3's BV-to-Sobolev comparison then gives a
canonical `TauCeti.W1p` element with weak gradient `g`.

Also establish the radial-profile comparison. Pin the representative for `r > 0` by
`v(r) = sup {t > 0 | ω_n r^n < |{u > t}|}`, with value zero for an empty set and the
extended nonnegative supremum until finiteness is proved. Superlevel volumes are finite
for `t > 0` by the `L¹` bound. Prove agreement with I2's Schwarz rearrangement, finiteness
of `v(r)` for `r > 0`, and absolute continuity of `v` on every compact subinterval of
`(0,∞)`. Derive this from the established radial `W¹,¹` representative by the weak
derivative comparison on annuli, including vanishing of tangential gradient components;
build the radial restriction and composition lemmas against PDE's canonical
weak-derivative API here. Use monotonicity to transport a.e. agreement with the continuous
profile to pointwise agreement with the pinned `v`. Establish

```
n ω_n ∫₀^∞ |v'(r)| r^(n−1) dr ≤ ∫ ‖∇u‖.
```

Use GMT G2's polar integration to identify
`g(x) = v'(‖x‖) • (x / ‖x‖)` a.e. away from zero. Prove
`r^(n−1) v(r) → 0` as `r ↓ 0` from the weighted derivative bound and `n ≥ 2`.
As corollaries of the established identity `D(u*) = g · volume`, deduce that the
derivative has no jump part across spheres, no Cantor part over a null set of radii,
and no contribution at the origin. Extend the norm comparison to real-valued inputs
by rearranging `|u|` and proving its weak-gradient bound using the canonical
positive-part/truncation calculus and
`|u| = u⁺ + (−u)⁺`. A BV bound or strict smooth approximation alone does not exclude
a singular derivative in the rearranged limit. These comparisons use I4 and are not
inputs to its proof.

For `n ≥ 2`, `p = n/(n−1)`, prove on the whole space

```
‖u‖_p ≤ (n ω_n^(1/n))⁻¹ |Du|(ℝⁿ),                u ∈ BV(ℝⁿ).
```

Derive it from coarea, layer cake, and I4, with the integral Minkowski inequality and
its equality analysis made explicit. Prove membership in `Lᵖ`; the norm expression alone
is not sufficient. Equality for a nonzero real-valued `u` holds exactly when
`u = c χ_(ball a r)` a.e., with `c ≠ 0`, `r > 0`. Establish the nesting and proportionality
of superlevel sets and the absence of sign cancellation required for this classification;
do not merely classify each level set separately as a ball. Treat the zero function
separately. Give the `W¹,¹` corollary and nonattainment by nonzero `W¹,¹` functions, as well
as normalized smooth near-extremizers approximating a ball indicator. This is the sharp
endpoint complement to PDE's general Sobolev embedding theory.

## I6 — Full planar Jordan theorem and compatibility

Prove the geometric and parameterized statements in the scope section, using actual
Lebesgue area, Hausdorff length, and total variation. Supply the equivalence of the
parameterized hypotheses with the existing `IsJordanCurve` trace plus rectifiability.
Derive area positivity and finiteness, length positivity and finiteness, and the
orientation-independent inequality.

Give both compatibility results: the planar finite-perimeter specialization via GMT G6,
and the AC/arclength area–energy specialization via I3 and Green's theorem. They must
use the same inside and the same length. For the finite-perimeter equality argument,
prove that the Jordan inside is regular open, that equality a.e. with a ball implies
actual equality of the inside with the ball, and hence that its frontier is the circle.
For the curve argument, transport equality of the arclength trace back to the original
curve, without imposing constant speed on that original parametrization. Prove the
converse for every continuous rectifiable simple parametrization of a circle.

## Acceptance examples and completion

Prove the disk/circle and `n`-ball formulas with the exact constants; an ellipse and a
rectangle have strict planar inequality unless the domain is a disk (in particular every
nondegenerate ellipse with unequal axes and every rectangle are strict). Compute annulus
area and perimeter and prove strictness. Give separated unions of two positive-radius
balls as strict examples. Check a punctured ball: it has equality for perimeter and a.e.
ball rigidity, while literal ball equality fails. Check a circle traversed twice: its
trace is a circle, but its parameterized length and winding-weighted area reflect
multiplicity and it is not a simple-curve equality case. Include a circle parametrized
by `φ(t) = (t + C(t))/2` on `[0,1]`, where `C` is the Cantor–Lebesgue function constructed
in GMT's acceptance examples. Prove that `φ` is an increasing homeomorphism which is not
AC, and that the resulting circle parameter is continuous, simple, rectifiable and not
AC. This tests the full geometric statement beyond AC parameters. Verify the BV
extremizers and smooth near-extremizers.

Completion requires the full inequality **and** equality statements, the geometric bridges,
and the reusable APIs of I1–I5. An outer-neighborhood-volume inequality without the
perimeter comparison, a smooth-only theorem, a supplied area/perimeter identity, or an
equality hypothesis assumed as input does not discharge the target. Proofs must use the
ordinary kernel-checked Mathlib/Tau Ceti foundation, with no additional mathematical axioms,
and the final declarations must have explicit integrability and finiteness hypotheses.

## References and existing formalizations

- Francesco Maggi, [*Sets of Finite Perimeter and Geometric Variational Problems*](https://cvgmt.sns.it/paper/1880/),
  for finite-perimeter isoperimetry and symmetrization. GMT's roadmap owns the underlying
  measure and boundary theory.
- Cagnetti–Colombo–De Philippis–Maggi,
  [*Rigidity of equality cases in Steiner's perimeter inequality*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.1639),
  §1.2 and Theorem A, for the necessary interval-section condition used in I4. Translation
  rigidity for a single symmetrization needs additional hypotheses.
- Bianchi–Gardner–Gronchi–Kiderlen,
  [*The Pólya–Szegő inequality for smoothing rearrangements*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.09833),
  Theorem 5.8, Theorem 6.3 and Corollary 6.5, for the Lipschitz convex-integrand estimate,
  Sobolev membership, and the gradient comparison, including the uniform-integrability
  argument at the `p = 1` endpoint. I5 requires only Schwarz rearrangement at that endpoint.
- [The Brunn–Minkowski exposition by Terence Tao](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2011/09/16/the-brunn-minkowski-inequality-for-nilpotent-groups/)
  includes the Euclidean Prékopa–Leindler argument.
- Joel Tropp's [*Lectures on Convex Geometry*](https://tropp.caltech.edu/notes/Tro18-Lectures-Convex-LN.pdf),
  Lecture 8, supplies the parallel-volume and intrinsic-volume normalization, including
  lower-dimensional convex bodies.
- [Freek Wiedijk's isoperimetric entry and HOL Light proof](https://www.cs.ru.nl/~freek/100/hol.html#43)
  provide a classical planar comparison: arbitrary rectifiable simple closed curves and
  geometric circle equality.
- **Humanfia's [public Lean source archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/humanfia-lab/lean-eval-source/tree/main/problems/isoperimetric_inequality)**
  contains a higher-dimensional bounded-set inequality using volume and Hausdorff measure
  of the topological frontier. It is relevant prior work for I1 and I4; the canonical
  finite-perimeter theory and equality cases remain intrinsic requirements here.
- **Jonathan Ho's [isoperimetric repository](https://github.com/hojonathanho/isoperimetric)**,
  also distributed [in LeanPool](https://github.com/LeanPool/lean-pool/tree/main/LeanPool/Isoperimetric),
  develops Prékopa–Leindler, Brunn–Minkowski, and outer-neighborhood volume inequalities.
  These are relevant to I1–I2. A neighborhood inequality still requires its bridge to
  geometric perimeter and rigidity.
- **[kim-em/isoperimetric](https://github.com/kim-em/isoperimetric)** is a parallel development
  directed at the classical isoperimetric theorem. Cite and examine its mathematical
  results as existing work; neither its implementation nor any chosen dependencies
  prescribe this roadmap's design or discharge a milestone without its full requirements.

# Roadmap: finite étale covers of punctured spectra and local purity

**Summary.** This roadmap builds the theory of finite étale covers of the punctured spectrum of a
Noetherian local ring and proves purity for regular local rings (Stacks, Lemma 58.21.3 (0BMA);
SGA 2, Exposé X, Théorème 3.4): for a regular local ring `A` of dimension `≥ 2`, every finite
étale cover of the punctured spectrum of `A` extends to a finite étale cover of `Spec A`. It then
globalizes: over a Noetherian scheme, a finite étale cover of an open `U` extends across every
point of the complement at which purity holds (Stacks, Lemma 58.21.6 (0EY7)). The route is that
of Stacks, Sections 58.19–58.21: finite normal algebras over a local ring, completion, full
faithfulness of restriction to a hypersurface section, the local Lefschetz extension theorem
(Lemma 58.20.7 (0BLM)), and an induction on the dimension whose base case uses miracle flatness
for a Cohen–Macaulay target and the discriminant of a finite free algebra. Mathlib has schemes,
finite and étale morphisms, the categories `MorphismProperty.Over`, regular local rings, adic
completion, local cohomology, discriminants and trace forms; Tau Ceti has finite étale schemes over
a base and regular local rings as domains; SchemeAndStackFoundations specifies depth,
Cohen–Macaulay rings, Serre's criterion, henselian pairs and formal completion. None of them has
finite étale covers of punctured spectra or local purity.

These results are the common input of two roadmaps:
[PurityOfBranchLocus](../PurityOfBranchLocus/README.md) (Zariski–Nagata purity of the branch locus,
Stacks 0BMB) and [AbhyankarLemma](../AbhyankarLemma/README.md) (extension of covers unramified in
codimension one and Abhyankar's lemma for a regular divisor, Stacks 0EYE–0EYH).

| Layer | Title | What it delivers |
|---|---|---|
| [0](#layer-0-commutative-algebra-inputs) | Commutative algebra inputs | miracle flatness for a Cohen–Macaulay target, the discriminant criterion for étaleness of a finite free algebra |
| [1](#layer-1-finite-étale-covers-of-punctured-spectra) | Finite étale covers of punctured spectra | purity for a local ring, finite normal algebras, completion, restriction to a hypersurface, the local Lefschetz extension theorem |
| [2](#layer-2-local-purity-and-extension) | Local purity and extension | purity for regular local rings, spreading out from a local scheme, extension across points where purity holds |

```text
Mathlib + Tau Ceti → Layer 0 → Layer 1 → Layer 2
SchemeAndStackFoundations §§0.6, 0.9, 0.14, 0.17, 2.7, 4.7–4.8, 4.13 ──→ Layers 0, 1, 2
PurityOfBranchLocus §0.3 (0AFS) ─────────────────────────────────────────────→ Layer 2 §2.1
```

The §0.3 regular-local localization targets of PurityOfBranchLocus are independent of local
purity. Their target-level order is §0.3 → this roadmap's §2.1 → PurityOfBranchLocus §2.1;
the whole-roadmap arrows do not reverse this prerequisite order.

The end theorems are `IsLocalRing.purityHolds_of_isRegularLocalRing` and
`Algebra.etale_of_finiteNormal_of_isRegularLocalRing` (0BMA, §2.1), and
`finiteEtale_extend_of_purity` (0EY7, §2.2).

**This roadmap owns** the punctured spectrum of a local ring, the restriction of finite étale
covers to it, and the notion "purity holds for `A`" (Stacks, Section 58.20 (0BM7)); Stacks, Lemmas
58.20.1 (0BM8), 58.20.2 (0BLK), 58.20.3 (0BM9), 58.19.3 (0BLH), 58.20.4 (0BLL), 58.19.4 (0BLI),
58.17.1 (0EL8), 58.19.6 (0BM6), 58.19.7 (0BLJ) and 58.20.7 (0BLM), and Algebraic and Formal

(Discriminants, Lemma 49.3.1 (0BJF), affine form); purity for regular local rings (Lemma 58.21.3

## Conventions

1. Rings are commutative. Schemes and morphisms are Mathlib's `Scheme` and `Scheme.Hom` in a fixed
   universe `u`. Hypotheses such as Noetherian, normal and regular are written on the statement
   that uses them, never folded into a definition.
2. **Statement form.** Every target is stated in Mathlib's and Tau Ceti's vocabulary, against the
   pinned libraries, and that statement is the target. Where the Stacks Project states the same
   result in a different form, the target cites the tag, carries Mathlib's `@[stacks XXXX]`
   attribute, and says how the two forms correspond; targets with no Stacks counterpart are marked
   *API*.
3. *Normal* is Stacks, Definition 10.37.11 (00GV), written in Mathlib's vocabulary: every
   localization at a prime is a domain and integrally closed,
   `∀ p : Ideal B, p.IsPrime → IsDomain (Localization.AtPrime p) ∧ IsIntegrallyClosed (Localization.AtPrime p)`.
   For a local ring it is `IsDomain` together with `IsIntegrallyClosed`.
4. The dimension of a local ring is `ringKrullDim`; depth is SchemeAndStackFoundations'
   `IsLocalRing.depth`.
5. **Finite normal algebras.** A *finite normal algebra* over a Noetherian local domain `A` is a
   finite `A`-algebra `B` that is normal (Convention 3) **and torsion free as an `A`-module**
   (Mathlib `Module.IsTorsionFree A B`). Stacks, Lemma 58.20.3 (0BM9) and Lemma 58.21.3 (0BMA),
   part (2), state no torsion-freeness condition, and as written both are false: for `A` normal
   local of dimension `≥ 2`, `B = A × A/𝔪` is finite and normal, `Spec B → Spec A` is étale over
   the punctured spectrum (its second factor lies over the closed point), and `B` is not flat over
   `A`; it is not `Γ(V, 𝒪_V)` for any finite étale `V` over the punctured spectrum. Torsion
   freeness removes exactly the factors supported at the closed point, and the Stacks proofs then
   apply unchanged. §1.2 and §2.1 state the corrected forms and record the counterexample as a
   Check.
6. Names: ring-level statements live in the `Algebra` and `IsLocalRing` namespaces; scheme-level
   statements in `AlgebraicGeometry`. The suggested forms are in `TauCetiRoadmap.LocalPurity`.

## Layer 0: commutative algebra inputs

### 0.1 Miracle flatness

Prove `flat_of_isCohenMacaulay` (Stacks, Lemma 10.128.1 (00R4)): a local homomorphism `R → S` of
Noetherian local rings with `R` regular, `S` Cohen–Macaulay and
`ringKrullDim S = ringKrullDim R + ringKrullDim (S ⧸ (maximalIdeal R).map (algebraMap R S))` makes
`S` flat over `R`. Prove `flat_of_normal_dim_two` (*API*): a finite injective local homomorphism
`A → B` with `A` regular local of dimension two and `B` a normal local domain makes `B` flat over
`A` (`B` has dimension two by going down and the dimension formula, satisfies `(S_2)` by
`serre_normality_criterion`, and so is Cohen–Macaulay). ModularCurves §4D's miracle flatness
between regular local schemes of equal dimension is the case of `flat_of_isCohenMacaulay` with `S`
regular.
*Needs:* SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.17 (`Ring.IsCohenMacaulay`,
`Ring.IsCohenMacaulay.of_isRegularRing`, `isCohenMacaulay_iff_forall_satisfiesSerreS`), §4.13
(`serre_normality_criterion`); Mathlib `Module.Flat`, `IsRegularLocalRing`, `Algebra.HasGoingDown`.

**Checks.**
- `test_flat_needs_cohenMacaulay`: `k⟦x, y⟧ → k⟦x, y⟧[z]/(z², xz, yz)` is finite and local with
  target of dimension two and depth zero, so not Cohen–Macaulay, and it is not flat.

### 0.2 The discriminant criterion

Prove `Algebra.etale_iff_traceForm_nondegenerate`: a finite-dimensional algebra `B` over a field
`K` is étale (`Algebra.Etale K B`) iff its trace form `Algebra.traceForm K B` is nondegenerate.
This is the field case in the proof of Discriminants, Lemma 49.3.1 (0BJF); for `B` a field it is
Mathlib's `traceForm_nondegenerate_tfae` (0BIL), and the general case reduces to it through the
decomposition of a reduced finite-dimensional algebra into fields and the nilpotence of the
nilradical. Prove `Algebra.etale_iff_isUnit_discr` (Stacks, Lemma 49.3.1 (0BJF), affine form over
a local base): for a local ring `A`, a finite free `A`-algebra `B` and a basis `b` of `B` over `A`,
`Algebra.Etale A B ↔ IsUnit (Algebra.discr A b)`. The proof base-changes `b` to the closed fibre
(`Algebra.TensorProduct.basis`; the trace matrix commutes with base change) and uses that a finite
free algebra over a local ring is étale iff its closed fibre is. Prove the localization form
`Algebra.isUnit_discr_localization_iff` (*API*): for a prime `𝔭` of `A`, the image of
`Algebra.discr A b` in `A_𝔭` is a unit iff `B_𝔭` is étale over `A_𝔭` (`Algebra.trace_localization`).
*Needs:* Mathlib `Algebra.discr`, `Algebra.traceForm`, `traceForm_nondegenerate_tfae`,
`Algebra.trace_localization`, `Algebra.TensorProduct.basis`, `Algebra.Etale`, `Module.Free`.

**Checks.**
- `test_discr_dual_numbers`: for a field `k` of characteristic `≠ 2`, `k[x]/(x²)` with basis
  `1, x` has discriminant `0` and is not étale over `k`.
- `test_discr_quadratic`: for `A = ℤ_(p)` with `p` odd and `d` a unit of `A`, `A[x]/(x² − d)` with
  basis `1, x` has discriminant `4d`, a unit, and is étale over `A`; for `d = p` the discriminant
  is `4p` and it is not étale.

## Layer 1: finite étale covers of punctured spectra

Throughout, `(A, 𝔪)` is a Noetherian local ring, `X = Spec A` and `U = X ∖ {𝔪}`.

### 1.1 The punctured spectrum and purity for a local ring

Define `IsLocalRing.puncturedSpectrum A : (Spec A).Opens`, the complement of
`IsLocalRing.closedPoint A`, and the restriction functor from finite étale schemes over `Spec A`
to finite étale schemes over `U` as pullback along its inclusion. Define
`IsLocalRing.PurityHolds A`: the restriction functor is essentially surjective (Stacks, Section
58.20 (0BM7), the definition in the first paragraph; Stacks assumes `A` Noetherian, and every
statement using the definition does). API: `puncturedSpectrum_eq_iSup_basicOpen` (`U` is the union
of the basic opens `D(x_i)` for generators `x_i` of `𝔪`), `isCompact_puncturedSpectrum`, and
`restrictPunctured_faithful`: for `IsLocalRing.depth A ≥ 1` the restriction functor is faithful.
*Needs:* Tau Ceti `FiniteEtaleScheme`; Mathlib `MorphismProperty.Over.pullback`,
`PrimeSpectrum.basicOpen`, `IsLocalRing.closedPoint`; SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.17
(`IsLocalRing.depth`).

### 1.2 Finite normal algebras

Prove `spec_sections_of_depth` (Stacks, Lemma 58.20.1 (0BM8)): a finite morphism `π : Y ⟶ X` with
`IsLocalRing.depth 𝒪_{Y,y} ≥ 2` at every closed point `y` of `Y` is isomorphic over `X` to the
spectrum of `Γ(π⁻¹ U, 𝒪_Y)`. Prove `extends_iff_sections_finiteEtale` (Stacks, Lemma 58.20.2
(0BLK)): for `IsLocalRing.depth A ≥ 2` and `V` finite étale over `U`, `V` is the restriction of a
finite étale scheme over `X` iff `Γ(V, 𝒪_V)` is finite étale over `A`. Prove `finiteNormalEquiv`
(Stacks, Lemma 58.20.3 (0BM9), **with the correction of Convention 5**): for `A` a normal local
domain of dimension `≥ 2`, let `FiniteNormalPuncturedEtaleAlg A` be the full subcategory of
`CommAlgCat A` on finite normal, torsion-free `A`-algebras `B` such that
`Algebra.IsEtaleAt A 𝔮` for every prime `𝔮` of `B` not lying over `𝔪`, with ordinary algebra
homomorphisms as morphisms. Global sections reverses arrows, so the target is an
**anti-equivalence** `FEt U ≌ (FiniteNormalPuncturedEtaleAlg A)ᵒᵖ`, not an equivalence to the
unopposed algebra category. Its quasi-inverse takes the spectrum of an algebra and restricts it
to `U`; identify both composites with the identity. Moreover, `V` is the restriction of a finite
étale scheme over `X` iff `Γ(V, 𝒪_V)` is étale over `A`. When replacing the prototype `FEt U`
by Tau Ceti's newer `FiniteEtaleScheme U` (not at this roadmap's pin), identify the carrier
equivalence and show that it commutes with restriction and pullback; otherwise the sections
functor does not transport automatically.
*Needs:* §1.1; SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.17 (depth), §4.13 (`serre_normality_criterion`);
Mathlib `integralClosure`, `IsIntegralClosure`, `Algebra.IsEtaleAt`.

**Checks.**
- `test_closed_point_factor`: for `A = k⟦x, y⟧`, the algebras `A` and `A × A/𝔪` are finite and
  normal and are étale at every prime not lying over `𝔪`; only `A` is torsion free, and `A × A/𝔪`
