## Layer 2: local purity and extension

### 2.1 Purity for regular local rings

Prove `IsLocalRing.purityHolds_of_isRegularLocalRing` and
`Algebra.etale_of_finiteNormal_of_isRegularLocalRing` (Stacks, Lemma 58.21.3 (0BMA)): for `A`
regular local of dimension `d ≥ 2`, (1) `IsLocalRing.PurityHolds A`; (2) **with the correction of
Convention 5**, every finite normal `A`-algebra `B` (torsion free) with `Algebra.IsEtaleAt A 𝔮` for
every prime `𝔮` of `B` not lying over `𝔪` satisfies `Algebra.Etale A B`. The proof is by induction
on `d`, as in Stacks: (1) and (2) are equivalent by `finiteNormalEquiv`, since `A` is normal
(PurityOfBranchLocus §0.3 gives `IsRegularRing A` from `IsRegularLocalRing A`, then
SchemeAndStackFoundations §4.13 `IsRegular.isNormal` applies to `Spec A`). For `d = 2`, localize
at each maximal ideal `𝔮` of `B` and apply the **general** `flat_of_isCohenMacaulay` to
`A → B_𝔮`, not the finite-local helper: `B_𝔮` need not be finite as an `A`-module. It is a
normal local domain of dimension two by integrality, going down and the dimension formula; its
closed fibre over `A` has dimension zero because `B` is finite, and normality gives `(S₂)`,
hence Cohen–Macaulayness in dimension two. The finite-local `flat_of_normal_dim_two` remains a
separate corollary, not the localization argument. `Module.flat_of_isLocalized_maximal` now gives
flatness of `B` over `A`, hence freeness (`Module.free_of_flat_of_isLocalRing`); for a basis `b`,
if `Algebra.discr A b` were not a unit
it would lie in a prime `𝔭` minimal over it, of height at most one by Krull's principal ideal
theorem (`Ideal.height_le_one_of_isPrincipal_of_mem_minimalPrimes`), so `𝔭 ≠ 𝔪`, and
`Algebra.isUnit_discr_localization_iff` (§0.2) contradicts étaleness over `A_𝔭`; so `B` is étale by
`Algebra.etale_iff_isUnit_discr`. For `d ≥ 3`, an element `f ∈ 𝔪 ∖ 𝔪²` gives `A ⧸ Ideal.span {f}`
regular of dimension `d − 1` (Tau Ceti `TauCeti.IsRegularLocalRing.quotient_span_singleton`), and
`finiteEtale_extend_of_hypersurface` (§1.4) lifts the inductive extension; regular local rings
have depth `d` by a local parameter induction using
`TauCeti.IsRegularLocalRing.quotient_span_singleton` and the SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.17
depth/regular-element API. This local Cohen–Macaulay consequence does not assume
`IsRegularRing A` before 0AFS is available.
*Needs:* §§0.1, 0.2, 1.2, 1.4; PurityOfBranchLocus §0.3 (0AFS);
SchemeAndStackFoundations §§0.17, 4.13; Tau Ceti
`TauCeti.IsRegularLocalRing.quotient_span_singleton`; Mathlib `Ideal.height_le_one_of_isPrincipal_of_mem_minimalPrimes`,
`Module.free_of_flat_of_isLocalRing`, `Module.flat_of_isLocalized_maximal`.

**Checks.**
- `test_closed_point_factor_not_etale`: for `A = k⟦x, y⟧` and `B = A × A/𝔪`, `B` is finite and
  normal, étale at every prime not lying over `𝔪`, and not étale over `A`; it is excluded by
  torsion freeness.
- `test_purity_needs_regular`: over a field `k` of characteristic `≠ 2`, for
  `A = k[x², xy, y²]` localized at the origin, the cover given by `k[x, y]` localized at the origin
  is finite étale over the punctured spectrum and does not extend to a finite étale cover of
  `Spec A`; so `IsLocalRing.PurityHolds A` fails for this normal, non-regular local ring of
  dimension two.

### 2.2 Spreading out and extension across points where purity holds

Prove `spread_from_localScheme` (Limits, Lemmas 32.20.3 (0BQ5) and 32.20.4 (0EY3)): for a scheme
`S`, a retrocompact open `U ⊆ S` and `s ∉ U`, with `V = Spec 𝒪_{S,s} ×_S U`, finitely presented
schemes over `U` and over `Spec 𝒪_{S,s}` whose restrictions to `V` are isomorphic glue to a finitely
presented scheme over an open `U' ⊇ U ∪ {s}`, uniquely up to shrinking `U'`; and if both are
separated, proper, finite or étale, the glued scheme has the same property after shrinking `U'`.
The proof applies SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.9 `finite_presentation_limits` to `Spec 𝒪_{S,s}` as
the limit of its affine open neighbourhoods. Prove `finiteEtale_extend_of_purity` (Stacks, Lemma
58.21.6 (0EY7)): for a Noetherian scheme `X` and an open `U ⊆ X` with
`IsLocalRing.PurityHolds 𝒪_{X,x}` for every `x ∉ U`, restriction from finite étale schemes over
`X` to finite étale schemes over `U` is essentially surjective. The proof is Noetherian induction
on the complement, extending across the generic point of an irreducible component of `X ∖ U` by
`spread_from_localScheme`. Prove `restrictOpen_fullyFaithful_of_depth` (*API*): for a locally
Noetherian scheme `X` and an open `U` with `IsLocalRing.depth 𝒪_{X,x} ≥ 2` for every `x ∉ U`,
restriction from finite étale schemes over `X` to finite étale schemes over `U` is fully faithful
(a finite étale scheme over `X` is the relative spectrum of a finite locally free algebra, whose
sections extend uniquely across `X ∖ U` by SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.6 `coherent_hartogs`).
Prove the corollary `finiteEtale_extend_of_regular_codimTwo` (*API*): for a locally Noetherian
scheme `X` and an open `U` such that `𝒪_{X,x}` is a regular local ring of dimension `≥ 2` for every
`x ∉ U`, restriction is essentially surjective. On each affine open it is
`finiteEtale_extend_of_purity` with `purityHolds_of_isRegularLocalRing`, and the local extensions
glue by `restrictOpen_fullyFaithful_of_depth` (regular local rings of dimension `d` have depth `d`).
*Needs:* §2.1; SchemeAndStackFoundations §§0.6, 0.9, 0.17; Mathlib `IsNoetherian`,
`IsLocallyNoetherian`, `Scheme.Opens`, `IsAffineOpen`.

# Roadmap: Markov chains and renewal processes

Develop the theory of homogeneous Markov chains on countable state spaces and
ordinary renewal processes with nonnegative i.i.d. increments. The main results
are recurrence classification, convergence to equilibrium, the elementary and
Blackwell renewal theorems, renewal equations, and the limiting excess-life law.

Build the surrounding library: transition kernels and path laws, stopping-time
identities, return cycles and occupation measures, renewal measures and convolution,
and the connections between exponential renewals and Poisson processes.
`README.md` is the definitive specification; `Suggested.lean` records selected
interfaces and is not an exhaustive checklist.

Suggested homes: `TauCeti/Probability/MarkovChain/` and
`TauCeti/Probability/Renewal/`. Extend existing modules for shared process and
kernel facts.

## Scope and dependencies

This roadmap owns homogeneous discrete-time chains on nonempty countable measurable
spaces with measurable singletons, ordinary renewal processes with nonnegative i.i.d.
increments, and their connections to homogeneous Poisson processes.

| Material | Owner and interface consumed here |
| --- | --- |
| Scalar probability laws, their convolution and moment identities | [StandardDistributions](../StandardDistributions/README.md), Layers 0–5 and 7; use the existing Poisson, exponential, geometric, Gaussian and uniform APIs |
| Markov-chain path laws and recurrent excursion decomposition | [Exchangeability](../../Completed/Exchangeability/README.md), Layer 8; consume `TauCeti.Probability.markovChainLaw` and the excursion API, and connect them to the return-time conventions below |
| Random measures, point measures, Poisson construction and characterization | [PointProcesses][pp], Layers 0, 1 and 4 |
| Restriction, mapping, independent marking, thinning and superposition | [PointProcesses][pp], Layer 6 |

Layer 7 specifies the temporal Poisson interfaces consumed here. Build missing

## Conventions

**Chains.** Write `κ : ProbabilityTheory.Kernel S S` with `IsMarkovKernel κ`.
The state space has `[Countable S] [Nonempty S] [MeasurableSpace S]` and
`[MeasurableSingletonClass S]`. No topology on the sample space is required.
Write $p_n(x,y) := (\kappa^n)(x,\{y\})$ and
$\mathbb P_x := \mathrm{markovChainLaw}(\delta_x,\kappa)$.
Distributions are probability measures, not a second probability-vector structure.
Give adapters to `PMF` and, for finite state spaces, row-stochastic matrices.

On a path $X$, distinguish the first entrance
$H_A := \inf\{n\geq 0:X_n\in A\}$ from the first return
$T_x^+ := \inf\{n\geq 1:X_n=x\}$; the empty infimum is infinity.
Use `WithTop ℕ` and Mathlib's `hittingAfter`, with starting indices zero and one.
Return-time means are extended nonnegative integrals; nonreturn with positive
probability gives infinite mean. Set $m_x := \mathbb E_x T_x^+$ and
$r_x := (m_x^{-1})_{\mathbb R}$, taking the inverse in `ℝ≥0∞` before `toReal`.
This gives $r_x=0$ when $m_x=\infty$; it avoids Lean's real-valued integral of
a nonintegrable function being mistaken for an expectation.

**Renewals.** Let $T_1,T_2,\ldots$ be measurable i.i.d. variables in $[0,\infty)$,
with common probability law $F$ and $F(\{0\})<1$. Zero increments are allowed.
Set

$$
S_0 := 0,\qquad S_n := \sum_{i=1}^n T_i,\qquad
N_t := \sum_{n\geq1}\mathbf1_{\{S_n\leq t\}}.
$$

Use `ℝ≥0` for time and increments and an extended count before proving finiteness.
The Lean sequence is indexed from zero: `T 0` represents $T_1$ and `S n` sums
`Finset.range n`. The artificial $S_0$ is not counted, but genuine arrivals at zero
are counted; thus $N_0$ need not vanish. Define $N_t$ as a natural number on the
full-measure nonexplosion event and give it the value zero on the exceptional event.
Prove measurability and invariance of laws under this choice.

Write $\mu := \int t\,F(dt)\in(0,\infty]$, $r := (\mu^{-1})_{\mathbb R}$ and
$m(t) := \mathbb E N_t$. Distinguish the law $F$ from its cdf
$F_{\leq}(t) := F([0,t])$. Convolution integrals include both endpoints of $[0,t]$.
The renewal measure is
$U := \sum_{n\geq0} F^{*n}$ with $F^{*0}:=\delta_0$; hence
$U([0,t])=1+m(t)$, including when $F$ has an atom at zero.

**Point processes.** Retain multiplicities. Use measurable maps into `Measure E`
and the integer-valued/point-measure interfaces of PointProcesses. A sigma-finite
intensity need not be finite on compact sets; use the locally finite carrier only
under its additional hypotheses. The homogeneous temporal Poisson specialization
has no points at zero and counts $(0,t]$, which agrees with the renewal convention
when increments are strictly positive.

## Layer 0: Kernels, laws and simulation

1. Prove that countable transition weights $p(x,y)\geq0$ with row sums one
   determine a unique Markov kernel. Provide singleton evaluation, `PMF`
   conversion, finite stochastic-matrix conversion, and compatibility with
   composition, powers and pushforward of initial laws.
2. Extend `markovChainLaw` with time-$n$ marginal $\kappa^n\circ\nu$,
   arbitrary finite-time cylinder probabilities, uniqueness from the initial law
   and prefix recursion, and measurable dependence on the starting state.
   Expose the path-law kernel $x\mapsto\mathbb P_x$ needed by Layer 1.
3. For a measurable process on any probability space, prove equivalence between
   its path law being `markovChainLaw ν κ` and the finite-path product formula.
   Transfer statements through this equality of laws; do not impose a canonical
   sample space on users.
4. Construct a measurable countable-state sampler from a uniform variable on
   $[0,1)$ for each probability law, and a sampler measurable jointly in the
   current state and the uniform variable for a kernel. Include finite and
   infinite enumerations, zero weights, and endpoint conventions. Prove that
   iterating the sampler with independent uniforms gives `markovChainLaw`.

Completion examples: an absorbing two-state chain, a deterministic cycle, and
a nearest-neighbor random walk on the integers. Check that kernel powers recover
their elementary transition laws.

## Layer 1: Deterministic and strong Markov properties

1. Define the filtration-relative one-step property by conditional expectations
   of bounded measurable real test functions. Include adaptation. Prove its
   equivalence to the prefix-law recursion for the natural filtration, with the
   initial law specified separately. Derive the multi-step conditional law using
   kernel powers.
2. Prove the path-valued Markov property: conditional on information through time
   $n$, the shifted future has law $\mathbb P_{X_n}$. Provide both bounded-test
   identities and event identities, with their measurability hypotheses.
3. Prove the strong Markov version for a stopping time
   $\tau:\Omega\to\mathrm{WithTop}\,\mathbb N$, on $\{\tau<\infty\}$,
   conditional on the stopped sigma-algebra. Values of $X_\tau$ and the shifted
   path outside that event must not affect the assertion. Give the simpler
   almost-surely finite specialization.
4. Provide stopping-time and measurability lemmas for entrances, returns,
   successive visits, shifted paths and concatenation. Starting at $x$, prove
   that $\mathbb P_x(T_x^+<\infty)=1$ implies infinitely many returns almost
   surely, by iterating the strong Markov property. This supplies the hypothesis
   of the existing excursion decomposition. Derive the i.i.d. return-gap law
   and prove that each gap equals excursion length plus one. Relate its existing
   visit-time convention to `hittingAfter` only on the event where the visit exists.

## Layer 2: State classification and occupation

1. Define reachability by $\exists n,\ p_n(x,y)>0$, communication by mutual
   reachability, and irreducibility by communication of every pair. Prove the
   equivalence-relation API, closed-class characterization and restriction to a
   closed class as a Markov kernel on a subtype.
2. Define recurrence by $\mathbb P_x(T_x^+<\infty)=1$, transience by its failure,
   positive recurrence by recurrence and $m_x<\infty$, and null recurrence by
   recurrence and $m_x=\infty$. Write $\rho_x:=\mathbb P_x(T_x^+<\infty)$,
   $V_x:=\sum_{n\geq1}\mathbf1_{\{X_n=x\}}$ for the number of positive-time visits,
   and $G(y,x):=\sum_{n\geq0}p_n(y,x)\in[0,\infty]$. Prove the dichotomy:
   $\mathbb P_x(V_x\geq k)=\rho_x^k$ for every $k\geq0$, so a recurrent $x$ has
   $V_x=\infty$ $\mathbb P_x$-almost surely, while for a transient $x$ the variable
   $1+V_x$ is geometric with parameter $1-\rho_x$ and
   $\mathbb E_xV_x=\rho_x/(1-\rho_x)<\infty$. Prove the Green-function identities
   $G(x,x)=(1-\rho_x)^{-1}$ in `ℝ≥0∞` and
   $G(y,x)=\mathbb P_y(H_{\{x\}}<\infty)\,G(x,x)$, and deduce

   $$x\text{ recurrent}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \sum_{n\geq0}p_n(x,x)=\infty.$$

   For every initial law $\nu$, prove that the total number of visits
   $\sum_{n\geq0}\mathbf1_{\{X_n=x\}}$ has $\mathbb P_\nu$-mean
   $\mathbb P_\nu(H_{\{x\}}<\infty)\,G(x,x)$; hence visits to a transient state are
   almost surely finite from every initial law.
3. If $x$ reaches $y$ and $x$ is recurrent, prove that $y$ is recurrent and
   $\mathbb P_x(H_{\{y\}}<\infty)=\mathbb P_y(H_{\{x\}}<\infty)=1$. Deduce that
   recurrence and transience are class properties, that a recurrent class is
   closed, and that an irreducible recurrent chain satisfies
   $\mathbb P_\nu(H_{\{y\}}<\infty)=1$ for every initial law $\nu$ and every $y$.
   Prove that positive and null recurrence are class properties, using the
   occupation limits of item 4. Every finite closed communicating class is
   positive recurrent. On a finite nonempty state space there is a closed
   communicating class, and the chain enters the union of closed communicating
   classes almost surely.
4. For $V_y(n):=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{X_k=y\}}$, prove
   $V_y(n)/n\to r_y$ almost surely under $\mathbb P_y$. Under an arbitrary
   initial law $\nu$, the limit is
   $\mathbf1_{\{H_{\{y\}}<\infty\}}r_y$. Prove the corresponding expectation
   limit $\mathbb P_\nu(H_{\{y\}}<\infty)r_y$ by bounded convergence.
   Supply the infinite-mean i.i.d. strong-law consequence by truncation, rather
   than using a finite-mean theorem outside its hypotheses.

Check a finite cycle (positive recurrent), simple symmetric random walk on
$\mathbb Z$ (null recurrent), and the walk with right-step probability
$p\in(0,1)\setminus\{1/2\}$ (transient). Prove the return/hitting estimates needed
for these classifications; their recurrence labels are not assumptions.

## Layer 3: Equilibrium and coupling

1. Use `Kernel.Invariant` for stationarity and `Kernel.IsReversible` for detailed
   balance. Prove their countable singleton formulas and the finite matrix
   adapters. Consume the existing implication from reversibility to invariance.
2. For an irreducible chain, prove that an invariant probability exists exactly
   when the chain is positive recurrent. Construct it by expected occupation in
   one return cycle, prove normalization and invariance, and prove uniqueness
   and $\pi(\{x\})=1/m_x$. No aperiodicity is needed for this result.
3. Define $d(x)$ as the gcd of positive return lengths, with gcd of the empty
   set zero; a chain is aperiodic when every state has period one.
   Prove constancy on communication classes. For $d(x)=1$, prove
   eventual positivity of all return lengths; for an irreducible aperiodic
   chain, prove eventual positivity of transitions between each fixed pair.
   Prove the additive-semigroup lemma: a subset of positive integers closed under
   addition and with gcd one contains every sufficiently large integer.
4. Build independent product chains, prove their path laws and stationary-product
   laws, and prove irreducibility and aperiodicity of the product of two
   irreducible aperiodic chains. For two chains with the same transition kernel,
   construct the meeting-time coupling and show that following one chain after
   their first meeting preserves the other marginal law. Bound the total-variation
   distance of item 5 at time $n$ by twice the probability of not having met
   by $n$. Whenever the product kernel is irreducible and recurrent, prove that
   the two coordinates meet almost surely for arbitrary initial laws, by Layer
   2.3 applied to the product chain. For an irreducible aperiodic positive
   recurrent kernel, the product kernel has invariant probability
   $\pi\otimes\pi$ and is therefore positive recurrent.
5. Measure total variation with Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.tvDist`
   ([mathlib4 #37730][tv-pr]), which takes values in $[0,2]$ on probability
   measures. On a countable space prove
   $\mathrm{tvDist}(\mu,\mu')=\sum_y|\mu(\{y\})-\mu'(\{y\})|$; the coupling bound
   of item 4 reads $\mathrm{tvDist}\leq2\,\mathbb P(\text{no meeting by }n)$.
   For an irreducible aperiodic positive recurrent chain and every initial
   probability $\nu$, prove $\mathrm{tvDist}(\nu\kappa^n,\pi)\to0$.
   For an irreducible aperiodic null recurrent or transient chain, prove
   $(\nu\kappa^n)(\{y\})\to0$ for each $y$ by cases on the product chain. If
   it is transient, $(\nu\kappa^n)(\{y\})^2$ is the probability that the product
   chain started from $\nu\otimes\nu$ is at $(y,y)$ at time $n$, which tends to
   zero by Layer 2.2. If it is recurrent, then $y$ is recurrent because
   $p_n(y,y)^2\leq p_n(y,y)$, hence null recurrent. Couple the chains
   started from $\nu$ and $\nu\kappa^i$ to get
   $|(\nu\kappa^n)(\{y\})-(\nu\kappa^{n+i})(\{y\})|\to0$ for each fixed $i$. By the strong Markov property at the first visit to $y$
   after time $n$, prove
   $\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^k(\nu\kappa^{n+i})(\{y\})\leq(1+\mathbb E_yV_y(k))/k$
   uniformly in $n$; Layer 2.4 makes the right side small. Do not turn the
   pointwise limit into total-variation convergence to the zero measure.
6. Formalize the hard-core sampling example on a finite nonempty simple graph.
   For activity $\lambda>0$, the state space consists of independent vertex
   sets and $\pi(I)\propto\lambda^{|I|}$. A step chooses a vertex uniformly,
   deletes it, then inserts it with probability $\lambda/(1+\lambda)$ when
   no neighbor is occupied. Prove detailed balance, irreducibility, aperiodicity
   and convergence. Specialize $\lambda=1$ to uniform sampling of independent sets.

## Layer 4: Ordinary renewal processes and renewal measures

1. Construct the i.i.d. increments on product space and transfer to arbitrary
   realizations. Prove measurability of arrivals and counts, $S_n\to\infty$
   almost surely, and simultaneous finiteness of $N_t$ for all finite $t$.
   Establish monotonicity, right continuity, and the inverse relations
   $N_t\geq n\iff S_n\leq t$ for $n\geq1$ and
   $S_{N_t}\leq t<S_{N_t+1}$ on the nonexplosion event.
2. Prove finite moments of every positive integer order for $N_t$ on each
   bounded time interval, using a comparison with increments in $\{0,a\}$
   with $a>0$ and positive chance of $a$. This supplies the local integrability
   needed below even when $\mu=\infty$.
3. Define convolution powers and $U$ as above using existing measure convolution.
   Prove $U$ is finite on bounded intervals, $U=\delta_0+F*U$, and
   $m(t)=\sum_{n\geq1}F^{*n}([0,t])$. Prove monotonicity and right continuity
   of $m$. Extend $m$ by zero on negative times and identify the restriction
   of its Stieltjes measure to the half-line with $U-\delta_0$. In particular,
   the measure has mass $m(0)$ at zero; it is not determined by increments
   $m(t)-m(s)$ for $0\leq s<t$ alone.
4. Work out deterministic increments $T_i=a>0$ and increments in $\{0,a\}$
   with $\mathbb P(T_i=a)=q\in(0,1]$. Give the count law and renewal function,
   including $m(0)=(1-q)/q$. For exponential increments of rate $\lambda>0$,
   derive the Poisson count law and $m(t)=\lambda t$ from scalar sum laws.

## Layer 5: Renewal limits

1. Prove $N_t/t\to r$ almost surely and $m(t)/t\to r$ as $t\to\infty$,
   including $\mu=\infty$. Prove uniform integrability of $N_t/t$ for
   $t\geq1$ using the comparison from Layer 4; also obtain $L^1$ convergence.
2. Under finite second moment and strictly positive variance $\sigma^2$ of
   $T_1$, identify its extended mean with a finite positive real $\mu$ and prove

   $$\frac{N_t-t/\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{t/\mu^3}}
     \ \xrightarrow{\mathrm{law}}\ \mathcal N(0,1).$$

   State this using Mathlib convergence in distribution, with a real-time limit
   or the equivalent assertion along every sequence $t_n\to\infty$.
   Build the inversion and rounding estimates from the scalar i.i.d. CLT.
3. Define lattice laws by support in $a\mathbb N$ for some $a>0$, without a
   translation. Prove existence and uniqueness of a maximal span when the law
   is lattice and $F(\{0\})<1$. For maximal span $a$, prove the lattice
   Blackwell limit

   $$m(a(n+1))-m(an)\longrightarrow ar.$$

   Set $q:=1-F(\{0\})$ and let $L$ have the conditional law of $T_1/a$
   given $T_1>0$. Build the chain on
   $C:=\{j\in\mathbb N:\mathbb P(L>j)>0\}$ that moves from $j>0$ to
   $j-1$ and from zero to a fresh $L-1$. Prove irreducibility, identify its
   return-time law as the law of $L$, and show its period is one by maximality
   of the span. Let $(R_n)_{n\geq0}$ be this chain started at zero, and prove
   $U(\{an\})=\mathbb P_0(R_n=0)/q$ for every $n\geq0$.
   Prove $\mathbb E L=\mu/(aq)$, including infinite mean. Layer 3 then
   yields the displayed limit. These identities account for zero-increment
   clusters rather than treating the original interarrival law as strictly positive.
4. For nonlattice $F$, prove, for every $h\geq0$,
   $m(t+h)-m(t)\to hr$. This includes infinite mean. Prove the local renewal bound
   $U([t,t+h])\leq U([0,h])$ for $t,h\geq0$ by conditioning at the first
   arrival at or after $t$, counting $S_0$ in $U$. Prove the limit by Feller's
   argument (vol. II, Chapter XI): by the local bound, every sequence $t_k\to\infty$
   has a subsequence along which the translates of $U$ by $-t_k$ converge vaguely
   on $\mathbb R$ to a Radon measure $\eta$ with $\eta=\eta*F$. Prove that for
   nonlattice $F$ every such measure with $\sup_x\eta([x,x+1])<\infty$ is a
   multiple $c$ of Lebesgue measure.
   Identify $c=r$ from $\int_{[0,t]}\mathbb P(T_1>t-s)\,U(ds)=1$ for $t\geq0$:
   pass to the limit by dominated convergence, using the local bound, when
   $\mu<\infty$, and by Fatou's lemma, giving $c=0$, when $\mu=\infty$.
   The local bound alone does not establish the limit.

## Layer 6: Renewal equations and excess life

1. For measurable real $h$ bounded on each $[0,t]$, define
   $(h*F)(t):=\int_{[0,t]}h(t-s)\,F(ds)$.
   Prove measurability, local boundedness, linearity, the convolution associativity
   needed for iteration, and absolute convergence of $\sum_{n\geq0}(h*F^{*n})(t)$
   uniformly on bounded time intervals. Use Layer 4's local finiteness of $U$.
2. Prove existence and uniqueness among measurable locally bounded solutions of
   $g=h+g*F$, with $g=h*U$. Give the equivalent formula $g=h+h*(U-\delta_0)$.
   At zero, prove $g(0)=h(0)/(1-F(\{0\}))$. Recover the renewal equation for
   $m$ with forcing $F_{\leq}$.
3. Prove the key renewal theorem for every nonnegative, nonincreasing,
   Lebesgue-integrable $h:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$: for nonlattice $F$,
   $(h*(U-\delta_0))(t)\to r\int_0^\infty h(s)\,ds$.
   Deduce the same limit for $h*U$ using $h(t)\to0$.
   Use Layer 5's uniform renewal-increment bound and prove the step-function
   approximations needed to justify the limit. Direct Riemann integrability in
   greater generality is outside scope.
4. Define the excess $E_t:=S_{N_t+1}-t$, prove measurability, and show that
   $e_x(t):=\mathbb P(E_t\leq x)$ solves the renewal equation with forcing
   $h_x(t):=F_{\leq}(t+x)-F_{\leq}(t)$ for each $x\geq0$.
   Prove the excess-tail representation with forcing
   $\overline F(t+x):=\mathbb P(T_1>t+x)$, which is nonincreasing.
   For nonlattice $F$ with finite mean, derive

   $$\mathbb P(E_t\leq x)\longrightarrow
     \frac1\mu\int_0^x \mathbb P(T_1>s)\,ds.$$

   Prove that the limit is a probability distribution and identify its density
   as $\overline F(x)/\mu$. Apply Layer 6.3 to the tail forcing, not directly to
   $h_x$, which need not be nonincreasing. For $\mu=\infty$, lattice or not,
   prove $\mathbb P(E_t\leq x)\to0$ for every finite $x$, using
   $\{E_t\leq x\}\subseteq\{N_{t+x}-N_t\geq1\}$ and Layer 5.3 or 5.4.

## Layer 7: Connections to Poisson processes

Consume the temporal specialization of [PointProcesses][pp], Layers 0, 1 and 4:
measurable point measures on the half-line, their count and arrival-time maps,
and the equivalence between a homogeneous Poisson random measure of intensity
$\lambda\,dt$, Poisson stationary independent increments of its count process,
and i.i.d. exponential gaps. Use $\lambda>0$, no point at zero, simplicity and
nonexplosion. PointProcesses Layer 6 supplies marking, thinning and superposition.

General enumeration of point measures, Poisson construction and uniqueness,
Laplace functionals, mapping and marking theorems, and stationary Palm renewal
laws belong to PointProcesses. The targets here connect its temporal API to
Layers 0–5:

1. Map the Layer 4 renewal construction with exponential increments to
   $\sum_{n\geq1}\delta_{S_n}$. Prove equality of count processes and path
   laws with the PointProcesses construction, including measurability of the
   conversions. Derive $N_t/t\to\lambda$ from Layer 5.
2. For $\lambda>0$ and a nonexplosive, nondecreasing, right-continuous
   integer-valued process with measurable coordinates and $N_0=0$, prove the microscopic characterization:
   it is a rate-$\lambda$ Poisson process exactly when it has stationary
   independent increments and, as $h\downarrow0$,

   $$\mathbb P(N_h=1)=\lambda h+o(h),\qquad
     \mathbb P(N_h\geq2)=o(h).$$

   Use the scalar Poisson limit theorem and control the probability that any
   subdivision interval contains two or more jumps. The conclusion includes
   simplicity. State path hypotheses on one event of probability one.
3. Prove that $(N_{t+s}-N_t)_{s\geq0}$ has the original Poisson-process law
   and is independent of the natural history at each deterministic $t$.
   Extend independence from cylinders to the generated sigma-algebra. For
   $\Delta>0$, identify $N_{n\Delta}$ as the Layer 0 chain with transition
   law $i+\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda\Delta)$.
4. As compatibility checks, derive the temporal thinning and superposition
   identities through the PointProcesses operations. Bernoulli thinning with
   $p\in[0,1]$ gives independent processes of rates $p\lambda$ and
   $(1-p)\lambda$; adding independent processes adds their rates. Treat
   zero rate as the identically zero process, separately from the positive-rate
   exponential-gap characterization.

## Completion checks

Every new definition must expose measurability, evaluation and extensionality
lemmas, the relevant law-transfer facts, and compatibility with the underlying
Mathlib or TauCeti object. Every milestone includes the examples and boundary
cases in its specification. Check in particular:

* A deterministic cycle has an invariant probability but does not converge to
  it from a point mass unless its length is one; aperiodicity belongs in Layer 3.5.
* The absorbing chain and the recurrent one-state chain distinguish entrance
  at zero from first return at one. A transient missing return has infinite mean.
* Deterministic renewal increments expose endpoint and lattice-span conventions;
  increments in $\{0,a\}$ expose the genuine atom of the count at time zero.
* The nonlattice excess-life limit has total mass one precisely under the
  finite-mean hypothesis used in Layer 6.4.
* The temporal Poisson adapters count $(0,t]$, agree with exponential-renewal
  counts, and preserve independence under thinning, including $p=0,1$.

Compilation of the suggested signatures checks their types, not the truth of
their admitted theorems or completion of these milestones.

TauCetiRoadmap/MassFormula:
# Roadmap: counting totally ramified extensions of a local field, and Serre's mass formula

The [local fields and ramification roadmap](../LocalFieldsRamification/README.md) builds the
arithmetic of a finite extension of a non-archimedean local field: total ramification, Eisenstein
generators, monogenicity, the different and the discriminant, and the tame criterion. This
roadmap is that theory's counting consumer. It asks how *many* such extensions there are, and
proves the answer — the **mass formula** of [Serre 1978]: inside a fixed separable closure, the
totally ramified extensions of degree `n` of a local field `K` satisfy

```text
∑_{L ∈ σ_K(n)} q^{-c(L)} = n,          c(L) = d(L) − n + 1
```

where `q` is the residue cardinality and `d(L)` the discriminant exponent, together with its
isomorphism-class form `∑_{M} 1 / (#Aut_K(M) · q^{c(M)}) = 1`. It is the local counting statement
behind mass heuristics for global field counting, and nothing like it is upstream.

The machinery the count needs is not ramification theory, and that is what makes this a separate
roadmap: a **quantitative Newton estimate** over a complete discrete valuation ring (Mathlib's
`hensels_lemma` is that estimate over `ℤ_[p]` only, and `HenselianLocalRing` lifts a simple root
with no distance bound, hence no count), the **lattice-index scaling law** for Haar measure over
such a ring (Mathlib's `Measure.addHaar_image_linearMap` is real-vector-space only), and the
parametrization of `σ_K(n)` by the **Eisenstein region** of coefficient space. The first two are
stated over an arbitrary discrete valuation ring (complete, for the Newton estimate; with finite
residue field, for the index) and are reusable well outside this roadmap.

Suggested home: `TauCeti/NumberTheory/LocalField/MassFormula/`, with the two general layers
placed by subject instead: quantitative Newton lifting in
`TauCeti/RingTheory/DiscreteValuationRing/`, the lattice index in
`TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FreeModule/` beside Mathlib's `ℤ` analogue, and the Haar scaling law in
`TauCeti/MeasureTheory/Group/`.

## Scope

This roadmap owns the **counting** of totally ramified extensions of a local field: the set
`σ_K(n)` as an object, the wild exponent `c` as its weight, the analytic and measure-theoretic
machinery that evaluates the count, and the mass formulas with the finiteness, convergence and
orbit statements that accompany them.

It does not own the arithmetic of the individual extension. **Total ramification, Eisenstein
generators, monogenicity, the different, the discriminant, and the tame criterion belong to the
[local fields and ramification roadmap](../LocalFieldsRamification/README.md)**, which is where
they are specified and where their API accrues; the contract this roadmap consumes from it is
listed below. It also does not own higher ramification groups, Herbrand functions or Hasse–Arf
(same roadmap); local class field theory; adic or Huber-theoretic geometry over `K`, which is the
[adic spaces roadmap](../../Completed/AdicSpaces/README.md); or archimedean local fields, which
`IsNonarchimedeanLocalField` excludes and which never enter.

## Standing conventions

Pinning these matters more than usual: the objects are junk-tolerant by design, and an
implementor who picks a different model will not be able to state the summit.

- **The base field.** `K` carries
  `[Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [UniformSpace K] [IsUniformAddGroup K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`.
  Spell the hypotheses out; do not bundle them. Mathlib's instances then supply
  `IsDiscreteValuationRing 𝒪[K]`, `Finite 𝓀[K]`, `CompactSpace 𝒪[K]`, `CompleteSpace K` and
  `IsAdicComplete 𝓂[K] 𝒪[K]` by `inferInstance`; consume them, never re-prove them.
- **The residue cardinality is written inline as `Nat.card 𝓀[K]`**, and the residue
  characteristic as `ringChar 𝓀[K]`; `q` below abbreviates the former in prose only, as `σ_K n`
  and `c L` abbreviate `totallyRamifiedOfDegree K n` and `wildExponent L`. Do not introduce a `q`
  or `p` abbreviation. A weight `q^{−k}` is spelled `1 / (Nat.card 𝓀[K] : ℝ≥0∞) ^ k`.
- **Extensions live inside a separable closure.** An extension is a term of
  `IntermediateField K (SeparableClosure K)`. This is Serre's setting and it is load-bearing: in
  equal characteristic `p` the inseparable Eisenstein polynomials (`X^p − π`) must not be counted,
  and working inside `SeparableClosure K` excludes them by construction rather than by a side
  hypothesis. ⚠ The consumed roadmap states its ramification theory for a finite extension `L/K`
  as such; the bridge to subextensions of `SeparableClosure K` is this roadmap's Layer 0, which
  installs the consumed `finiteIntermediateField*` adapters.
- **The discriminant exponent is the consumed one.** `d L` is the consumed
  `discriminantExponent`, totalized over arbitrary subextensions by the wrapper
  `intermediateFieldDiscriminantExponent`; for a totally ramified extension its different
  exponent `v_L(𝔡)` and the valuation of its discriminant ideal in `K` agree, since the residue
  degree is `1` (the consumed `discriminantExponent_eq_inertiaDegree_mul_differentExponent`). Do
  not introduce a second discriminant.
- **Junk is tolerated, `0 < n` is not optional.** For `L` infinite over `K`, or for `n = 0`, these
  definitions take junk values. Every statement about `σ_K n` therefore carries `0 < n`, and
  membership in `σ_K n` is what makes a statement honest. Do not add finiteness hypotheses to
  definitions to avoid junk; add them to theorems.
- **Sums are in `ℝ≥0∞`.** Theorems 1 and 2 are stated with `∑'` valued in `ℝ≥0∞`, where the
  possibly infinite sum needs no convergence side condition and equality with `n` (resp. `1`)
  already encodes convergence. The convergence remark is a *separate* statement over `ℝ` as
  `Summable`; state both and relate them, and do not merge them.
- **Representative sets are a predicate, not a quotient.** `IsRepresentativeSet n R` says that
  `R ⊆ σ_K n` and every `L ∈ σ_K n` is `K`-isomorphic to exactly one member of `R`; Theorem 2
  quantifies over every such `R`. This is Serre's phrase verbatim and avoids `Quotient.lift`
  well-definedness obligations for `c` and `#Aut`.
- **The coefficient space and its measure.** A monic degree-`n` polynomial is its coefficient
  vector `a : Fin n → K`, with `a i` the coefficient of `X ^ i`. The measure is the additive Haar
  measure of `Fin n → K` normalized so that the integer box `Fin n → 𝒪[K]` has volume `1`; by
  uniqueness of Haar measure this is the product of the normalized coordinate measures, but the
  product structure is needed only inside proofs, so neither `Measure.pi` nor σ-finiteness appears
  in any statement.
- **Valuations in an extension are `IsDiscreteValuationRing.addVal`**, `ℕ∞`-valued. No topology on
  `L` enters any counting statement or estimate: completeness of the ring of integers of `L` is
  the algebraic `IsAdicComplete`, and all estimates are `addVal` estimates — the spelling the
  consumed `addVal_sum_eisenstein_powerBasis` exports. The consumed structure adapters put the
  canonical topology and valuation on a subextension carrier only inside the Layer 0 wrappers;
  no statement here hypothesizes a second uniform structure.

## The build, in layers

The ordering is the dependency order. As each layer makes the next layer's *types* expressible in
`TauCeti/`, its milestones go into `Suggested.lean` (with `sorry`).

### Layer 0: the counting invariants

- **`σ_K(n)`**, the set of subextensions of `SeparableClosure K` that are totally ramified of
  degree `n` over `K`, built on the consumed `IsTotallyRamified` through the wrapper
  `intermediateFieldIsTotallyRamified`, which installs the consumed `finiteIntermediateField*`
  adapters and carries the comparison theorem the consumer contract requires. With the bridge
  lemmas the count needs: `σ_K(1) = {K}`; every member is `K⟮x⟯` for `x` a root of an
  Eisenstein polynomial of degree `n`, which is the consumed
  `isTotallyRamified_iff_exists_eisenstein_generator` transported to this setting; conversely,
  `K⟮x⟯ ∈ σ_K(n)` for every root `x ∈ SeparableClosure K` of a degree-`n` Eisenstein polynomial
  over `𝒪[K]`, which transports the consumed statement that an Eisenstein root generates a
  totally ramified extension in which it is a uniformizer (that roadmap's README item, cited
  above) and is the direction Layer 3's root-count identity and Layer 4's orbit count apply; and
  membership is preserved by the image of any `K`-embedding into `SeparableClosure K`, a
  corollary of the converse.
- **The wild exponent `c L := d L + 1 − n`** in truncated `ℕ`-subtraction, where `d` is the
  consumed `discriminantExponent` through its wrapper `intermediateFieldDiscriminantExponent`.
  Mathlib's `pow_sub_one_dvd_differentIdeal`, read through the consumed `differentExponent` and
  `discriminantExponent_eq_inertiaDegree_mul_differentExponent` (`e = n`, `f = 1`), gives
  `n − 1 ≤ d L`, which makes the truncation faithful, so `c` is Serre's nonnegative integer; with
  the consumed tame criterion it gives `c L = 0 ⟺ ¬ (ringChar 𝓀[K] ∣ n)`. State both here as the
  corollaries of Mathlib and the consumed facts that they are, not as fresh developments.
- **Invariance of `c` under `K`-isomorphism.** A `K`-isomorphism carries integral bases to
  integral bases with the same discriminant, so `d`, hence `c`, is an invariant of the class.
  The arithmetic invariance is the consumed `discriminantExponent_eq_of_algEquiv` (with
  `differentExponent_eq_of_algEquiv` beside it); the target here is only its transport through
  the wrapper to `wildExponent`, junk case included, which is the regrouping Theorem 2 runs
  along.
- **The box and cube corollaries of the power-basis orthogonality.** The consumed
  `addVal_sum_eisenstein_powerBasis` gives, at an Eisenstein generator `ξ` of degree `n`, that
  the terms of `∑_{i<n} c_i ξ^i` have pairwise distinct valuations — the `i`-th is
  `n · addVal(c_i) + i`, distinct modulo `n` — so no cancellation is possible and the valuation
  of the sum is the minimum of the terms'. The targets here are its family-level consequences: a
  ball of the ring of integers is a box in power-basis coordinates — the ball `v_L ≥ r` is
  `∏_{i<n} π^{⌈(r − i)/n⌉} · 𝒪[K]`, that is `c_i ∈ 𝓂[K] ^ ((r − i) ⌈/⌉ n)` for every `i`, with
  the `ℕ`-truncated ceiling division `(r − i) ⌈/⌉ n = (r − i + n − 1) / n`, so the `i`-th factor
  is `𝒪[K]` itself when `r ≤ i` — and at a radius `r = n · ρ` it is the cube with every factor
  `π^ρ · 𝒪[K]`. These are the workhorse of Layers 2 and 3.

### Layer 1: quantitative Newton lifting over a complete discrete valuation ring

The Newton estimate is stated for an arbitrary complete (`IsAdicComplete`) discrete valuation
ring, since nothing in it uses the local field; the local-field case is an instance. The local
constancy of the root count is stated over `K` and quantifies over Layer 0's `σ_K n`.

- **Newton iteration with an estimate.** If `addVal (F y₀) > 2 · addVal (F' y₀)`, the iteration
  `y ↦ y − F y / F' y` converges to a root `z` of `F` with
  `addVal (z − y₀) ≥ addVal (F y₀) − addVal (F' y₀)`, and `z` is the unique root in that ball.
  Uniqueness is the algebraic statement that two roots `z ≠ z'` of `F` satisfy
  `addVal (z − z') ≤ addVal (F' z)`, from the Taylor expansion of `F` at `z`; it uses no
  completeness, and it is the form the local fibre count of Layer 3 applies. ⚠ This is Mathlib's
  `hensels_lemma` (`Mathlib/NumberTheory/Padics/Hensel.lean`), stated there over `ℤ_[p]` only and
  in norm spelling, over an arbitrary complete discrete valuation ring in `addVal` spelling;
  `HenselianLocalRing` lifts a simple root modulo the maximal ideal and yields no distance bound.
  The estimate, not the existence, is what Layer 3 consumes.
- **Local constancy of the root count.** For a monic `f` over `𝒪[K]`, separable over `K`, there is
  a threshold `T`, depending on `f` and `n` only, such that every monic `g` with
  `g.coeff i − f.coeff i ∈ 𝓂[K]^T` for all `i` has exactly as many roots in `L` as `f` does, for
  every `L ∈ σ_K n`. The route is a Bézout
  certificate `U · f + V · f' = β` over `𝒪[K]` bounding the order of `f'` at every near-root
  uniformly, then Newton lifting in both directions.
- ⚠ **Not Krasner's lemma.** Mathlib's Krasner (`Analysis/Normed/Field/Krasner.lean`) is a
  normed-field statement about a *single* root generating an extension; what Layer 3 needs is a
  *count* that is uniform on a coefficient ball, which Krasner does not give. Keep the two apart
  and do not route this layer through the normed setting.

### Layer 2: lattices, index, and the Haar scaling law

The index is stated for an arbitrary discrete valuation ring with finite residue field of
cardinality `q`, for the same reason; it uses no completeness. The scaling law is over `K`, whose
`𝒪[K]` is such a ring.

- **The index of an image lattice.** For a matrix `M` over `𝒪[K]` with `Associated M.det (π^k)`,
  the quotient of the integer box `Fin n → 𝒪[K]` by its image under `M` has exactly `q^k`
  elements. Via `Submodule.quotientEquivPiSpan` (Smith normal form over the principal ideal ring
  `𝒪[K]`), the quotient splits into residue rings of the diagonal coefficients, whose product is
  associated to `M.det`. Mathlib's `AddSubgroup.index_eq_natAbs_det` is the `ℤ` analogue.
- **The scaling law.** For the Haar measure `μ` of `Fin n → K` normalized on the integer box,
  `μ (M '' S) = q^{−k} · μ S` for every measurable `S` — the non-archimedean analogue of
  `Measure.addHaar_image_linearMap`. State it in two forms. For `S` the box or any ball it is the
  index, with no side condition, and that is the form Layer 3 consumes. For general `S`,
  `μ (M '' ·)` is again a Haar measure, so the constant is read off the box by uniqueness of Haar
  measure (`isAddLeftInvariant_eq_smul_of_regular`), at the price of the hypothesis `μ.Regular`,
  which Mathlib's `addHaarMeasure` carries by instance and which no Layer 3 statement needs.
- **Boxes and balls.** The image lattice of a diagonal matrix is the coordinate box with `i`-th
  factor `π^{e i} · 𝒪[K]`, of volume `q^{−∑ e i}`; a ball is a translate of the lattice of a
  constant-radius box. With Layer 0's orthogonality this computes the volume of a ball of the ring
  of integers of `L` in power-basis coordinates, which is the only other volume the summit needs.

### Layer 3: the Eisenstein region and the parametrization

- **The Eisenstein region** `E_n ⊆ (Fin n → K)`: every coefficient in `𝓂[K]`, with the constant
  term of valuation exactly that of a uniformizer. State the bridge the parametrization runs on:
  `a ∈ E_n` exactly when the coefficients are integral and the polynomial over `𝒪[K]` they
  define is `Polynomial.IsEisensteinAt 𝓂[K]`. Its measure is `q^{−n} · (1 − q^{−1})`.
- **Almost every Eisenstein polynomial is separable** ([Serre 1978, eq. (3)]): the non-separable
  locus is null. In equal characteristic this is where the inseparable polynomials are discarded,
  and it is the reason the count is over subextensions of `SeparableClosure K`.
- **The root count.** For `L ∈ σ_K n`, `rootCount L a` is the number of roots of the monic
  polynomial with coefficient vector `a` lying in `L`, counted with multiplicity. On the
  full-measure separable locus all multiplicities are `1`. Almost everywhere on `E_n`,
  `∑_{L ∈ σ_K n} rootCount L a = n`: an Eisenstein polynomial is irreducible, and each of its `n`
  roots generates exactly one member of `σ_K n`.
- **Almost-everywhere measurability of the root count.** For each `L ∈ σ_K n`, state
  `AEMeasurable (fun a => (rootCount L a : ℝ≥0∞)) (μ.restrict (eisensteinSet K n))`.
  Layer 1 makes the root count locally constant on the separable Eisenstein locus; the
  non-separable locus is null, giving measurability for the restricted measure.
- **Countability of the family.** For `0 < n`, state
  `(totallyRamifiedOfDegree K n).Countable`. At the coefficient vector of an Eisenstein generator
  of each `L`, local constancy gives an open piece of `E_n` of positive Haar measure on which
  `rootCount L` is positive. For any finite subfamily, the sum of the root-count integrals is at
  most `n · μ(E_n)`, by the almost-everywhere root-count identity. This finite bound forces the
  family of positive integrals, hence `σ_K n`, to be countable, without using Theorem 1.
- **The local fibre count** ([Serre 1978, Lemma 1]): for `L ∈ σ_K n` with Eisenstein generator `ξ`
  of minimal polynomial `f`, and `d = d L` the consumed discriminant exponent through its wrapper —
  which is `addVal (f' ξ)`, since `𝒪_L = 𝒪[K][ξ]` makes Mathlib's `conductor_mul_differentIdeal`
  (with `conductor_eq_top_of_adjoin_eq_top`) read `differentIdeal = (f' ξ)`, and the residue degree
  is `1` — and for every `ρ` with `d + n ≤ n · ρ`: a monic `g` of degree `n` over `𝒪[K]` has a
  root in the cube `ξ + π^ρ · 𝒪_L` of radius `π^ρ`, that is `addVal (y − ξ) ≥ n · ρ`, if and only
  if `addVal (g ξ) ≥ n · ρ + d`, and then exactly one. Existence is Layer 1 at `ξ`, where
  `addVal (g' ξ) = d`, so the root lands at distance `≥ n · ρ`; uniqueness is that the threshold
  transports the derivative order to any root `z` of `g` in the cube, `addVal (g' z) = d`, and two
  distinct roots `z ≠ z'` would then give `d = addVal (g' z) ≥ addVal (z − z') ≥ n · ρ`; the
  converse is the Taylor expansion of `g` at a root in the cube. By the power-basis orthogonality
  the condition `addVal (g ξ) ≥ n · ρ + d` is a box in coefficient space, of measure
  `q^{−(n · ρ + d)}`, which is `q^{−d}` times the volume `q^{−n · ρ}` of the cube in power-basis
  coordinates: the lattice whose volume the integral below computes. ⚠ `ρ` must be taken large
  enough: for `K = ℚ_2` and `ξ = √2`, where `d = 3`, the cube at `ρ = 1` is `ξ + 2 · 𝒪_L` and
  contains both roots of `X² − 2`.
- **The integral of the root count** ([Serre 1978, Lemmas 2 and 3, eqs. (5)–(13)]): for each
  `L ∈ σ_K n`, `∫_{E_n} rootCount L = q^{−(d L + 1)} · (1 − q^{−1})`. The change of variables runs
  in power-basis coordinates: a ball of the ring of integers is the ideal generated by a suitable
  element, in coordinates the image lattice of the matrix of multiplication by it, whose
  determinant is that element's norm — so Layer 2 supplies the factor `q^{−d L}` with no Jacobian,
  no conjugates and no Vandermonde.

### Layer 4: the mass formulas

- **Theorem 1** ([Serre 1978, Thm. 1]): for `0 < n`, `∑' L : σ_K n, 1 / q ^ c L = n` in
  `ℝ≥0∞`. Integrate the root-count identity of Layer 3 over `E_n`, interchange the sum and
  integral using `MeasureTheory.lintegral_tsum` with Layer 3's countability and
  almost-everywhere measurability targets, and divide by the measure of the region.
- **The finiteness dichotomy** ([Serre 1978, Rmk. 1°]): `σ_K n` is infinite if and only if `K` has
  equal characteristic `p` and `p ∣ n`. Both directions are targets. The forward direction follows
  from Theorem 1 together with the uniform bound `c L ≤ n · natCastValuation K n h`, for
  `h : (n : K) ≠ 0`, which is available exactly outside the asserted case — the consumed upper
  bound of `differentExponent_bounds_of_wild` at `e = n`, its `natCastValuation L n` being
  `n · natCastValuation K n h` since `L / K` is totally ramified;
  the converse is an explicit family — the Eisenstein polynomials `X^n + π^m X + π` for `m ≥ 1`
  have `d = n · m`, pairwise distinct, hence generate infinitely many distinct members.
- **Convergence** ([Serre 1978, Rmk. 1°]): `Summable fun L : σ_K n => 1 / (q : ℝ) ^ c L`, the
  real-valued restatement, a corollary of Theorem 1 through `ENNReal.summable_toReal`; it carries
  information only in the infinite case.
- **The orbit count** ([Serre 1978, Rmk. 3°]): for `L ∈ σ_K n`, the number of `M ∈ σ_K n` that are
  `K`-isomorphic to `L`, times `#Aut_K(L)`, is `n`. `L / K` is separable of degree `n`, so it has
  exactly `n` embeddings into `SeparableClosure K`; each image lies in `σ_K n` by Layer 0; and the
  embeddings with a given image form a torsor under `Aut_K(L)`.
- **Theorem 2** ([Serre 1978, Thm. 2]): for every `R` with `IsRepresentativeSet n R`,
  `∑' M : R, 1 / (#Aut_K(M) · q ^ c M) = 1` in `ℝ≥0∞`. Theorem 1 regrouped along isomorphism
  classes, using the invariance of `c` from Layer 0 and the orbit count.
- **The tame count**, as a corollary worth stating: when `¬ (ringChar 𝓀[K] ∣ n)`, every `c L = 0`,
  so `σ_K n` is finite with exactly `n` elements.

## Worked examples (acceptance criteria, keeping the definitions honest)

Discharge these alongside the layers; they catch a vacuous `σ`, a wrong normalization of the
measure, and an off-by-one in `c`.

- **`n = 1`:** `σ_K 1 = {K}` with `d = c = 0`, and Theorem 1 reads `1 = 1`.
- **Tame:** for `K = ℚ_p` with `p` odd and `n = 2`, `σ_K 2` has exactly two elements (`ℚ_p(√p)`
  and `ℚ_p(√(u p))` for `u` a non-residue unit), both with `c = 0`, so the sum is `2`. This is the
  tame count above in its smallest instance.
- **Wild, and the sharpest test of `c`:** for `K = ℚ_2` and `n = 2`, `σ_K 2` has six elements —
  `ℚ_2(√−1)` and `ℚ_2(√−5)` with `d = 2`, hence `c = 1`; and `ℚ_2(√±2)`, `ℚ_2(√±10)` with `d = 3`,
  hence `c = 2`. Theorem 1 reads `2 · 2^{−1} + 4 · 2^{−2} = 2`. An implementation that gets `c`
  off by one fails here and nowhere earlier. ⚠ Those two discriminant values are the `ℚ_2(i)` and
  `ℚ_2(√2)` cases of the consumed roadmap's own worked examples; agreeing with them is the check
  that the consumed `d` and the `c` here are the same invariant.
- **Equal characteristic:** for `K = 𝔽_p((t))` and `n = p`, `σ_K n` is infinite, yet the real
  series converges — the two halves of Remark 1° on the same example.
- **The measure of the Eisenstein region** is `q^{−n}(1 − q^{−1})`, and the integral of
  `rootCount L` over it is `q^{−(d L + 1)}(1 − q^{−1})`; summing over `L` recovers `n` times the
  measure of the region. Checking the two constants against each other catches a misnormalized
  Haar measure, which is otherwise invisible until the summit.
- **Galois case of the orbit count:** for `L / K` Galois in `σ_K n`, `#Aut_K(L) = n` and the
  isomorphism class of `L` inside `σ_K n` is `{L}`.

## Ordering

Layer 0 comes first and rests on the consumed contract. The Newton estimate of Layer 1 and all of
Layer 2 are independent of Layer 0 and of each other — general statements about discrete
valuation rings; the local constancy of the root count quantifies over `σ_K n` and needs Layer 0.
Layer 3 needs 0–2; Layer 4 needs Layer 3, except for the orbit count, which needs only Layer 0.

## Long horizon (a roadmap for a future roadmap; do not attempt it here)

Serre's formula was refined by Krasner into a count of the totally ramified extensions of given
degree *and* given discriminant, and generalized by Bhargava into a mass formula over all étale
extensions of a local field, which is the local input to the conjectured densities of number-field
discriminants. Both are natural continuations and neither is specified here; they are named to
mark the direction, not to be worked on under this roadmap.

# Morse–Novikov homology and dynamical Reidemeister torsion

Build the Morse theory of closed real one-forms, from the completed group-ring
algebra to geometric trajectory complexes and their topological comparison.
Count periodic return orbits with their multiplicities and Lefschetz signs,
and prove that Novikov torsion multiplied by the dynamical zeta function equals
cellular Reidemeister torsion. The resulting library includes nonintegral period
classes, noninjective period homomorphisms, torsion in abelian deck groups,
continuation, Euler structures, and explicit circle, mapping-torus and knot-surgery
calculations.

## Scope, conventions and suppliers

The geometric setting is a finite-dimensional real smooth Hausdorff second-countable
closed connected manifold X. The Novikov complex does not require X to be oriented.
The torsion comparison assumes χ(X)=0; retain the zero convention when a field
component is not acyclic. Smooth one-forms use
[DifferentialGeometry 0–1](../DifferentialGeometry/README.md)'s common smooth-form
carrier and exterior derivative, with its pullback and de Rham comparisons.
A closed one-form α is Morse if its local potentials have nondegenerate critical
points. This predicate includes neither Morse–Smale transversality nor periodic-orbit
nondegeneracy. Use the metric dual V=α♯, and count trajectories of **−V**.

Choose a connected regular abelian covering π:X̃→X on which π*α is exact, with
specified deck-group identification H. Periods factor as
`π₁(X)→H₁(X;ℤ)→H→ℝ`; denote the final homomorphism by P. Write H additively,
monomials as e^h, and use **N=−P** in the Novikov completion. A primitive f̃ satisfies
`f̃(h·x)=f̃(x)+P(h)`. Thus e^h shifts critical values by P(h), and completed chains
are finite above each potential threshold. A downward closed orbit γ has
`N([γ])=−∫γ α>0`. Neither injectivity nor discreteness of N is assumed.
For S¹ use ℝ/ℤ, identified with `Circle` by t↦exp(2πit), and pull back
DG's `circleAngularForm/(2π)` to obtain the angular form with integral 1. The Laurent variable t is the
monomial of the generator of H≅ℤ with **N(h)>0**, not a silently chosen positive
angular deck generator. In the exact N=0 circle example, separately fix
t as the positive angular deck generator; no N(t)>0 condition applies.

The algebraic coefficient ring R is any commutative ring. Torsion over ℤ and
rational characteristic-zero field components is its own layer; do not assume a
Novikov ring over an arbitrary ring is a field. Every geometric deck group H is
finitely generated, proved using a finite CW model of X. N1's completion algebra
also treats arbitrary abelian groups, without claiming a finite field decomposition
in that generality.

## Order and acceptance

N1 is independent of geometry. N2 uses native Morse/flow topology and HF M/F0;
N3 consumes N1–N2 and AT/GT cellular suppliers. N4's algebra runs independently
of N2–N3, then applies to their based complexes. N5 consumes N1–N2. N6 uses all
five, including its own Lefschetz and knot/surgery adapters; N7 constructs the
Euler carrier before using it to refine N6. Generic ordinary Morse homology is
not proved using the dynamical torsion theorem, and Novikov homology comparison
is not used to infer torsion invariance without its based comparison factor.

Acceptance requires all three circle chain calculations, an irrational-period
noninjective-kernel completion example with finite tied leading coefficients,
a deck group with finite torsion and partially acyclic total-quotient components,
return-map iterate signs in both dimension parities (the three circle calculations supply odd dimension): an attracting and a
repelling orbit on a surface, and the orientation-reversing circle mapping
torus (Klein bottle) with ζ=(1+t)/(1−t). Check period doubling algebraically
by (1+x)/(1−x²)=1/(1−x), and the algebraic cyclic-cover norm/self-slide identities for
H=ℤ⊕ℤ/2 and h=(2,1), using divisibility 2 in H/T. For the
irrational noninjective example fix H=ℤ³ and N(a,b,c)=a+√2b,
with coefficient ring ℤ and kernel generated by (0,0,1); verify finite tied
leading supports and an infinite series whose periods escape each cutoff.
For partial acyclicity use the algebraic two-term complex over H=ℤ/2,
N=0, differential 1−g from degree 1 to degree 0: its two rational components have differential 0 and 2,
so its torsion components are 0 and 1/2. This is explicitly an algebraic
acceptance example, not an asserted geometric fibred example. Include the mapping-
torus Lefschetz/determinant comparison and the two knot-surgery examples. Every
coefficient, lift, orientation and monodromy change is checked by its naturality
formula. Suggested.lean gives representative completion, based-chain, flow and
coefficient interfaces; this README specifies the full mathematical targets.

# Morse functions, sublevel topology and Morse–Bott attachments

Develop the finite-dimensional topology of Morse and Morse–Bott functions:
intrinsic Hessians and indices, normal forms, genericity, deformation of
sublevels, handles and cells, proper exhaustions, strong inequalities and
critical-submanifold attachments and compact-trapped gradient convergence.
The resulting library supplies geodesic Morse theory,
[AffineMorseLefschetz](../AffineMorseLefschetz/README.md) and Hamiltonian moment-map topology.

## Scope, conventions and dependencies

Use finite-dimensional real smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifolds with
boundaryless models. Compactness, properness, a lower bound, and compactness of
a particular level band are separate hypotheses. A Morse function means smooth

## M3. Approximation and proper Morse exhaustions

On native smooth maps `C^∞⟮I,M;ℝ⟯`, define strong C^k neighborhoods by a
locally finite compact chart family and a positive tolerance on each member,
bounding every coordinate derivative of order≤k. Define the strong smooth
topology as generated by these neighborhoods for all finite k, without
unbounded derivative orders varying per chart. Prove chart-family independence
and agreement with compact C^k seminorm neighborhoods when M is compact.
Prove every smooth function can be approximated by Morse functions in this
topology. Use native local
linear perturbations and DG Sard, multiply them by cutoffs, and run a compact

fixed compact set and with tails preserving earlier C² nondegeneracy. Prove

fine error bounds for every prescribed finite-order neighborhood. This gives the global theorem without an unstated Baire
space or transversality theorem on a function space.

For a proper bounded-below input preserve those properties by a global C⁰
error less than 1. Prove existence of a smooth proper bounded-below exhaustion

already Morse, with compact-support control for local perturbations. Include
