### 5.2 Compact inverse systems and topological Nakayama

Standing assumptions: compact modules are compact Hausdorff topological abelian groups with a
continuous action of a profinite ring; inverse systems are indexed by ℕ or by a directed set with
countable cofinal subset.

References: RJW Proposition 13.13 and its proof, p. 193, where the inverse limit of the sequences 0
→ E⁺_{n,1} → U⁺_{n,1} → Gal(M⁺_n/L⁺_n) → 0 is taken; RJW justifies its exactness by the terms being
finitely generated ℤ_p-modules (Mittag-Leffler), whereas the statement below derives it from
compactness of the terms, which is the statement arithmetic uses. The same exactness along a tower
with surjective transition maps is `exists_forall_map_succ_eq_and_forall_eq_of_surjective`
(`TauCeti.Topology.Compactness.InverseSystem`) of Tau Ceti ProfiniteProPGroups, layer 9; its
directed case is `exists_forall_map_eq_of_compact_t2`, and exactness on the left is the
closed-embedding formality. Built on Mathlib `Submodule.eq_bot_of_le_smul_of_le_jacobson_bot`.

**Topological Nakayama.** For Λ = O⟦T⟧ (more generally a compact local ring with finite residue
field and maximal ideal 𝔪) and a compact Hausdorff topological Λ-module M with continuous action Λ ×
M → M, prove: M = 0 if M/𝔪M = 0; M is finitely generated over Λ if M/𝔪M is finite, by lifts of a
finite spanning set; and a map of compact Λ-modules is surjective if it is surjective modulo 𝔪.
Compactness of M replaces the finite-generation hypothesis of the algebraic Nakayama lemma (no
source in this roadmap's register; the statement is the standard topological Nakayama lemma, and is
stated here as the specification). *Needs:* the maximal ideal (ϖ, T) of Λ (§4.3), Tau Ceti
`exists_forall_map_succ_eq_and_forall_eq_of_surjective`, Mathlib
`Submodule.eq_bot_of_le_smul_of_le_jacobson_bot`.

**Checks.**
- M = Λ with its adic topology: M/𝔪M = 𝔽 is finite and M is generated by one element.
- M = ∏_n 𝔽 (a compact Λ-module with trivial T-action): M/𝔪M = M is infinite and M is not finitely
  generated.
- The lemma fails for the discrete module ℚ_p/ℤ_p, whose quotient by p is zero.

### Examples

- The two-term complex [Λ --a--> Λ] in degrees −1, 0 has even parity, H⁰ = Λ/(a), and its
  determinant line sits in Q as a^{−1}Λ = char(Λ/(a))^{−1}; placed in degrees 0, 1 the image is aΛ.
- The swap of the two summands of A² acts by −1 on ⋀² A², the witness of the Koszul sign.

## Layer 6: coefficient orders, Fitting ideals and transposes

The ring theory of coefficient orders used by integral Brumer–Stark and Euler-system arguments, in
the setting of Dasgupta–Kakde: character group rings O[G] with their evaluation at characters, the
lattice and unit theory, the sharp involution and the contragredient dual; quadratic presentations
and the comparison of their Fitting ideals; higher Fitting ideals, their chain and their behaviour
under extensions and fibre products; compound matrices and higher adjugates; exterior powers and the
annihilator of a cokernel; and transposed presentations. The initial Fitting ideal itself is §4.5.
The layer states no Gorenstein property and no duality theorem (see Scope and ownership): the
contragredient dual below is a module structure on Hom_R(M, R), and nothing is asserted about its
exactness or about biduality. The generic compound-matrix and higher-adjugate algebra is stated in
the `Matrix` namespace, shared with every consumer of minors, not under this roadmap's prefix.

Standing assumptions for this layer: the setting of Dasgupta–Kakde §2.2: p is an odd prime; G is a
finite abelian group, G = G_p × G′ with G_p its p-Sylow subgroup and G′ of order prime to p; O is
the valuation ring of a finite extension K of ℚ_p with finite residue field k, containing all values
of all characters of G, that is `HasEnoughRootsOfUnity O (Monoid.exponent G)`; Ĝ = Hom(G, Oˣ) has
order #G (`CommGroup.card_monoidHom_of_hasEnoughRootsOfUnity`). The idempotents e_ω and their
relations are those of `charIdempotent` (§4.6), stated there for a complete discrete valuation ring
O with finite residue field of characteristic p and a finite abelian H with p ∤ #H, here with H =
G′. The hypothesis on Ψ enters only through the locality of R_Ψ (§6.1): a statement holds for every
Ψ for which R_Ψ is a local ring and a finite O-module. R is an arbitrary commutative ring with no
noetherian or finiteness hypothesis beyond the stated ones; Fitt_R(M) = Fitt⁰_R(M) is the initial
Fitting ideal of §4.5 of a finitely presented R-module M (the convention of Dasgupta–Kakde, Appendix
B.2, p. 93), and Fitt^i_R(M) for i ≥ 1 is Tau Ceti's `fittingIdeal R M i`. For a ∈ R and an ideal J
of R, a^# = σ^{−1}(a) ∈ R^# and J^# = σ^{−1}(J); for R = R_Ψ and σ = # this is the notation of the
sharp involution of §6.1.

### 6.1 Character group rings and their duals

References: Dasgupta–Kakde §2.2, p. 15. Built on Mathlib `HasEnoughRootsOfUnity`, `Monoid.exponent`
and `MonoidAlgebra.mapDomainAlgHom`. The proposed namespace is `TauCeti`.

**Evaluation of the group ring at characters and the joint evaluation.** For a commutative ring O, a
commutative group G and a character ψ : G → O^× (a group homomorphism; the trivial character is 1;
the maps need no finiteness), the character evaluation ev_ψ : O[G] → O is the O-algebra homomorphism
Σ_g a_g g ↦ Σ_g a_g ψ(g), the lift of g ↦ ψ(g) through the universal property of the monoid algebra;
it is the Tau Ceti declaration `TauCeti.DiagonalizableGroup.point` ψ with value algebra A = O and is
not defined again; define `TauCeti.charEval` as an abbreviation for it. For a set Ψ of characters
define the joint evaluation ev_Ψ : O[G] → ∏_{ψ∈Ψ} O, x ↦ (ev_ψ(x))_{ψ∈Ψ}; this is the new
construction. Following Dasgupta–Kakde, ψ(x) means ev_ψ(x) for x ∈ O[G]. Its API is `charEval` (ev_ψ
: O[G] →ₐ[O] O, Σ a_g g ↦ Σ a_g ψ(g): abbreviation of `TauCeti.DiagonalizableGroup.point` ψ with R =
A = O), the value on a·g (ev_ψ(a·g) = a·ψ(g) for a ∈ O, g ∈ G:
`TauCeti.DiagonalizableGroup.point_single` specialised to A = O), the value on g (ev_ψ(g) = ψ(g):
`TauCeti.DiagonalizableGroup.point_single_one` specialised to A = O), the trivial-character rule
(the trivial character evaluates by the augmentation: ev_1(a·g) = a), the augmentation identity (as
a ring homomorphism, ev_1 is the coefficient-sum augmentation `TauCeti.MonoidAlgebra.augmentation` O
G : O[G] → O) and the vanishing on the group sum (for G finite, O a domain and ψ ≠ 1: ev_ψ(Σ_{g∈G}
g) = 0, row orthogonality; this item assumes G finite and O a domain). Prove separately
`TauCeti.jointEval_injective`: the joint evaluation at all characters is injective, for G finite and
O a domain with `HasEnoughRootsOfUnity O (Monoid.exponent G)`. *Lean:* `TauCeti.charEval`,
`TauCeti.jointEval` and `TauCeti.jointEval_injective`.

- G trivial: ev_1 : O[G] → O is bijective.
- If G has an element h ≠ 1 and O ≠ 0, no single ev_ψ is injective: it kills h − ψ(h)·1 ≠ 0.

**Character group rings.** In the Dasgupta–Kakde setting, for a subset Ψ ⊆ Ĝ define the character

non-maximal O-order in ∏_{ψ∈Ψ} O and is never replaced by that product; it is not Gorenstein in
general. Ψ ⊆ Ĝ is arbitrary: Ψ = ∅ gives the zero ring, Ψ = {1} gives O through the augmentation,
Ψ = Ĝ gives O[G]. No Gorenstein property is part of the definition, and none is asserted anywhere in

### 6.2 Transposed presentations

References: Dasgupta–Kakde §6.1, equation (80), p. 40; Appendix A.4, proof of Lemma A.8, p. 86.
Built on Mathlib `Module.dualProdDualEquivDual`, `Module.dual_projective` and `Module.dual_finite`.
The proposed namespaces are `TauCeti.ContragredientDual` and `TauCeti.PresentationTranspose`.

**The contragredient dual.** For a ring isomorphism σ : S → R of commutative rings (σ = # : R^# → R
for R = R_Ψ, or # : R → R for R = O[G], ℤ_p[G], ℤ[G]) and an R-module M, define the contragredient
dual M^* = Hom_R(M, R) as the S-module with (s·φ)(x) = φ(σ(s)·x), the module structure
`Module.compHom` along σ; for R = R_Ψ this is Dasgupta–Kakde's rule (r·φ)(x) = φ(r^#·x). Prove that
a linear map f : M → N induces the S-linear f^* : N^* → M^*, φ ↦ φ∘f, functorially, and that for M =
R^m, M^* is free over S on the dual basis. The source states the rule for ℤ[G]-modules, with M^* =
Hom_{ℤ[G]}(M, ℤ[G]), and applies it to modules over a character group ring R = R_Ψ; for an R-module
the dual is Hom_R(M, R), the reading that Lemma 6.1 requires, and the general form with a ring
isomorphism σ : S → R covers both. Its API is `TauCeti.ContragredientDual` (Hom_R(M, R) with the
S-module structure along σ), `toDual` (the underlying functional in `Module.Dual` R M),
`smul_apply`, `ofDual` (the element of M^* with underlying functional φ ∈ `Module.Dual` R M;
`ofDual` and `toDual` are mutually inverse additive bijections between `Module.Dual` R M and M^*),
`ext` (two elements of M^* are equal iff their underlying functionals take the same value at every x
∈ M) and `toDual_smul` (toDual(s·φ) = σ(s)·toDual(φ) in `Module.Dual` R M: `toDual` is a
σ-semilinear bijection from M^* onto Mathlib's dual, the identity on functionals). *Needs:* `sharp`
(§6.1).

**Checks.**
- R = S = O[G], σ = #, φ = id ∈ Hom_R(R, R): (g·φ)(1) = g^{−1}.
- σ = id: (s·φ)(x) = s·φ(x), the ordinary dual.
- R = O[G] with O ≠ 0, σ = #, g ∈ G with g^{−1} ≠ g: (g·id)(1) = g^{−1} ≠ g in O[G], so the
  contragredient structure differs from the ordinary one.

**The transpose of a finite projective presentation.** For a commutative ring R, a ring isomorphism
σ : S → R, and a presentation P_1 →f P_0 → M → 0 by finitely generated projective R-modules, define
the transpose attached to it as M^tr = coker(f^* : P_0^* → P_1^*), an S-module through the
contragredient structure (for R = R_Ψ, S = R^# and σ = #). Its carrier is the Tau Ceti cokernel
`TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose` f (any ring, any presentation map), with scalars restricted along
σ. The transpose depends on the presentation, not on M alone: for a square presentation with matrix
(a_ij) it is quadratically presented over S by (σ^{−1}(a_ji)). Dasgupta–Kakde write the presentation
as P_0 → P_1 → M with the indices swapped (Dasgupta–Kakde §6.1, (81), p. 40). Minimal presentations,
the stable category and the translate D Tr (Tau Ceti QuiverRepresentations Layer 6) are not used or
rebuilt here; the uniqueness theorem
`TauCeti.IsMinimalProjectivePresentation.nonempty_linearEquiv_auslanderReitenTranspose` compares two
minimal projective presentations, over any ring, whereas the presentations of Dasgupta–Kakde are not
assumed minimal, and over ℤ[G] minimal presentations need not exist (ℤ/2 has no projective cover
over ℤ). That the transpose is unique up to projective summands, tr(f) ⊕ (Q_1 ⊕ P_0)^* ≅ tr(g) ⊕
(P_1 ⊕ Q_0)^* for any two projective presentations, is Tau Ceti
`TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose.nonempty_linearEquiv_prod_dual`
(`TauCeti.Algebra.Module.AuslanderReiten.StableTranspose`), with the converse
`nonempty_linearEquiv_prod_of_linearEquiv`; this construction only restricts scalars along σ. Its
API is `TauCeti.PresentationTranspose` (coker(f^*) with the S-module structure along σ; carrier
`TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose` f), `mk` (the quotient map P_1^* →ₗ[S] M^tr: the function
`TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose.mk` on the underlying functional; it is S-linear for the
contragredient structure on P_1^* because the map is R^op-linear and s ∈ S acts on both sides as
op(σ(s))), `mk_eq_zero_iff` (mk φ = 0 iff φ factors through f: an abbreviation of
`TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose.mk_eq_zero_iff`), `mk_surjective` (the quotient map mk is
surjective: an abbreviation of `TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose.mk_surjective`), `lift` (an
S-linear map g : P_1^* → N to an S-module N with g(φ ∘ f) = 0 for every φ ∈ P_0^* factors through mk
by a unique S-linear map lift g : M^tr → N, and lift g (mk φ) = g φ; it is
`TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose.lift`, with `lift_mk` and `hom_ext`, applied after regarding N as
an R^op-module through op(r) ↦ σ^{−1}(r)) and `toARTranspose` (the underlying additive group is
`TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose` f). *Needs:* `TauCeti.ContragredientDual`,
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation` (§6.3). *Lean:* `TauCeti.PresentationTranspose`, with its additive
group and S-module instances.

**Checks.**
- The transpose of id : R → R is 0.
- The presentation R² → R, (a, b) ↦ a, of the zero module has transpose ≅ S, not 0: a transpose
  belongs to a presentation, not to M.
- The transpose of R →(a) R is ≅ S/(σ^{−1}(a)).

**The Fitting ideal of the transpose.** (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 6.1.) Let R be a character group ring
(more generally a commutative ring with a ring isomorphism σ : R^# → R) and M a quadratically
presented R-module with square matrix (a_ij). The transpose M^tr attached to that presentation is
quadratically presented over R^# with matrix (a_ji^#); this is the construction
`quadraticPresentation` of `TauCeti.PresentationTranspose`. Prove Fitt_{R^#}(M^tr) = Fitt_R(M)^#.
The identity concerns the transpose of the stated quadratic presentation: adding a nonzero free
relation summand makes the zeroth Fitting ideal of the transpose 0 (Dasgupta–Kakde, Lemma 6.1, p.
40). *Needs:* `TauCeti.PresentationTranspose`, the Fitting ideal of a quadratic presentation (§6.3),
`sharp` (§6.1), `TauCeti.fittingIdeal` (§4.5). *Lean:*
`TauCeti.PresentationTranspose.fittingIdeal_eq`.

Prove next the free form of the next statement: for a presentation P_1 → P_0 → M → 0 with P_1 and
P_0 free of ranks t and t + s, the zeroth Fitting ideal of the transpose is the ideal of the t × t
minors of the transposed matrix, which is Fitt^s_R(M)^#.

**Higher Fitting ideals and transposes with excess generators.** (Dasgupta–Kakde (171), proof of
Lemma B.4.) Let R be a commutative ring with a ring isomorphism σ : R^# → R, and let P_1 →f P_0 → M
→ 0 be an exact sequence of R-modules with P_1 and P_0 finitely generated projective of constant
ranks t and t + s (locally t relations and t + s generators), where a finitely generated projective
module has constant rank t when its localisation at every prime ideal is free of rank t
(`Module.rankAtStalk`). Prove that the zeroth Fitting ideal over R^# of the transpose M^tr attached
to f is Fitt^s_R(M)^#: Fitt^0_{R^#}(M^tr) = Fitt^s_R(M)^#. The identity concerns the transpose of
this presentation; in Dasgupta–Kakde the presentation is V^θ → B^θ → ∇ → 0 over ℤ[G], with B^θ free
of rank t + s and V^θ projective of constant rank t. No freeness is assumed: over ℤ[G] a projective
module of constant rank need not be free, and ℤ[G] is not a finite product of local rings. M and
M^tr are finitely presented, being cokernels of maps between finitely generated projective modules:
such a module is finitely presented (`Module.finitePresentation_of_projective`), its dual is again
finitely generated projective (`Module.dual_finite`, `Module.dual_projective`), and the quotient of
a finitely presented module by a finitely generated submodule is finitely presented
(`Module.finitePresentation_of_surjective`); the R^#-structure of M^tr is a transport along the ring
isomorphism σ (Dasgupta–Kakde, proof of Lemma B.4, equation (171), p. 93). *Needs:*
`TauCeti.PresentationTranspose`, the free form above, `sharp`, Tau Ceti `fittingIdeal`,
`fittingIdeal_baseChange`, the initial Fitting ideal (§4.5). *Lean:*
`TauCeti.PresentationTranspose.fittingIdeal_eq_excess`.

### 6.3 Quadratic presentations and the initial Fitting ideal

References: Dasgupta–Kakde §2.3, p. 16. Built on Mathlib's `Matrix` lemma `adjugate_mul`,
`lTensor_exact` and `mem_nonZeroDivisors_iff`. The proposed namespaces are `TauCeti` and
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation`.

**Quadratically presented modules.** Let R be a commutative ring. Define a quadratic presentation of
an R-module N to consist of an integer m ≥ 1, an m×m matrix φ over R and a surjection π : R^m → N
whose kernel is the image of φ : R^m → R^m; N is quadratically presented over R if it has one,
equivalently N ≅ coker(φ) for a square matrix φ of size m ≥ 1. m ≥ 1 is part of the definition (the
zero module is presented by R →(1) R). Its API is `TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation` (the data (m ≥ 1,
φ ∈ M_m(R), π : R^m ↠ N) with range(φ) = ker(π)), `size` (the size m ≥ 1), `rel` (the square
relation matrix φ), `gen` (the surjection π : R^m → N), `ext` (two quadratic presentations of N with
the same size m, the same matrix φ and the same map π are equal) and
`TauCeti.IsQuadraticallyPresented` (N has a quadratic presentation over R). *Lean:*
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation` and `TauCeti.IsQuadraticallyPresented`.

**Checks.**
- R/(a) has a quadratic presentation of size 1 with determinant a.
- The zero module is quadratically presented (m = 1, φ = (1)); m = 0 is excluded.
- R^m (m ≥ 1) has a quadratic presentation with φ = 0.

**The Fitting ideal of a quadratic presentation.** Prove that if N has a quadratic presentation R^m
→φ R^m → N → 0, then Fitt_R(N) = (det φ); in particular Fitt_R(N) is principal. *Needs:*
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation`, the initial Fitting ideal (§4.5). *Lean:*
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation.fittingIdeal_eq`.

**Locally quadratic presentations.** Define a locally quadratic presentation of an R-module M to be
an exact sequence P_1 →f P_0 →π M → 0 with P_0, P_1 finitely generated projective R-modules of the
same constant rank r (rank of (P_i)_𝔭 equal to r at every prime 𝔭, that is `Module.rankAtStalk` P
𝔭 = r for every prime 𝔭 of R, the rank of the free R_𝔭-module P_𝔭). Prove that every quadratic
presentation is locally quadratic, and that over a ring with finitely many maximal ideals — for
instance a local ring, or a finite product of local rings such as ℤ_p[G], O[G] and the character
group rings R_Ψ — a module with a locally quadratic presentation is quadratically presented, because
finitely generated projective modules of constant rank over such a ring are free (Dasgupta–Kakde
Remark A.7, for ℤ_p[G]): for r ≥ 1 the presentation becomes R^r → R^r → M → 0 after a choice of
bases, and for r = 0 the module M is 0, presented by R →(1) R. An arbitrary ℤ_p[G]-algebra is not a
finite product of local rings (ℤ_p[G][X] has infinitely many maximal ideals), and over a general
ring a locally quadratic presentation need not be quadratic: for a non-principal ideal I of a
Dedekind domain R, I ↪ R ↠ R/I is locally quadratic of rank 1, but R/I is not quadratically
presented. For the ℤ_p[G]-algebras R of Remark A.7 the presentation is the base change of the
locally quadratic presentation over ℤ_p[G]; that one is quadratic, and its base change to R is
quadratic by `QuadraticPresentation.baseChange` (Dasgupta–Kakde, Remark A.7, p. 86). Its API is
`IsLocallyQuadraticPresentation` (P_1 →f P_0 →π M → 0 exact with P_i finitely generated projective
of the same constant rank), `QuadraticPresentation.isLocallyQuadraticPresentation` (a quadratic
presentation is locally quadratic), `IsLocallyQuadraticPresentation.isQuadraticallyPresented` (over
a local ring a locally quadratic presentation gives a quadratic presentation),
`IsLocallyQuadraticPresentation.isQuadraticallyPresented_pi` (over a finite product of local rings a
locally quadratic presentation gives a quadratic presentation),
`IsLocallyQuadraticPresentation.isQuadraticallyPresented_of_finite_maximalSpectrum` (over a ring
with finitely many maximal ideals a locally quadratic presentation gives a quadratic presentation;
the local case and the case of a finite product of local rings are instances) and
`IsLocallyQuadraticPresentation.baseChange` (for a ring map R → R′, the base change P_1 ⊗_R R′ → P_0
⊗_R R′ → M ⊗_R R′ → 0 of a locally quadratic presentation is a locally quadratic presentation of the
same rank). *Needs:* `TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation`. *Lean:* the case of a ring with finitely many
maximal ideals is `TauCeti.isQuadraticallyPresented_of_finite_maximalSpectrum`, stated directly for
a presentation by finite projectives of the same constant rank; `IsLocallyQuadraticPresentation`
itself is specified here only.

**Checks.**
- A quadratic presentation (φ, π) is a locally quadratic presentation.
- R = ℤ_p × ℤ_p, I = ℤ_p × 0: the presentation I ↪ R ↠ R/I is not locally quadratic (ranks of I are
  1 and 0).
- 0 → 0 → 0 → 0 is locally quadratic of rank 0.

as a set, and B/K is a finite-index subring of that product, so the preceding inputs apply; K = 0
when every D_i is infinite. This K is not the conductor {b ∈ B : bB′ ⊆ B}. Use them in the forms
`natCard_quotient_range_toLin'_of_det_ne_zero`, `natCard_quotient_range_toLin'_subring`,
`natCard_quotient_range_toLin'_quotient_of_finite` and `mem_nonZeroDivisors_tfae_of_finiteIndex_pi`,
with the hypotheses stated above. *Lean:* the second and third inputs are
`TauCeti.natCard_quotient_range_toLin'_subring` and
`TauCeti.natCard_quotient_range_toLin'_quotient_of_finite`, with an `example` showing that an ideal
K of finite index does not suffice (B = ℤ, K = (2), A = (4) give cokernels of orders 4 and 2); the
first and fourth inputs are specified here only.

The PID input states
`Nat.card ((Fin m → D) ⧸ LinearMap.range (Matrix.toLin' A)) = Nat.card (D ⧸ Ideal.span {A.det})`
for a square matrix A over a principal ideal domain D with A.det ≠ 0; no finite-residue-field or
completeness hypothesis is needed, and `Nat.card` is 0 for an infinite quotient.
This roadmap supplies the generic PID input in
`TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/FreeModule/CardQuotient.lean` using Mathlib's Smith-normal-form API;

#(D/(π^k)) = (#k_D)^k when det A is associated to π^k. The Smith-normal-form argument has this
single generic library home; MassFormula supplies the residue-cardinality specialization and

**The order of a quadratically presented module over a finite-index order.** (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma
2.4.) Let B be a subring of finite additive index of a finite product B′ = ∏_i D_i of principal
ideal domains, each possibly a field, finite or infinite, of any characteristic (for instance B is a
character group ring R_Ψ ⊆ ∏_{ψ∈Ψ} O). Let N be a quadratically presented B-module with Fitt_B(N) =
(x) for a non-zerodivisor x of B such that B/(x) is finite. Prove that N is finite
and #N = #(B/(x)). This is the source's generality; when every D_i is infinite, in particular in
characteristic zero, which covers every use (R_Ψ ⊆ ∏ O), the ideal K of the proof is 0 and x is
already a non-zerodivisor of B′ (Dasgupta–Kakde, Lemma 2.4, p. 16–17). *Needs:*
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation`, the Fitting ideal of a quadratic presentation, the four inputs
above, the initial Fitting ideal (§4.5). *Lean:* `TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation.card_eq`.

### 6.4 Compound matrices and higher adjugates

References: Dasgupta–Kakde, proof of Lemma 3.9, p. 26. Built on Mathlib's `Matrix` lemma
`det_transpose`, `Set.powersetCard.compl` and `Module.Basis.exteriorPower`. The namespace is
`Matrix`.

**Compound matrices.** For a commutative ring R, finite linearly ordered index types and an ι×κ
matrix A over R, define the r-th compound matrix C_r(A) as the matrix indexed by r-subsets S ⊆ ι and
T ⊆ κ whose (S, T) entry is the minor det A[S, T] (rows S and columns T in increasing order);
r-subsets are `Set.powersetCard`, enumerated increasingly by the inverse of
`Set.powersetCard.ofFinEmbEquiv`. Prove that it is the matrix of ⋀^r A : ⋀^r R^κ → ⋀^r R^ι in the
bases e_T = e_{t_1} ∧ ⋯ ∧ e_{t_r} (t_1 < ⋯ < t_r) of Mathlib's exterior-power bases. Its API is
`compound` (C_r(A)_{S,T} = det A[S, T]), the exterior-power identity (C_r(A) is the matrix of
`exteriorPower.map` r (`toLin'` A) in the bases `Module.Basis.exteriorPower` r of the standard
bases), `compound_mul` (C_r(AB) = C_r(A)C_r(B), Cauchy–Binet), the unit rule C_r(1) = 1, the first
compound (C_1(A)_{{i},{k}} = A_{ik}) and the second compound (for i < j in ι and k < l in κ,
C_2(A)_{{i,j},{k,l}} = `Matrix.pairMinor` A (i, j) (k, l), the 2×2 minor; for r = 2,
`Matrix.compound_mul` is its Cauchy–Binet formula, Tau Ceti's `pairMinor_mul`). Prove along the way
the sign of the complement shuffle (stated as `Set.powersetCard.sign_permOfDisjoint_compl` below)
and the generalised Laplace expansion. *Lean:* `Matrix.compound` and `Matrix.compound_mul`.

**Checks.**
- C_1(A)_{{i},{k}} = A_{ik} for a 2×3 matrix.
- C_2 of the 2×2 matrix (a b; c d) is (ad − bc).
- For r larger than the number of rows there are no r-subsets: C_3 of a 2×3 matrix is empty.

**Higher adjugates.** For a square m×m matrix A over a commutative ring and 0 ≤ r ≤ m, with indices
Fin m, define the r-th higher adjugate adj_r(A) as the matrix indexed by r-subsets with entry
adj_r(A)_{T,S} = (−1)^{ΣS+ΣT} det A[Sᶜ, Tᶜ] (complementary minor; ΣS the sum of the elements of S;
with 0-based or 1-based element sums the sign is the same, since both change by 2r). Prove
C_r(A)·adj_r(A) = det(A)·I and adj_r(A)·C_r(A) = det(A)·I (generalized Laplace expansion), and that
adj_1 is the adjugate and adj_m = (1). Its API is `higherAdjugate` (adj_r(A)_{T,S} = (−1)^{ΣS+ΣT}
det A[Sᶜ, Tᶜ]), `sum_compound_mul_compound_compl` (generalised Laplace expansion: for r-subsets S,
S′ of Fin m, Σ_T (−1)^{ΣS′+ΣT} det A[S, T] det A[S′ᶜ, Tᶜ] is det A if S′ = S and 0 if S′ ≠ S, the
sum over the r-subsets T), `det_eq_sum_compound_mul_compound_compl` (generalised Laplace expansion
along the rows S, the case S′ = S of `sum_compound_mul_compound_compl`: for an r-subset S of Fin m,
det A = Σ_T (−1)^{ΣS+ΣT} det A[S, T] det A[Sᶜ, Tᶜ], the sum over the r-subsets T),
`sum_compound_mul_compound_compl_eq_zero` (the case S′ ≠ S of `sum_compound_mul_compound_compl`: for
r-subsets S ≠ S′ of Fin m, Σ_T (−1)^{ΣS′+ΣT} det A[S, T] det A[S′ᶜ, Tᶜ] = 0),
`Set.powersetCard.sign_permOfDisjoint_compl` (for an r-subset T of Fin m, the shuffle that sorts T
followed by Tᶜ (`Set.powersetCard.permOfDisjoint`) has sign (−1)^{ΣT − r(r−1)/2}, ΣT the sum of the
elements of T as natural numbers) and `compound_mul_higherAdjugate` (C_r(A)·adj_r(A) = det(A)·I).
*Needs:* `compound`, the generalised Laplace expansion. Prove along the way that the image of ⋀^r f,
for f with matrix A, is controlled by the r×r minors: det(A) times ⋀^r R^m lies in the span of the
image of the compound matrix (the input of §6.7). *Lean:* `Matrix.higherAdjugate` and
`Matrix.compound_mul_higherAdjugate`.

**Checks.**
- For a 3×3 matrix, adj_1 agrees with `Matrix.adjugate`.
- For a 3×3 matrix, adj_3(A) = (1).
- adj_r(1_3) = 1 for every r ≤ 3.

### 6.5 Higher Fitting ideals

References: Dasgupta–Kakde, Appendix B.2, first paragraph, p. 93. Built on Tau Ceti
`TauCeti.fittingIdeal`, `fittingIdeal_eq_minorsIdeal_ker`, `fittingIdeal_monotone`,
`fittingIdeal_baseChange`, and Mathlib's `Matrix` lemma `det_succ_row`.

The higher Fitting ideals Fitt^i_R(M), i ≥ 0, are Tau Ceti's `TauCeti.fittingIdeal R M i` (a91d3aaf,
`RingTheory/FittingIdeal/{Basic,Generators,BaseChange}.lean`), defined for every finite module M
through the minors ideal `Submodule.minorsIdeal` (determinants of dual functionals) of the kernel of
any surjection from a finite free module, with our indexing. Everything this layer needs about them
is in that library and is consumed, not restated: independence of the presentation
(`fittingIdeal_eq_minorsIdeal_ker` for any surjection from a finite free module,
`fittingIdeal_eq_minorsIdealOfSet` from any generating set of the kernel, with no finiteness of the
generating set), invariance under linear equivalence (`fittingIdeal_congr`), monotonicity under
surjections (`fittingIdeal_le_of_surjective`), the chain Fitt^i ⊆ Fitt^{i+1}
(`fittingIdeal_monotone`), Fitt^i = R once M is generated by i elements
(`fittingIdeal_eq_top_of_surjective`), Fitt⁰(R/I) = I (`fittingIdeal_quotient_zero`), Fitt^{i+r}(M ⊕
R^r) = Fitt^i(M) for i, r ≥ 0 (`fittingIdeal_prod_add_finrank`), with Fitt^j(M ⊕ R^r) = 0 for j < r
(the subtraction formula Fitt^j(M ⊕ R^r) = Fitt^{j−r}(M) is used only for j ≥ r), the jumps of a
free module, Fitt^i(R^n) = 0 for i < n and R for i ≥ n (`fittingIdeal_eq_bot_of_lt_finrank`,
`fittingIdeal_eq_top_iff_finrank_le`), the fibre criterion `fittingIdeal_le_iff_lt_finrank` (Fitt_k
≤ 𝔭 iff k < the dimension of the fibre at 𝔭), base change along any ring map
(`fittingIdeal_baseChange`, with no flatness hypothesis) and its localisation form
(`fittingIdeal_eq_map` with `IsLocalizedModule.isBaseChange`); Fitt^0 is the initial Fitting ideal
of §4.5. The statements of §6.2 and §6.6 are made on that declaration. The one statement of this
subsection is the translation to matrices that Dasgupta–Kakde's arguments read off.

**Fitting ideals in matrix form.** For a presentation R^m →A R^n → M → 0 with relation matrix A (the
columns of A generate the kernel of the surjection R^n → M), prove that Fitt^i_R(M) is the ideal
generated by the (n − i)×(n − i) minors of A, which is R for i ≥ n and 0 for i < n − m. This is a
translation of Tau Ceti's `fittingIdeal_eq_minorsIdeal_ker` and `fittingIdeal_eq_minorsIdealOfSet`,
whose minors ideal is stated with dual functionals rather than matrix entries, and nothing else
(Dasgupta–Kakde, Appendix B.2, first paragraph, p. 93). *Needs:* Tau Ceti
`fittingIdeal_eq_minorsIdeal_ker`, `fittingIdeal_eq_minorsIdealOfSet`, Mathlib's `Matrix` lemma
`det_succ_row`. *Lean:* `TauCeti.fittingIdeal_eq_span_minors`, with the Fitt¹ part of the third
check as an `example`.

**Checks.**
- Fitt^i(R^n) = 0 for i < n and R for i ≥ n, read off the zero relation matrix.
- Fitt⁰(R/(a)) = (a) and Fitt^i(R/(a)) = R for i ≥ 1, read off the 1×1 matrix (a).
- R/(a) ⊕ R/(b) has Fitt⁰ = (ab), Fitt¹ = (a, b) and Fitt² = R, read off the diagonal matrix diag(a,
  b); a definition taking the (n − i)×(n − i) minors of the wrong index would give Fitt¹ = (ab).

### 6.6 Fitting ideals of extensions and fibre products

References: Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 2.6, p. 18. Built on Mathlib's `Matrix` lemma
`det_fromBlocks_zero₂₁` and `Module.finitePresentation_of_ker`.

First prove the relation matrix of an extension: for 0 → A → B → C → 0 with A and C presented by
relation matrices ψ_A and φ_C, lifts c̃_j of the generators of C satisfy relations Σ_j
(φ_C)_{jk}·c̃_j = Σ_i X_{ik}·a_i for some matrix X, and the kernel of the combined generator map is
generated by the columns of the block matrix [[ψ_A, −X], [0, φ_C]].

**An extension of quadratically presented modules is quadratically presented.** (Dasgupta–Kakde
Lemma 2.6, second assertion.) Let R be a commutative ring and 0 → A → B → C → 0 an exact sequence of
R-modules, A identified with its image in B, with A quadratically presented by (n, ψ_A, π_A) and C
quadratically presented by (m, φ_C, π_C). Prove that B is quadratically presented, of size n + m, by
the block upper-triangular matrix [[ψ_A, −X], [0, φ_C]] and the generators a_1, ⋯, a_n, c̃_1, ⋯,
c̃_m, where a_i = π_A(e_i), the c̃_j ∈ B are lifts of the π_C(e_j), and X is an n×m matrix with Σ_j
(φ_C)_{jk}·c̃_j = Σ_i X_{ik}·a_i for every k; the determinant of this matrix is det ψ_A·det φ_C. The
presentation of B depends on the choice of the lifts c̃_j and of X; its size n + m and its
determinant det ψ_A·det φ_C do not. The sign of X comes from moving the lifted relation to the other
side; it does not affect the determinant, and replacing each a_i by −a_i turns −X into X. *Needs:*
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation`, the relation matrix of an extension.

**Fitting ideals of extensions with a quadratically presented quotient.** (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 2.6,
first assertion.) Let R be a commutative ring and 0 → A → B → C → 0 an exact sequence of R-modules
with C quadratically presented and A finitely presented. Prove that B is finitely presented and
Fitt_R(B) = Fitt_R(A)·Fitt_R(C). Finite generation suffices to define `TauCeti.fittingIdeal`;
finite presentation of A supplies a finite relation matrix for the block-matrix proof. Then B is
finitely presented, as an extension of finitely presented modules
(`Module.finitePresentation_of_ker`). The source states the identity over an arbitrary commutative
ring; this target retains finite presentation for that proof, with the convention of Appendix B.2
(arXiv v3 PDF p. 93). *Needs:*
`TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation`, the Fitting ideal of a quadratic presentation, the relation matrix
of an extension, the initial Fitting ideal (§4.5). *Lean:* `TauCeti.fittingIdeal_eq_mul_of_exact`,
with B finitely presented as a hypothesis, which also carries the previous statement for the
property of being quadratically presented.

**Checks.**
- For A = 0 and B = C, the formula is Fitt_R(C) = R·Fitt_R(C).
- A split extension B = A ⊕ R/(a) gives Fitt_R(B) = Fitt_R(A)·(a).
- The nonsplit sequence 0 → ℤ/p → ℤ/p² → ℤ/p → 0 for a prime p gives (p²) = (p)·(p).

**Fitting ideals of two extensions of a common quotient.** (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 2.7.) Let B, B′ be
quadratically presented R-modules with exact sequences 0 → A → B → C → 0 and 0 → A′ → B′ → C → 0, A
and A′ finitely presented. Prove Fitt_R(A)·Fitt_R(B′) = Fitt_R(A′)·Fitt_R(B). A and A′ finitely
presented makes the fibre product B ×_C B′ finitely presented, as an extension of B by A′; the
source leaves this implicit (its modules are finitely generated over noetherian rings, where A and
A′ are automatically finitely presented) and fixes the convention in Appendix B.2 (Dasgupta–Kakde,
Lemma 2.7 and proof, p. 18). *Needs:* `TauCeti.QuadraticPresentation`, the extension formula above,
the initial Fitting ideal (§4.5). *Lean:* `TauCeti.fittingIdeal_mul_comm_of_exact`.

### 6.7 Exterior powers and annihilators

References: Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 3.9, p. 25–26. Built on Mathlib `exteriorPower.map_surjective`,
`exteriorPower.map_comp` and `Module.annihilator`.

**Fitting ideals annihilate exterior-power cokernels.** (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 3.9.) Let R be a
commutative ring and N ⊆ M R-modules with N finitely generated and M finitely presented, so that M/N
is finitely presented and Fitt_R(M/N) is defined. Prove that for every r ≥ 1, Fitt_R(M/N)
annihilates the cokernel of ⋀^r_R N → ⋀^r_R M. *Needs:* `compound`, the determinant control of the
image of ⋀^r (§6.4), the initial Fitting ideal (§4.5). *Lean:*
`TauCeti.fittingIdeal_le_annihilator_exteriorPower_cokernel`.

### Examples

- O a domain, G of prime order p with p not a unit in O: R_Ĝ ≅ O[G] contains no coordinate
  idempotent δ_ψ of ∏_{Ĝ} O, so it is a proper suborder; and for G = ⟨g, h⟩ with Ψ = {1, ψ_1, ψ_2}
  as in §6.1, R_Ψ/(ζ − 1) has a two-dimensional socle, the witness that character group rings need
  not be Gorenstein (the second check on character group rings in §6.1).
- Ψ = {ψ} with ψ(τ) = ζ a primitive cube root of unity: τ − ζ ∈ ker α_Ψ but τ^{−1} − ζ ∉ ker α_Ψ,
  so # is an isomorphism R_Ψ → R_{Ψ^#} and not an endomorphism of R_Ψ.
- The presentation R² → R, (a, b) ↦ a, of the zero module has transpose S ≠ 0: the transpose belongs
  to the presentation.
- Over R = ℤ_p × ℤ_p the presentation ℤ_p × 0 ↪ R ↠ R/(ℤ_p × 0) is not locally quadratic (ranks 1
  and 0), and over a Dedekind domain a non-principal ideal gives a locally quadratic presentation of
  rank 1 of a module that is not quadratically presented.
- C_2 of (a b; c d) is (ad − bc); adj_1 of a 3×3 matrix is `Matrix.adjugate` and adj_3 = (1).

TauCetiRoadmap/PerfectoidSpaces:
# Roadmap: perfectoid rings and spaces

**Summary.** Perfectoid spaces are the adic spaces on which Frobenius can be inverted: locally they
are adic spectra of perfectoid Tate rings, complete uniform Tate rings with a pseudouniformiser `ϖ`
such that `ϖ^p` divides `p` and Frobenius is an isomorphism `R°/ϖ → R°/ϖ^p`. This roadmap builds
their theory in that generality, with no perfectoid base field and with products of mixed- and
equal-characteristic rings allowed: almost mathematics over an arbitrary basic setup; perfectoid
Tate rings, tilts, Fontaine's `θ` and the classification of untilts by primitive ideals; the tilting
homeomorphism, perfectoid rational localisation, the sheaf theorem with almost acyclicity of `O⁺`,
and perfectoid spaces with fibre products; almost purity and the étale site; injections,
immersions, Zariski closed immersions and separatedness; cofiltered limits and finite-stage descent
of étale objects; `κ`-small perfectoid spaces and the pro-étale calculus; and tilde-limits and
Frobenius-controlled towers, sousperfectoid frames and spaces, analytic approximation,
perfectoid torsor presentations and the affinoid perfectoid basis of the rigid pro-étale site. The end results are the tilting equivalence
`Perfd/X ≃ Perf/X♭` with `X_ét ≃ X♭_ét`, the almost purity theorem (for a perfectoid Tate ring
`R`, `FÉt(R) ≃ FÉt(R♭)`, every finite étale `R`-algebra is perfectoid, and `S°` is almost finite
étale over `R°`), and the pro-étale calculus on which DiamondsAndVStacks builds its topologies.

Everything rests on Tau Ceti's Huber rings and adic spaces (the Foundations of adic spaces roadmap,
`TauCetiRoadmap/AdicSpaces/README.md`, called AdicSpaces below, and its implementation under
`TauCeti.RingTheory.Huber` and `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.AdicSpace`) and on Mathlib's Witt vectors,
perfection, `PreTilt` and `WittVector.fontaineTheta`. The outputs are the geometric inputs of
pro-étale descent and diamonds (DiamondsAndVStacks) and of perfectoid Shimura varieties
and period spaces downstream. The analytic étale interfaces come from AdicEtaleGeometry;
this roadmap proves their perfectoid specializations.

## Conventions

Fix a prime `p`. A perfectoid Tate ring is complete and Hausdorff, uniform, and has a
pseudouniformiser `ϖ` with `ϖ^p | p` in `R°` such that Frobenius `R°/ϖ → R°/ϖ^p` is an isomorphism;
injectivity of Frobenius is automatic and the condition does not depend on `ϖ`. No perfectoid base
field is fixed; statements that hold only over a perfectoid field say so. A perfectoid Tate pair
`(R, R⁺)` is a Tau Ceti Huber pair with `R` perfectoid; `R°` is its maximal ring of integral elements
and `R°°` the topologically nilpotent elements. `Perfd` denotes perfectoid spaces of all
characteristics, a full subcategory of Tau Ceti's `PreAdicSpace` (sheafy pre-adic spaces covered by
affinoid perfectoid opens, P2.10), and `Perf` its characteristic-`p` subcategory, with `p = 0` in all
sections; `X♭` is the tilt, `♯` the sharp map,
which is multiplicative and continuous but not additive. Almost mathematics is always with respect
to a stated basic setup `(V, m)`: `m` idempotent with `m ⊗_V m` flat; for a perfectoid Tate ring the
setup is `(R°, R°°)`, equivalently the root ideal `(ϖ^{1/p^∞})` of a pseudouniformiser with compatible
`p`-power roots, and the two setups on `R⁺ ⊆ R°` are compared explicitly. "Almost zero", "almost
isomorphism", "almost finite étale" and "almost acyclic" are relative to that setup; an almost
statement is never silently upgraded to an actual one.

Rings of integral elements are open, integrally closed and contained in `R°`; completed colimits of
Tate pairs complete the colimit of the plus rings `ϖ`-adically and invert `ϖ`. "qcqs" means
quasicompact and quasiseparated; morphisms of perfectoid spaces are morphisms of adic spaces.
Tilde-limits carry both the topological condition and the affinoid density condition. Cardinals:
`κ`-smallness is tested on affinoid covers, and uniformly `κ`-small means `κ'`-small for a single
`κ' < κ` (P6.2); the cutoff cardinals are strong limits and may be singular.

Each target below is written with its hypotheses in the sentence, its source locator in parentheses
(short keys are resolved in the References), its API as named lemmas and its unit tests as `Checks`;
`Suggested.lean` gives typed forms for a subset of these targets and Checks. Existing definitions keep their library namespaces.
The names of definitions, lemmas and Checks in the target paragraphs are the names proposed for the
formalisation. A subsection whose targets are carried by declarations of `Suggested.lean` ends with
a `Lean:` line listing them, and the layer's Examples paragraph lists its Lean `example`s; a
target, definition or Check not named on a `Lean:` line is specified in this README only and has no
Lean declaration yet. Names of other roadmaps' declarations are theirs.

## How to read the build

P0 and P1 are independent until the almost setup of a perfectoid ring: P0 builds almost mathematics
over an arbitrary basic setup up to almost finite étale algebras, the almost cotangent complex and
finite étale lifting; P1 builds perfectoid Tate rings, tilts, perfectoid fields, `θ`, untilts and
the tilting equivalence of rings. P2 turns the ring theory into geometry (the tilting homeomorphism,
rational localisation, the sheaf theorem, perfectoid spaces and their fibre products), P3 proves
almost purity and builds the étale site, P4 the injections, immersions and separatedness, P5 the
cofiltered limits and finite-stage descent, P6 the `κ`-small calculus and pro-étale morphisms, P7 the
tilde-limits and Frobenius-controlled towers. Build order is by declarations: construct the
almost-algebra and module categories and the algebra adjunction in P0.8 before P0.16's
change-of-setup equivalence, then prove P0.8's `moduleEquiv`, its comparisons and the closed
monoidal structure. Construct P0.9's unitization before P0.25; its faithful-flatness comparison
uses P0.11 and is proved in P0.25. Construct `uniformTilt` in P1.7 before P1.4's perfectoid
specialization, and its comparisons with that specialization afterwards. Construct P1.24's
integral predicate and Frobenius criterion before P1.20's integral-to-Tate criterion.
A target's `*Needs:*` clause names the prerequisite declarations, the subsections of other
roadmaps and the library declarations it rests on, and each layer's Dependencies paragraph collects
the subsections of other roadmaps that the layer uses. P4.4 and the targets built on it use the
completed direct limit of P5.1–P5.3, which depends only on P1 and P2. Each subsection ends with the
Lean declarations that carry it, when there are any; targets without Lean are stated here only,
their carriers being formalisation tasks in their own right.

Each definition requires three discriminating Checks on its own carrier, including a
computed value and a degenerate case or non-example. Arithmetic identities, facts solely
about imported objects, repetitions of a target, and laws true of every morphism of the
same kind are supplementary calculations; they do not count toward these three Checks.
In particular, the following named calculations are supplementary wherever they occur:

## Layer P0: almost mathematics over a basic setup

Almost mathematics is developed over an abstract basic setup `(V, m)`, so that it can be
instantiated later for `(R°, R°°)` and for the root ideal of a pseudouniformiser without
circularity. The layer builds the almost category as the Serre quotient of `V`-modules by almost
zero modules, with the functor of almost elements and the left adjoint `M_!`; the closed symmetric
monoidal structure; almost algebras with the left adjoint `B_!!`; almost finite generation and
presentation, flatness, projectivity, duals and traces, and the rank decomposition; flat, unramified,
étale and finite étale morphisms with the trace-form criterion and the comparison with Mathlib's
finite étale algebras; inversion of an element of `m`; almost Kähler differentials, the cotangent
complex of a ring map and the almost cotangent complex with its deformation theory; faithfully flat
descent; tight ideals, henselian pairs and modules over complete almost algebras; finite étale
lifting modulo a tight ideal; and almost sheaves with almost sheaf cohomology and almost Čech
complexes on a site.

### P0.1 basic setup `(V, m)`

The layer opens with the basic setup itself, its two standing examples and the firm-module model of
the almost category.

**Basic setup `(V, m)`: an idempotent ideal with flat `m ⊗ m`.** (*almost-basic-setup*) Let `V` be a
commutative ring (`[CommRing V]` in universe `u`) and `m` an ideal of `V`. A basic setup is a pair
`S = (V, m)` such that (i) `m` is idempotent, `m·m = m` (Mathlib `IsIdempotentElem m` in the
semiring `Ideal V`), and (ii) the `V`-module `m̃ := m ⊗_V m` is flat. Condition (i) is Gabber–Ramero's
basic setup, the only hypothesis they use before (2.5.14); it makes almost zero modules closed under
extensions ([GR] §2.1, (2.1.1), p. 7). Condition (ii) is the flatness they assume from (2.5.14) on
and use earlier for the exactness of `M ↦ M_!` in Corollary 2.2.22; it is imposed here once for all
almost mathematics of this roadmap, and every setup used here satisfies it: root ideals and maximal
ideals of valuation rings with non-finitely-generated maximal ideal satisfy condition (A) below, and
`m = V` is flat ([GR] §2.1, (2.1.1), p. 7, and (2.5.14), p. 32). Conventions: a `V`-module
`M` is almost zero if `m·M = 0`; a `V`-linear map is an almost isomorphism if its kernel and
cokernel are almost zero; `m̃` always denotes the tensor product `m ⊗_V m` (it maps onto
`m·m = m`, isomorphically when `m` is flat); the classical limit is `m = V`, which recovers ordinary
commutative algebra ([GR] §2.1, Example 2.1.2(i)-(ii), p. 7). Condition (A): `m` is a filtered union
of principal ideals; condition (B): for every `k ≥ 1` the `k`-th powers of elements of `m` generate
`m`. For an idempotent `m`, (A) implies (B): `x ∈ m = m^k` is a sum of products of `k` elements of
`m`, which lie in a common principal ideal `(z)`, so each product lies in `(z^k)`; without
idempotence (A) does not imply (B), as `(t) ⊆ 𝔽_p[t]` shows. (A) together with `m·m = m` implies
(ii) by *filtered-principal-union-tilde-flat* (P0.2). A basic setup is data, not a type class, because one
ring carries several setups: for a perfectoid Tate ring `R`, `(R°, R°°)` and `(R⁺, the root ideal of a pseudouniformiser)`, compared in layer P1. Bhatt's variant of the setup, with `m` itself flat, is a
special case ([Bhatt] §4.1, Assumption 4.1.2, p. 17). In `Almost`, define `BasicSetup` as the
structure with fields `ideal : Ideal V`, `isIdempotentElem : IsIdempotentElem ideal` and

### P0.2 the root setup of compatible p-power roots

**The basic setup of an element with compatible p-power roots.** (*root-ideal-basic-setup*) Let `V`
be a commutative ring, `p ≥ 2` an integer and `(ϖ_n)_{n≥0}` a sequence in `V` with

and no perfectoid hypothesis enter: the construction is purely algebraic. Then `(V, m)` is a basic
setup, the root setup of `(ϖ_n)`: `m` is the increasing union of the principal ideals `ϖ_n V`,
`m·m = m`, and `m̃` is flat by condition (A). A `V`-module `M` is almost zero for it iff `ϖ_n M = 0`
for all `n` ([Bhatt] §4.1, Example 4.1.3, p. 18; cf. [ECD] §3, Definition 3.21, p. 19).

`ϖ_n` is a nonzerodivisor, each `ϖ_n V` is free of rank one, `m` is flat and countably generated,

nonzerodivisor hypothesis is used only for this clause. Replacing `(ϖ_n)` by the shifted sequence
`(ϖ_{n+k})_n`, or by any sequence `(ϖ'_n)` with `ϖ'_n V = ϖ_{n+c} V` for all large `n`, gives the
same setup. This is the input layer P1 instantiates with a pseudouniformiser admitting compatible
`p`-power roots. Define `BasicSetup.ofCompatibleRoots` (given `p ≥ 2` and `ϖ : ℕ → V` with

definition. Prove `BasicSetup.mem_ofCompatibleRoots_ideal` (`x ∈ ideal ↔ ∃ n, ϖ n ∣ x`),
`BasicSetup.ofCompatibleRoots_isAlmostZero_iff` (`IsAlmostZero M ↔ ∀ n (x : M), ϖ n • x = 0`),
`BasicSetup.isIdempotentElem_span_roots` and `BasicSetup.flat_tilde_span_roots` (idempotence and

### P0.4 firm modules

**Firm modules: a small-hom model of the almost category.** (*firm-module-model*) Let `S = (V, m)`
be a basic setup (`m̃ = m ⊗_V m` flat; flatness is used for the exactness of `m̃ ⊗ −` and the closure
of firm modules under kernels), with `V : Type u` and `ModuleCat.{u} V`, so that `S.Firm : Type (u+1)`
with `Category.{u}`. A `V`-module `M` is firm if the multiplication map `m̃ ⊗_V M → M` is an
isomorphism; firm modules form a full subcategory `S.Firm` of `ModuleCat V`, closed under kernels,
cokernels and finite biproducts (hence abelian, with exact inclusion `j_!`). The functor
`j^* : ModuleCat V → S.Firm`, `M ↦ m̃ ⊗_V M`, is well defined (`m̃ ⊗ m̃ ≅ m̃`), exact, right adjoint to
`j_!`, and has a fully faithful right adjoint `j_* : N ↦ Hom_V(m̃, N)`; its kernel `{M : m̃ ⊗ M = 0}`
is exactly `S.almostZero` ([Bhatt] §4.1, Construction 4.1.5, pp. 18–19). By Mathlib's
`Abelian.isLocalization_isoModSerre_kernel_of_leftAdjoint`, `j^*` is a localization functor for the
almost isomorphisms `S.almostZero.isoModSerre`, which yields the instance
`MorphismProperty.HasLocalization.{u} S.almostZero.isoModSerre` whose localized category has
Hom-types in the universe `u` of the `V`-modules; the almost category of P0.5 is defined through it
([Bhatt] §4.1, Proposition 4.1.7(2) and proof, p. 21; [GR] §2.2, Proposition 2.2.21 and Corollary
2.2.22, p. 15). The categories `S.Firm` and `Almost.Module S` are equivalent; firm modules are the
modules of the form `M_!` (P0.6). Define `BasicSetup.IsFirm` (`Function.Bijective` of
`TensorProduct.lift (multiplication) : S.tilde ⊗[V] M → M`), `BasicSetup.Firm` (the full
subcategory on firm modules), `BasicSetup.firm` (the functor `ModuleCat V ⥤ S.Firm`,
`M ↦ S.tilde ⊗[V] M`), `BasicSetup.Firm.ι` (the inclusion, `j_!`) and `BasicSetup.closure`
(`N ↦ Hom_V(S.tilde, N)`, `j_*`); prove `BasicSetup.firmInclusionAdj` (`Firm.ι ⊣ S.firm`),
`BasicSetup.firmAdj` (`S.firm ⊣ S.closure`, with `S.closure` fully faithful), the kernel identity
`S.firm.kernel = S.almostZero`, `BasicSetup.hasLocalization` (the `HasLocalization.{u}` instance
with localized category `S.Firm`), firmness of `S.tilde` and
`BasicSetup.Firm.abelian` (`Abelian S.Firm`, kernels and cokernels computed in `ModuleCat V`).

the unit `N → (N^a)_*` and the natural map `(N^a)_! → N` are almost isomorphisms, and `M_! → M_*` is

### P0.8 almost algebras

**Almost algebras (commutative monoids in `V^a-Mod`) and their modules.** (*almost-algebras*) For a
basic setup `S = (V, m)`, an almost `V`-algebra is a commutative unital monoid object in the
symmetric monoidal category `Almost.Module S`: `Almost.Algebra S := CommMon (Almost.Module S)`
(Mathlib), with monoid morphisms ([GR] §2.2, (2.2.5), p. 12). For an almost algebra `A`,
`A_* = Hom(V^a, A)` is a commutative `V`-algebra (`a·b := μ ∘ (a ⊗ b) ∘ ν⁻¹`); `R ↦ R^a` from
commutative `V`-algebras to almost algebras is left adjoint to `A ↦ A_*`, with counit
`A ≅ (A_*)^a`, so `(−)_*` is fully faithful and `Hom_{Alg}(A, B) ≅ Hom_{V-alg}(A_*, B_*)`; every
almost algebra is `R^a` for `R = A_*` ([Sch12] §4, after Proposition 4.6, p. 19; [Bhatt] §4.2,
Remark 4.2.8, p. 25). An `A`-module is a module object over `A` (Mathlib `CategoryTheory.Mod`);
`A`-modules form an abelian, complete and cocomplete category `A-Mod`, closed symmetric monoidal
with `M ⊗_A N := (M_* ⊗_{A_*} N_*)^a`, and `A-Mod ≃ Almost.Module (S.baseChange A_*)`
by *change-of-basic-setup* (P0.16). An `A`-algebra is a morphism `A → B`. Convention:
module-theoretic notions for `A`-modules (flat, almost projective, almost finitely generated and
presented) are those of P0.11 and P0.10, evaluated through this equivalence on the `A_*`-module
`M_*`. Limits are computed on almost elements, `(lim D)_* ≅ lim D_*`. Colimits are almostified
last: `colim D ≅ (colim D_*)^a`, so free modules `((A_*)^{(I)})^a`, quotients and pushouts are `(−)^a`
of the corresponding constructions on almost elements ([GR] §2.2, Corollary 2.2.15 and 2.2.18, p.
14). The functor `(−)_*` preserves neither colimits nor epimorphisms: an almost element of the
target of an epimorphism lifts only after multiplication by an arbitrary `ε ∈ m` ([GR] §2.2, Remarks
2.2.14(ii) and 2.2.28(i), pp. 14–16), so no exactness or colimit-preservation statement is made for
`(−)_*`. Define `Almost.Algebra` (`CommMon (Almost.Module S)`), `Almost.Algebra.toAlmost`
(`CommAlgCat V ⥤ Almost.Algebra S`, `R ↦ R^a`), `Almost.Algebra.elements` (`A ↦ A_*`),
`Almost.Algebra.ModuleCat` (`A-Mod := CategoryTheory.Mod (Almost.Module S) A.X`),
`Almost.Algebra.free` (the free `A`-module `A^{(I)} := ((A_*)^{(I)})^a`, left adjoint to
`M ↦ (M_* as a set)`, [GR] 2.2.18), `Almost.Algebra.quotient` (for an ideal `I ↪ A`, the almost
algebra `A/I` with `A → A/I` an epimorphism), `Almost.Algebra.prod` (finite products with
`(A₁ × A₂)_* = A₁_* × A₂_*` and `A-Mod` decomposing accordingly) and `Almost.Algebra.tensor`
(pushouts `B ⊗_A C ≅ ((B_* ⊗_{A_*} C_*))^a`); prove `Almost.Algebra.adj` (`toAlmost S ⊣ elements S`),
`Almost.Algebra.counitIso` (`(A.elements)^a ≅ A`; `elements` fully faithful),
`Almost.Algebra.homEquiv` (`(A ⟶ B) ≃ (A.elements →ₐ[V] B.elements)`),
`Almost.Algebra.moduleEquiv` (`A-Mod ≌ Almost.Module (S.baseChange A.elements)`) and
`Almost.Algebra.monoidalCategory` (the closed symmetric monoidal structure on `A-Mod`). *Needs:*
P0.7 for the categories and algebra adjunction; Mathlib `CategoryTheory.CommMon`, `CategoryTheory.Mod`,
`CategoryTheory.MonObj`, `CategoryTheory.IsCommMonObj`. The declaration `moduleEquiv`, its
action and forgetful comparisons, and the closed monoidal structure use
*change-of-basic-setup* (P0.16), whose module categories and algebra adjunction are constructed here.

`Almost.Algebra.moduleEquiv_elements_action` identifies the almost elements of
`moduleEquiv.functor.obj M` naturally with `Hom(V^a, M.X)` as additive groups,

### P0.9 the left adjoint `B_!!` on algebras

**The left adjoint `B ↦ B_!!` of almostification on algebras.** (*almost-algebra-lower-shriek-shriek*)
For a basic setup `S = (V, m)` and an almost `V`-algebra `B`, `B_! = m̃ ⊗_V B_*` is a non-unital
`V`-algebra: it inherits a multiplication from `B` through `m̃ ⊗ m̃ ≅ m̃`, but no unit, since
`(V^a)_! ≅ m̃` and the unit comparison `m̃ → V` of the oplax monoidal functor `(−)_!` is not an
isomorphism unless `m = V` (P0.7). Its unitisation is `B_!! := (V ⊕ B_!)/I`, where `I` is the `V`-submodule spanned by the elements
`(xy, −x ⊗ y ⊗ 1)` for `x, y ∈ m`, is a unital commutative `V`-algebra with `B ≅ (B_!!)^a`, and
`B ↦ B_!!` is left adjoint to `R ↦ R^a`. The span is already the ideal of the unitalisation
`V ⊕ B_!` that Gabber–Ramero quotient by: in `B_! = m̃ ⊗_V B_*` one has
`(x ⊗ y ⊗ 1)·(x' ⊗ y' ⊗ b) = x ⊗ yx'y' ⊗ b = (xy)·(x' ⊗ y' ⊗ b)`, so
`(xy, −x ⊗ y ⊗ 1)·(v, b) = v·(xy, −x ⊗ y ⊗ 1)`, and the two descriptions of `I` agree. The
adjunction is between `A_!!`-algebras and `A`-algebras, for any almost algebra `A` with `B` an
`A`-algebra ([GR] §2.2, Proposition 2.2.27, p. 15). `B` is exact if
`0 → m̃ → V ⊕ B_! → B_!! → 0` is exact; every almost algebra is exact when `m̃ → m` is an isomorphism
(e.g. `m` flat), and `V^a × B` is always exact ([GR] §2.2, Definition 2.2.25 and Remark 2.2.26,
p. 15). `B ↦ B_!!` commutes with all colimits, in particular with tensor products ([GR] §2.2, Remark
2.2.28(i), p. 16); the natural map `B_!! → B_*` is an almost isomorphism ([Bhatt] §4.2, Remark
4.2.8, p. 25); `B ↦ B_!!` preserves faithful flatness of morphisms but not flatness,
see *lower-shriek-shriek-faithful-flatness* (P0.25). Define `Almost.Algebra.shriekShriek`
(`Almost.Algebra S ⥤ CommAlgCat V`, `B ↦ B_!!`), `Almost.Algebra.IsExact` and
`Almost.Algebra.shriekShriekToElements` (the natural map `B_!! → B_*`); prove
`Almost.Algebra.shriekShriekAdj` (over `A`: `B ↦ B_!!` is left adjoint to `R ↦ R^a`),
`Almost.Algebra.shriekShriekUnitIso` (`B ≅ (B.shriekShriek)^a`), `Almost.Algebra.isExact_of_bijective`
(if `S.tilde → S.ideal` is bijective, every almost algebra is exact), `Almost.Algebra.isExact_prod`
(`V^a × B` is exact), `Almost.Algebra.shriekShriek_preservesColimits` (with `shriekShriekTensorIso : (B ⊗_A C)_!! ≅ B_!! ⊗_{A_!!} C_!!`). *Needs:* P0.8's categories and algebra adjunction.
The comparison `Almost.Algebra.shriekShriek_faithfullyFlat_iff` (`φ` faithfully flat
`↔ φ_!!` faithfully flat) is *lower-shriek-shriek-faithful-flatness* (P0.25), using this
unitization and P0.11's flatness theory.

### P0.10 almost finite generation and presentation

**Almost finitely generated, uniformly almost finitely generated and almost finitely presented
modules.** (*almost-finitely-generated-and-presented*) Let `S = (V, m)` be a basic setup, `R` a
`V`-algebra and `N` an `R`-module, `M = N^a` over `A = R^a`. `N^a` is almost finitely generated if
for every finitely generated ideal `m₀ ⊆ m` there are `n` and an `R`-linear `φ : Rⁿ → N` with
`m₀·coker φ = 0`; it is almost finitely presented if for every such `m₀` there is a complex
`R^k →ψ Rⁿ →φ N` with `m₀·coker φ = 0` and `m₀·ker φ ⊆ im ψ`
([GR] Proposition 2.3.10(i), (ii)(c), p. 18). Both conditions depend only on `N^a`.
For an arbitrary almost algebra `A`, apply these two formulas to `M_*` over `A_*` (P0.8).

The invariant uniform notion is `Almost.Module.UniformlyAlmostFG M n`: the isomorphism class of
`M` belongs to `U_n(A)`, the closure of the classes of `A`-modules generated by at most `n`
elements ([GR] Definition 2.3.8(iii), p. 17). The uniform structure is that of [GR]
Definition 2.3.1(ii), p. 16: for each finitely generated `m₀ ⊆ m`, a basic entourage consists of
pairs admitting a common source whose two maps have kernels and cokernels annihilated by `m₀`.
Thus the specified bound is an invariant of the almost module for every basic setup.

Separately, the ordinary-module predicate `BasicSetup.UniformlyAlmostFG N n` requires an
ordinary `φ : Rⁿ → N` with `m₀·coker φ = 0` for every finitely generated `m₀ ⊆ m`.
This implies membership of `N^a` in `U_n(A)` for every setup. Under condition (A),
`BasicSetup.IsFilteredPrincipal`, it is equivalent to that membership and is preserved by
almost isomorphisms with the same bound `n` ([GR] Remark 2.3.9, p. 18).
Without (A), this stronger predicate can depend on the ordinary representative, and evaluating it
on `M_*` does not characterize all representatives of `M`. The non-uniform predicates under (A)
also agree with Scholze's `ε`-formulation: for every `ε ∈ m` there is a finitely generated
(presented) `N_ε → N` with kernel and cokernel killed by `ε`
(*almost-finite-generation-epsilon-criterion*, P0.11; [Sch12] Definition/Proposition 4.7(iii), p. 19).
The Lean forms use `V`-modules over `S`; for `R`-modules use `S.baseChange R`.
In almost finite presentation, `k`, `n`, `ψ` and `φ` may depend on `m₀`, with no uniform kernel
condition ([GR] Proposition 2.3.10(ii)(c)). Define `BasicSetup.AlmostFG`
(`∀ m₀ ≤ S.ideal, m₀.FG → ∃ n (φ : (Fin n → V) →ₗ[V] N), ∀ ε ∈ m₀, ∀ x, ε • x ∈ range φ`),
`BasicSetup.UniformlyAlmostFG` (the ordinary-module predicate with `n : ℕ` fixed) and `BasicSetup.AlmostFP`
(`∀ m₀` f.g., `∃` complex `V^k —ψ→ Vⁿ —φ→ N` with `φ ∘ ψ = 0`, `m₀ • coker φ = 0` and
`m₀ • ker φ ≤ range ψ`); prove `BasicSetup.AlmostFP.almostFG` (almost finitely presented implies
almost finitely generated), invariance of `AlmostFG` and `AlmostFP` under almost
isomorphisms, `BasicSetup.UniformlyAlmostFG.iff_of_isAlmostIso` (under (A), an almost
isomorphism preserves the ordinary-module predicate with the same `n`),
`Almost.Module.almostFG_of_finite` (`Module.Finite R N → AlmostFG`;
`Module.FinitePresentation R N → AlmostFP`), `BasicSetup.AlmostFG.extension` and
`BasicSetup.AlmostFP.extension` (in a short exact sequence of ordinary `V`-modules,
almost f.g., respectively almost f.p., endpoints imply the same property for the middle term;
for `M` almost f.p., a quotient is almost f.p. iff the kernel is almost f.g.,

### P0.11 flatness and almost projectivity

**Flat, faithfully flat, almost projective and almost finite projective almost modules.**
(*almost-flat-projective-finiteness*) Let `S = (V, m)` be a basic setup, `A` an almost `V`-algebra
and `M` an `A`-module (`A-Mod` as in P0.8). `M` is flat if `M ⊗_A − : A-Mod → A-Mod` is exact,
faithfully flat if moreover `M ⊗_A N ≅ 0` implies `N ≅ 0`, almost projective if
`alHom_A(M, −) : A-Mod → A-Mod` is exact, and almost finite projective if it is almost projective
and almost finitely generated (P0.10); "uniformly almost finite projective" adds a uniform bound
([GR] §2.4, Definition 2.4.4, p. 23). Convention: categorical projectivity (`Hom(M, −)`
exact) is never used — `Almost.Module S` has no nonzero projective objects when `V` is local and
`m ≠ V` ([GR] §2.4, Example 2.4.5, p. 23; [Sch12] §4, Remark 4.8, p. 20). For a `V`-algebra `R` and
an `R`-module `N`: `N` flat (faithfully flat, projective) implies `N^a` flat (faithfully flat,
almost projective) over `R^a` ([GR] §2.4, (2.4.8), p. 24). Characterisations: the Tor and Ext
criteria *almost-flatness-tor-criterion*, the `ε`-factorisation
*almost-projective-epsilon-factorisation* (P0.11) and finite projective = flat + almost finitely
presented, *almost-finite-projective-iff* (P0.11). Define `Almost.Module.Flat` (`M ⊗_A −` preserves
finite limits), `Almost.Module.FaithfullyFlat` (flat and `M ⊗_A N ≅ 0 → N ≅ 0`),
`Almost.Module.AlmostProjective` (`alHom_A(M, −)` preserves epimorphisms) and
`Almost.Module.AlmostFiniteProjective` (`AlmostProjective ∧ AlmostFG`; uniformly with bound `n`);
prove `Almost.Module.flat_toAlmost` (`Module.Flat R N → Flat ((toAlmost _).obj N)`; likewise
`FaithfullyFlat`, and `Projective → AlmostProjective`), `Almost.Module.AlmostProjective.flat`,
`Almost.Module.Flat.tensor` (`Flat` and `AlmostProjective` are stable under `⊗_A` and under base
change `B ⊗_A −`), `Almost.Module.Flat.trans` (if `B` is a flat (almost projective, almost f.g.,
almost f.p.) `A`-algebra and `M` such a `B`-module, `M` is such an `A`-module, [GR] Lemma 2.4.7),
and `Almost.Module.flat_iff_tor` (`Flat (N^a) ↔ ∀ X i, 0 < i → IsAlmostZero (Tor_i^R(N, X))`);
the characterisations `Almost.Module.almostProjective_iff_factor` (for `M` almost f.g.:
`AlmostProjective M ↔ ∀ ε ∈ m, ∃ n u v, v ∘ u = ε • 𝟙` through `A^n`) and
`Almost.Module.almostFiniteProjective_iff` (`AlmostFiniteProjective M ↔ Flat M ∧ AlmostFP M`) are
proved with the supporting results *almost-projective-epsilon-factorisation* (P0.11) and
*almost-finite-projective-iff* (P0.11). *Needs:* P0.8; P0.10; Mathlib `Module.Flat`,
`Module.FaithfullyFlat`, `Module.Projective`, `CategoryTheory.Functor.PreservesEpimorphisms`.

Two supporting results. Tor and Ext criteria for almost flatness and almost projectivity
(*almost-flatness-tor-criterion*): for a basic setup `S`, a `V`-algebra `R` and `R`-modules `M, N`,
(i) there are natural isomorphisms `Tor_i^{R^a}(M^a, N^a) ≅ Tor_i^R(M, N)^a` and
`alExt^i_{R^a}(M^a, N^a) ≅ Ext^i_R(M, N)^a`, where `Tor^{R^a}` and `alExt` are the derived functors
of `⊗` and `alHom` on `R^a-Mod` (computed by flat resp. injective resolutions; Mathlib
`CategoryTheory.Abelian.Ext`); (ii) `N^a` is flat over `R^a` iff `Tor_i^R(N, X)` is almost zero for
all `R`-modules `X` and all `i > 0`; (iii) `N^a` is almost projective iff `Ext^i_R(N, X)` is almost
zero for all `X` and `i > 0`; (iv) `N^a` is faithfully flat iff it is flat and `N ⊗_R X` almost zero
implies `X` almost zero; (v) an almost projective module is flat ([GR] §2.4, (2.4.10), p. 24; [GR]
§2.4, Remark 2.4.12(i), p. 24; [Sch12] §4, Definition/Proposition 4.7(i), p. 19). Over `(K°, K°°)`, `M^a` is flat iff `Tor_1(M, K°/ϖ) = M[ϖ]` is almost zero, iff
`M_*` has no `ϖ`-torsion ([Sch12] Lemma 5.3(i)). The `ε`-criterion for almost finite generation and
presentation under condition (A) (*almost-finite-generation-epsilon-criterion*): for a basic setup
satisfying (A) (root and valuation setups), a `V`-algebra `R` and an `R`-module `N`, `N^a` is almost
finitely generated (resp. presented) iff for every `ε ∈ m` there are a finitely generated (resp.
presented) `R`-module `N_ε` and `N_ε → N` with kernel and cokernel killed by `ε`, and `N^a` is
uniformly almost finitely generated with bound `n` iff for every `ε ∈ m` there is `Rⁿ → N` with
cokernel killed by `ε`. For general basic setups, the non-uniform generation and presentation
criteria use finitely generated subideals `m₀ ⊆ m` as in P0.10; the fixed-rank ordinary-map
criterion implies the invariant uniform bound, with the converse asserted under (A)
([GR] §2.3, Remark 2.3.9, p. 18;
[Sch12] §4, Definition/Proposition 4.7(iii), p. 19).

**Checks.**

- `Almost.Module.Flat_test_valuation` (computation) — for `S = ofValuationRing K°` and `0 ≠ ϖ ∈ K°°`:
  `(toAlmost S).obj K°` is `Flat` and `(toAlmost S).obj (K° ⧸ ϖ)` is not `Flat` (its almost elements
  have `ϖ`-torsion).
- `Almost.Module.projectivity_test_classical` (compatibility) — for `S = classical V` and a `V`-module `N`:
  `Flat (N^a) ↔ Module.Flat V N`, `FaithfullyFlat (N^a) ↔ Module.FaithfullyFlat V N`, and
  `AlmostProjective (N^a) ↔ Module.Projective V N`.
- `Almost.Module.projectivity_test_zero` (degenerate) — the zero module is `Flat` and
  `AlmostProjective` but not `FaithfullyFlat` (unless `A ≅ 0`).
- `Almost.Module.almostProjective_test_unit_epsilon` (degenerate) — if some `ε ∈ m` is a unit then
  `m = V` and the factorisation `v ∘ u = ε • 𝟙` through `Aⁿ` of `almostProjective_iff_factor` is an
  honest splitting, so `AlmostProjective` is `Module.Projective` and the `ε`-criterion
  `N_ε → N` of *almost-finite-generation-epsilon-criterion* is an isomorphism from a finitely generated module; both
  reduce to the classical statements, as `Almost.Module.projectivity_test_classical` requires.

Supporting result: Flat + almost finitely presented ⟺ almost projective + almost finitely
generated (*almost-finite-projective-iff*, `Almost.Module.almostFiniteProjective_iff`): for a basic
setup `S`, an almost `V`-algebra `A` and an `A`-module `M`, (i) if `M` is almost projective and
almost finitely generated, `M` is almost finitely presented (and flat); (ii) if `M` is flat and
almost finitely presented, `M` is almost projective;
hence Scholze's "finite projective" (flat and almost finitely presented) coincides with almost
finite projective; (iii) if `A → B` is a monomorphism of almost algebras and `M` is an almost
finitely generated flat `A`-module with `B ⊗_A M` almost finitely presented over `B`, then `M` is
almost finitely presented ([GR] §2.4, Proposition 2.4.18, p. 26; [Sch12] §4, Proposition 4.10 and
the text after it, p. 20). Classically this says finitely presented flat modules are projective and
finitely generated projective modules are finitely presented. 

Almost projectivity via
`ε`-factorisations through free modules (*almost-projective-epsilon-factorisation*,
`Almost.Module.almostProjective_iff_factor`): for an almost algebra `A` and an `A`-module `M`,
(i) `M` is almost projective iff for every `ε ∈ m` there are a set `I` and `A`-linear maps
`M →u A^{(I)} →v M` with `v ∘ u = ε·1_M`; (ii) if `M` is almost finitely
generated, `M` is almost projective iff for every `ε ∈ m` there are `n(ε) ∈ ℕ` and
`M →u Aⁿ →v M` with `v ∘ u = ε·1_M`, and, under condition (A), `M` is uniformly almost finite projective with bound `n`
iff `n` can be taken independent of `ε`, Kedlaya–Liu's definition ([GR] §2.4, Lemma 2.4.15, p. 25, and the proof of Lemma 2.4.29, p. 28;
[KL15] §5.5, Definition 5.5.8, p. 132). For `P = L°a` over `K°a` (`L = K(√p)`, the odd-`p` `L` of
P0.10) the maps
`L° → (K°)² → L°` with composite `p^{1/p^{n−1}}` ([Bhatt] Example 4.2.7) exhibit `P` as uniformly
almost finite projective with bound `2`.

- `projectivity_test_classical` — flatness, faithful flatness and almost projectivity become the three ordinary module predicates in the classical setup.
- `projectivity_test_zero` — the zero object is flat, almost projective, almost finite projective, and uniformly so with bound zero; it is faithfully flat exactly when the tensor unit is zero.
- `projectivity_test_free` — the almostification of `Vⁿ` is almost finite projective with uniform bound `n`, including `n = 0, 1, 2`.
- `projectivity_test_torsion` — classically, `ℤ/2` is neither flat nor almost projective.
- `faithful_test_unit` — the tensor unit is faithfully flat in every setup.
- `uniformProjectivity_test_rank` — over a field in the classical setup, a free module of rank `r` has uniform projective bound `n` exactly when `r ≤ n`.

- `derived_test_torsion` — `Tor₁^ℤ(ℤ/2, ℤ/2) = ℤ/2` and `Ext¹_ℤ(ℤ/2, ℤ) = ℤ/2`;

### P0.12 duals and traces

**Duals, traces of endomorphisms and the trace form of an almost finite projective algebra.**
(*almost-dual-and-trace*) Provides the duality trace whose internal almost-module realization is
used by the algebra-trace and trace-form consumers. Supplied by PivotalSpherical §Layer 2 / Left
and right trace and the common spherical `trace`.
Convention gap: this roadmap proves the required almost duality, instantiates the supplier's
standard symmetric pivotal/spherical structure (§Layer 7), and identifies the internal map
`End_A(P)^a → A` with its tensor-unit-valued trace on endomorphisms.

Let `S` be a basic setup and `A` an almost `V`-algebra. For an `A`-module `M`, the dual is
`M* := alHom_A(M, A)` with evaluation `ev_{M/A} : M ⊗_A M* → A`. For `P` almost finite projective,
`ω_{P/A} : P ⊗_A P* → End_A(P)^a` is an isomorphism by
*tensor-hom-comparison-almost-projective*. On the full subcategory of almost finite projective
`A`-modules, prove closure under duals and tensor products and both triangle identities for the
evaluation and the coevaluation obtained from `ω_{P/A}⁻¹` applied to the identity; these give the
rigid symmetric category needed by the supplier. Retain `Almost.Module.trace` only as the local
internal realization `tr_{P/A} := ev_{P/A} ∘ ω_{P/A}⁻¹ : End_A(P)^a → A`. Its comparison with the
supplied trace is an equality of internal morphisms, natural on maps `L → End_A(P)^a` for every
test `A`-module `L`, using the corresponding contraction `L ⊗_A P → P`; at `L = A` it recovers
PivotalSpherical §Layer 2's trace through `alHom_A(A, A) ≅ A`.
The carrier's docstring is: “Internal almost-module realization of PivotalSpherical §Layer 2's
trace for `Almost.Algebra.trace` and trace-form consumers. The tensor–Hom/evaluation and scalar
identifications are proved here.”

Provides cross-object cyclicity for the almost endomorphism trace through the duality comparison.
Supplied by PivotalSpherical §Layer 2 / Cyclicity (`leftTrace_comm` and the common spherical trace).
Convention gap: both source objects must carry
the proved almost duality, and this roadmap translates composition between `ψ∘φ` and Lean's
left-to-right `f ≫ g` before transporting scalar traces through the internal comparison.

Provides tensor multiplicativity for the almost endomorphism trace. Supplied by PivotalSpherical
§Layer 2 / The left trace is monoidal (`leftTrace_tensor` and the common spherical trace).
Convention gap: this roadmap transports the
supplier's tensor-unit endomorphisms and unitor formula to multiplication in `A`, preserving the
chosen tensor/dual identifications.

For an `A`-algebra `B` which is almost finite projective as an `A`-module,
`μ : B → End_A(B)^a` (`b ↦`
multiplication by `b`, defined on almost elements; [Sch12] §4, Remark 4.15, p. 20) gives the almost
trace `Tr_{B/A} := tr_{B/A} ∘ μ : B → A` using the internal realization of PivotalSpherical
§Layer 2 ([GR] §4.1, (4.1.7), p. 74), the trace form
`t_{B/A} := Tr_{B/A} ∘ μ_{B/A} : B ⊗_A B → A` and `τ_{B/A} : B → B*`; `t_{B/A}` is perfect, by
definition, iff `τ_{B/A}` is an isomorphism ([GR] §4.1, (4.1.12), p. 75). Properties:
additivity on short exact sequences of almost finite projective modules;
`Tr_{C⊗_A B/C} = 1_C ⊗ Tr_{B/A}`; `Tr_{C/A} = Tr_{B/A} ∘ Tr_{C/B}` ([GR]
§4.1, Proposition 4.1.8(ii)-(iii), p. 74); `τ` is `B`-linear and compatible with base change.
Mathlib's `LinearMap.trace` (defined through a finite basis, and `0` when the module is not finite
free) is not used for almost finite projective modules; it agrees with `tr` on finite free modules
after almostification via AdicSpacesPartIII §R3.8 / *projective-module-trace*,
`LinearMap.projectiveTrace_eq_trace` and the internal comparison above.
Define `Almost.Module.dual` (`M*` with its evaluation), `Almost.Algebra.trace` (`Tr_{B/A} : B ⟶ A`),
`Almost.Algebra.traceForm` (`t_{B/A}` and `τ_{B/A}`) and `Almost.Algebra.IsPerfectTraceForm`
(`τ_{B/A}` is an isomorphism); prove `Almost.Module.dualTensorHomIso` (`ω_{P/A} : P ⊗_A P* ≅ End_A(P)^a` for `P` almost finite projective), `Almost.Module.trace_additive`, `Almost.Module.isReflexive`
(`P ≅ P**`), `Almost.Algebra.trace_baseChange`, `Almost.Algebra.trace_trans`,
`Almost.Algebra.trace_of_iso` (simp: if `A → B` is an isomorphism, `Tr_{B/A}` is its inverse) and

`η : C ⊗_A B* → (C ⊗_A B)*` is the dual base-change comparison, [GR] Lemma 4.1.13).
*Needs:* P0.7; P0.8; P0.11; PivotalSpherical §Layer 2 (trace, cyclicity and monoidality) and §Layer 7
(standard symmetric pivotal/spherical structure); AdicSpacesPartIII §R3.8 /
*projective-module-trace*; Mathlib `LinearMap.trace`, `Algebra.trace`, `Algebra.traceForm`.

Supporting result: `E ⊗ alHom(F, N) → alHom(F, E ⊗ N)` is an isomorphism for almost finite
projective `E` or `F` (*tensor-hom-comparison-almost-projective*). For a basic setup `S`, an almost
algebra `A` and `A`-modules `E, F, N`, the natural map `E ⊗_A alHom_A(F, N) → alHom_A(F, E ⊗_A N)`
is (i) an isomorphism if `E` or `F` is almost finite projective, if `E` is flat and `F` almost
finitely presented, if `F` is almost projective and `E` almost finitely presented, or if `E` is
almost projective and `F` almost finitely generated; (ii) a monomorphism if `E` is flat and `F`
almost finitely generated, or if `E` is almost projective; (iii) an epimorphism if `F` is almost
projective and `E` almost finitely generated ([GR] §2.4, Lemma 2.4.29, p. 27). Consequently, for `P`
almost finite projective, `ω_{P/A}` is an isomorphism ([GR] §2.4, Lemma 2.4.29(i)(b), p. 27), `P` is
reflexive ([GR] §2.4, Lemma 2.4.31(ii), p. 28), and
`B ⊗_A alHom_A(P, N) ≅ alHom_B(B ⊗_A P, B ⊗_A N)` for every `A`-algebra `B`; for `P = (Rⁿ)^a` free,

### P0.13 rank decomposition

**Rank decomposition of uniformly almost finite projective modules.**
(*rank-decomposition-of-finite-projective*) Let `S` be a basic setup satisfying condition (B)
(`k`-th powers generate `m`; automatic from flatness of `m̃` by [GR] Proposition 2.1.7(ii), p. 9; (B) is used for
the uniform continuity of `Λ^r`, [GR] Lemma 2.3.7(vi), and for Proposition 4.3.4), `A` an almost
`V`-algebra and `P` a uniformly almost finite projective `A`-module. Then `P` has finite rank:
`Λ^r_A P = 0` for some `r` ([GR] §4.3, Remark 4.3.10(i), p. 85). For `P` almost finite projective with
`Λ^r_A P = 0` there is a unique decomposition `A ≅ A_0 × A_1 × ⋯ × A_{r−1}` such that
`P_i := P ⊗_A A_i` has constant rank `i` over `A_i`: `Λ^{i+1}_{A_i} P_i = 0` and `Λ^i_{A_i} P_i` is
an invertible `A_i`-module (`Λ^i P_i ⊗ (Λ^i P_i)* ≅ A_i`); the decomposition is compatible with base change
`A → A'` ([GR] §4.3, Proposition 4.3.27, p. 88, with the standing finiteness hypothesis on p. 83;
[GR] §4.3, Definition 4.3.9(iv), p. 85; [Sch12] §4,
Theorem 4.11, p. 20, over `(K°, K°°)`, citing the book numbering). For `L°a` over `K°a`
(`L = K(√p)`, the odd-`p` `L` of P0.10): `r = 3` and `A = A_2` (constant rank `2`); for `A = K°a × K°a` and `P = K°a × 0`,
`A_1` is the first factor and `A_0` the second. *Needs:* P0.12; Mathlib `Module.Invertible`,
`ExteriorAlgebra.exteriorPower`.

`Almost.Module.rankDecomposition_baseChange` states compatibility for every almost-algebra
map `f : A → A'`, every almost finite projective module `P` over `S.baseChange A_*`, and every
`D : RankDecomposition P r`. It produces a rank decomposition of
`(Almost.Module.baseChange S f).obj P` and a comparison between the new tensor unit and the
scalar extension of the old one. Each new projector is the corresponding transported projector
conjugated by that comparison. No flatness or faithfulness of `f` is required; a factor may become
zero. This is the naturality of [GR] Proposition 4.3.27, p. 88.

**Checks.**

- `Almost.Module.rankFactors_test_zero` (degenerate) — `P = 0` has `Λ^1 P = 0`, so `r = 1` and the
  decomposition is `A = A_0`; a module of constant rank `0` is zero, since `Λ^1 P = P`; for a
  uniformly almost finite projective `P` with invariant bound `n`, `Λ^{n+1} P = 0`:
  `Λ^{n+1}` is uniformly continuous under (B) and vanishes on modules generated by at most `n`
  elements, hence on their closure `U_n(A)` ([GR] Lemma 2.3.7(vi), p. 17,
  and Remark 4.3.10(i), p. 85).

- `exterior_test_degree_zero` — `Λ⁰ M` is the tensor unit, including `M = 0`.
- `exterior_test_degree_one` — `Λ¹ M ≅ M`; constant rank zero therefore forces `M = 0`.
- `exterior_test_rank_two` — for `(V²)^a`, `Λ³ = 0` and `Λ² ≅ V^a`.
- `Almost.Module.rankFactors_test_one` — a rank-one free module has `r = 2`, with `A₁ = A` and `A₀ = 0`.
- `Almost.Module.rankFactors_test_two` — a rank-two free module has `r = 3`, with `A₂ = A` and `A₀ = A₁ = 0`.
  `RankDecomposition` expresses the factors by orthogonal idempotent endomorphisms of the tensor unit,
  whose sum is the identity. The factor modules are their images. On factor `i`, `Λ^{i+1} P` vanishes
  and the evaluation of `Λ^i P` against its dual is invertible. Thus the carrier records constant rank,
  not merely a list of ring factors. `rankDecomposition` constructs it and `rankDecomposition_unique`
  fixes its projectors uniquely; `RankDecomposition.unitIso` is the base decomposition.
- `rankFactors_test_zero`, `rankFactors_test_one`, `rankFactors_test_two` — for free ranks `0, 1, 2`,
  only the matching projector is the identity and the other projectors are zero.
- `rankFactors_test_empty` — an empty rank decomposition forces the base unit to be zero.
- `Almost.Module.rankDecomposition_infinite_support` (negative control) — let `k` be a field,
  `V = ∏_{i∈ℕ} k` with the classical setup, and `I = ⊕_{i∈ℕ} V δ_i ⊂ V`, where `δ_i` is the
  coordinate idempotent. For `P = I^a`, projectivity follows from the direct sum of the projective
  summands `V δ_i`, and `Λ²_V P = 0`: distinct summands have zero tensor product, and each summand
  is cyclic. Yet `P` is not almost finitely generated, since any finite set of generators has
  support in a common finite subset of `ℕ`. Its annihilator is zero, so a rank decomposition with
  `r = 2` would force the rank-zero projector to be zero and the rank-one projector to be the
  identity. But the image of evaluation `P ⊗ P* → V^a` is `I^a`, which misses `1`; evaluation is
  not invertible and `RankDecomposition S P 2` is empty. Thus vanishing of an exterior power does
  not replace the almost finite generation hypothesis in `rankDecomposition`.

### P0.14 flat, unramified, étale and finite étale morphisms

Almost finite étale algebras are built next: the morphism classes, the trace-form criterion,
inversion of an element of `m`, the comparison with Mathlib's finite étale algebras, almost Kähler
differentials and the cotangent complex of a ring map.

**Flat, unramified, étale and finite étale morphisms of almost algebras.**
(*almost-finite-projective-and-finite-etale-algebras*) Let `S` be a basic setup and `φ : A → B` a
morphism of almost `V`-algebras; view `B` as a `B ⊗_A B`-algebra through the multiplication
`μ_{B/A} : B ⊗_A B → B`, with kernel `I_{B/A}`; the module notions are those of P0.11 and P0.10,
applied to `B` as an `A`-module and as a `B ⊗_A B`-module. `φ` is flat (faithfully flat, almost
projective) if `B` is a flat (faithfully flat, almost projective) `A`-module; (uniformly) almost
finite if `B` is a (uniformly) almost finitely generated `A`-module; weakly unramified (unramified)
if `B` is a flat (almost projective) `B ⊗_A B`-module; weakly étale (étale) if flat and weakly
unramified (unramified) ([GR] §3.1, Definition 3.1.1(iii)-(iv), p. 39). `φ` is finite étale if it is
étale and `B` is an almost finitely presented `A`-module ([Sch12] §4, Definition 4.13, p. 20;
Gabber–Ramero's `A-Ét_afp`, [GR] §3.2, (3.2.27), p. 46; Kedlaya–Liu's and Bhatt's "almost finite

are finite étale over `A`. Equivalent descriptions: unramified iff there is a diagonal idempotent
`e ∈ (B ⊗_A B)_*` with `μ(e) = 1` and `I_{B/A,*}·e = 0` (*unramified-idempotent-characterisation* in P0.15,
Scholze's definition); for `B` almost finite projective over `A`, étale iff the trace form
`t_{B/A}` is perfect (P0.15). Convention: "finite étale" always means étale and almost finitely
presented; in the classical setup it is Mathlib's finite étale (P0.17), while Gabber–Ramero's
"étale" without finiteness is more general than EGA étale ([GR] §3.1, Remark 3.1.3(i), p. 39).
