The interfaces consumed by Part II are `IsAffinoidAlgebra`, the affinoid
norm and reduction theorems, `Sp`, affinoid subdomains, classical Tate
acyclicity, `RigidSpace`, rigid analytification and `rigidToAdic`. Part II's
R0.9 transports the algebraic predicate to its topological presentation;
its R1 names refer to these objects, not independent definitions.
Part III supplies coherent and proper-cohomology theorems after the classical
category and comparison functor. Its algebraic targets
*affinoid-completed-field-extension* and *almost-noetherian-integral-affinoid-modules*
use only the Tate, Banach and affinoid algebra floor, not their later
geometric applications.

Part III's affinoid complete-continuity condition agrees with
CompactOperators' `IsCompletelyContinuous`: over a noetherian affinoid,
containment in a finite submodule is equivalent to finitely generated image.
Use PFA's gauges, model spaces and countable-type APIs under those comparisons.
Part III retains the strict lattice condition, perturbation corollaries and
Kiehl applications; they do not create a second operator library.

Formal models, Raynaud's theorem, admissible blow-ups, dagger geometry,
eigenvariety gluing, automorphic forms and curve uniformisation are outside
this roadmap. The geometric contracts below fix the required scope rather
than inviting an independent implementation of those subjects.

## Conventions and foundations

1. Use `[NontriviallyNormedField K] [IsUltrametricDist K] [CompleteSpace K]`.
   Characteristic zero, discrete valuation and spherical completeness are
   additional hypotheses only where stated. Put
   `√|K×| = {r>0 : ∃ n≥1, ∃ c∈K×, r^n=|c|}`.
2. `Tₙ=K⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩` is the shared native restricted-series algebra at unit
   polyradius. Use coefficient-preserving equivalences for alternative
   presentations. Distinguished-variable conventions must agree with the
   supplier's iteration map, including the choice of first or last variable.
3. `IsAffinoidAlgebra K A` is a proposition: there is a surjective algebra
   map `Tₙ→A`. It does not select a norm or a topology. Quotient Gauss norms
   give complete algebra norms; §1 proves independence of their topology.
   Equivalent norms need not be equal or isometric.
4. Classical points are `MaximalSpectrum A`. The value `|f(x)|` uses the
   unique extension of `|·|` to the finite residue field `A/x`; no embedding
   into a chosen algebraic closure enters its definition. Define
   `|f|sup = sup_x |f(x)|`, with value zero for the zero algebra. Prove
   boundedness before using a real supremum.
5. Use `TauCeti.Huber.powerBoundedSubring` for `A°`, its native
   `topologicallyNilpotentIdeal` for `A°°`, and `Ã=A°/A°°`. Keep a presentation
   ring `A₀=π(Tₙ°)` separate from `A°`.
   Nilpotents remain in all algebra and sheaf carriers. Reduced affinoids
   are uniform; nonreduced affinoids use strong noetherianness for sheafiness.
6. Rational fractions are `A⟨f/g⟩=A⟨T⟩/(gTᵢ−fᵢ)` with `(g,f₁,…,fₘ)=A`.
   Rational domains require `|g(x)|≠0` and `|fᵢ(x)|≤|g(x)|`.
   All localisation and tensor comparisons commute with structure maps.
7. Use native `Ideal`, `Submodule`, `Module.Finite`, `Module.Projective`,
   tensor products, continuous linear maps, schemes, sites, sheaves and
   sheaf cohomology. An arbitrary module has an algebraic Čech complex;
   Banach topologies and strictness are asserted for finite modules.
8. Classical points and adic points are different carriers. The comparison
   preserves rational traces and ringed sites, not all underlying points.
   In particular, a higher-rank condition `v(T)<1` is not by itself a
   description of the adic image of the rigid open unit disc.

Mathlib supplies restricted-series predicates and Gauss norms, polynomial
and fraction-ring algebra, noetherian and Jacobson rings, maximal spectra,
normed quotients, finite-dimensional topology and categorical sites/sheaves.
The series, functional-analysis and adic suppliers extend this floor. The geometric
objects assigned here are construction targets on native sheaf and site
carriers, not opaque constants or structures with the desired theorems as fields.
Suggested homes are `TauCeti/RingTheory/Affinoid/` for the algebra and
`TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/Rigid/` for rigid spaces and comparisons, with
general G-site lemmas under `TauCeti/Topology/GTopology/`, sharing the adic
geometry's carriers. Production modules import proved mathematics, never a
roadmap's `Suggested.lean`.

### Existing library interfaces

The prototype uses Tau Ceti `a91d3aaf` and Mathlib `6b7abb3c`. Import
`TauCeti.RingTheory.MvPowerSeries.TateAlgebra.Basic`: the native restricted
subring already has its coefficient algebra, Gauss norm and completeness.
Use `MvPowerSeries.norm_eq_gaussNorm`, `NormMulClass` and the native
coefficient embedding rather than defining another normed Tate algebra.
`pointNorm` uses Mathlib's `spectralNorm` on the actual maximal-ideal quotient.

Follow Mathlib's [restricted-series carrier #42867](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42867)
and [Gauss-norm API #42871](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42871).
For boundedness, Huber rings and `Spa`, use the native Tau Ceti interfaces
and the comparisons directed by [#40013](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/40013),
[#42312](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42312),
[#38009](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/38009) and
[#42315](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42315).
Valuations are considered up to equivalence; a chosen representative is not
a replacement for `Spv`. Missing results are required in Tau Ceti in these
interfaces, independently of the timing of the Mathlib proposals.

## Layer 0: shared Tate inputs and weak stability

### 0.1 The imported Tate package

Use RestrictedPowerSeries §§2.4 and 5 for the complete multiplicative Gauss
norm, polynomial density, coefficient reduction `T̃ₙ≃K̃[X₁,…,Xₙ]`, bounded
evaluation and substitution, maximum modulus at a finite-residue-field point,
and the Zariski-dense maximum locus of a nonzero Tate series. Its Weierstrass
polynomials are monic of Gauss norm one; nonleading coefficients may have
norm one. Consume division, preparation, simultaneous distinguished charts
and the finite free quotient on `1,X,…,X^(s−1)` for degree `s`.

The same supplier owns noetherianity, factoriality, integral closedness,
the Jacobson property, `dim Tₙ=n`, finite maximal residue fields, polynomial
generation of maximal ideals, nearest-point results for Tate ideals and
strictness for finite Tate modules. The last property is specific input;
nearest points are not assumed to exist in every Banach subspace.

**Checks.** Transport constants, variables, products and coefficients through
the carrier comparison. Over `ℚ_p`, `p+T²` has maximum one at `T=1`, whereas
its value at zero is `|p|`; the reduction of `p+T+pT²` is `T`. For `n=0`
recover `K`, including its norm and residue field.

### 0.2 Weak stability and finite normalisation

Develop the valued-field weak-stability and weakly Cartesian finite-extension
API of [BGR] §§3.5.1–3.5.3: the bounded-functional criterion, the complete
and perfect cases, and the comparison of finite-extension norms. Coordinate
the complete countable-type Banach-space results with PFA §2.4. The
bounded-functional separation and weakly Cartesian results for the possibly
incomplete Gauss fraction field are targets here, following [BGR] 2.3.2/7
and §§3.5.1–3.5.3; they are not obtained by dropping the completeness
hypothesis of a Banach-space theorem.

Equip `Frac(Tₙ)` with the extended Gauss norm and prove it weakly stable
in every characteristic, using [BGR] 5.3.1/1 and 3.5.3/1–2. Apply the
Japanese-ring criteria of SchemeAndStackFoundations to prove that the integral
closure of `Tₙ` in every finite extension of its fraction field is finite.
The inseparable step uses [BGR] 4.1/3–4 and 4.4/2 and is part of the theorem.
Neither separability nor a discrete valuation may replace that step.

**Checks.** The zero-variable case agrees with finite extensions of `K`.
Test both a separable extension and a characteristic-`p` purely inseparable
extension. Keep the normed fraction field distinct from its completion;
completeness of `Tₙ` does not imply completeness of `Frac(Tₙ)`.

## Layer 1: affinoid algebras and their topology

### 1.1 Presentations and complete topology

Construct quotient norms, prove noetherianity and the Jacobson property,
closedness of ideals and closure under quotients and finite algebra
extensions. Construct `A⟨X⟩` from the shared relative-series interface,
with iteration and the continuous universal property for power-bounded
variable images. Surjections induce the expected quotient topologies.

Prove automatic continuity of algebra maps from a noetherian Banach
`K`-algebra to an affinoid by the closed-graph argument of [BGR] 3.7.5 and
6.1.3. Its algebraic inputs include finite-dimensionality of `A/𝔪^n` for
`n≥1` and
`⋂_{𝔪 maximal} ⋂_{n≥1} 𝔪^n=0`.
This is not the assertion `⋂_n 𝔪^n=0` for each fixed maximal ideal in an
arbitrary nonlocal ring. Deduce independence of presentation, equivalence
of complete algebra norms, and invariance of boundedness and integral
elements. Supply contractive renorming for an affinoid homomorphism.

Use the finite-module topology from PFA to prove
`isClosedEmbedding_of_finite_injective`: every finite injective affinoid
algebra map, equipped with complete algebra norms, is a closed topological
embedding. Continuity is a conclusion. Norm-one equality is not.

**Checks.** Quotient by zero and by the unit ideal; dual numbers; an
equivalent but differently scaled module norm. In `K×K`, powers of a fixed
maximal ideal have nonzero intersection, while the intersection over both
maximal ideals is zero.

### 1.2 Normalisation, points and dimension

For `A≠0`, construct a finite injective map `T_d→A` using distinguished
charts, and prove `d=dim A`. Establish finiteness in towers and the
torsion-free consequences when the target is a domain. Quotients by ideals
with maximal radical are finite-dimensional over `K`. Maximal ideals
contract to maximal ideals under affinoid algebra maps, and every maximal
residue field is finite. Deduce that affinoid domains are Japanese from §0.2.

For an affinoid **domain**, prove
`height_eq_ringKrullDim_of_isDomain`: every maximal ideal has height
`dim A` ([Conrad], Lemma 2.1.5). For general affinoids give the corresponding
componentwise statements, without asserting that all components have the
same dimension.

**Checks.** The cusp `K⟨X,Y⟩/(Y²−X³)` is finite over `K⟨X⟩` and has
dimension one. `(T²−p)` in `ℚ_p⟨T⟩` has quadratic residue field and
`|T(x)|=p^(−1/2)`. In `K⟨T⟩×K`, the maximal ideal `K⟨T⟩×0` has height
zero although the ring has dimension one. The zero algebra has no
normalisation injection from a Tate algebra.

Prove excellence of affinoid algebras in every characteristic, using the
shared excellent-ring criteria and [Conrad] §1.1's regularity arguments.
The supporting targets are regularity of Tate algebras, universal catenarity,
a nonempty regular locus in every affinoid domain, and geometrically regular
formal fibres at maximal ideals. Include the differential-rank regularity
criterion of [Conrad] Theorem 1.1.1 used in positive characteristic; finite
imperfection degree is not assumed. General excellent-ring permanence
stays in SchemeAndStackFoundations.

### 1.3 Tensor products and complete field extension

For `B=A⟨X⟩/I`, `C=A⟨Y⟩/J`, identify the affinoid pushout with
`A⟨X,Y⟩/(I,J)`. Prove its continuous universal property, presentation
independence, density of the algebraic tensor image and preservation of
surjections. Compare this construction with Part II R0.3's completed tensor
product. Density alone is not the completion theorem.

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.6, *affinoid-completed-field-extension*.**
Transport its algebraic theorem through the presentation comparison above.
For a complete isometric extension `L/K`, set `A_L=A⊗̂_K L`. Identify
it as affinoid over `L`, identify `Tₙ(K)_L` with `Tₙ(L)`, and transport
the faithful flatness of `A→A_L`. For finite `A`-modules with their
canonical topologies supply the topological `A_L`-linear isomorphism

`A_L ⊗_A M ≃ M ⊗̂_K L`,

sending `(a⊗l)⊗m` to `(am)⊗l` on elementary tensors. The left tensor is
algebraic and finite, with its finite-module topology. The right uses the
shared nonarchimedean completed tensor. State naturality and compatibility
with exact sequences and repeated field extension. No algebraicity or
spherical completeness of `L/K` is assumed. For finite `L/K`, compare to
the algebraic tensor model with its complete finite-module topology.

**Checks.** `M=A`, `L=K`, zero modules and
`A=K⟨T⟩, M=A/(T)`, where both sides are `L`. Source: [BGR] 6.1.1 and
[Conrad], Lemma 1.1.5; tensor construction from Part II R0.3, *completed-tensor-banach-module*.

### 1.4 Fraction algebras

Construct Weierstrass and Laurent fractions and their iterated
presentations. For rational fractions prove invertibility of `g`, the
power-bounded ratios, the continuous universal property and density of
`A[g⁻¹]`. Construct the appropriate quotient seminorm on that localisation
and identify its separated completion with `A⟨f/g⟩`. Identify it naturally
with the shared adic rational localisation. Specify the compared norms
before asserting an isometry. Sources: [BGR] 6.1.4–6.1.5, 7.2; Part II R0.3.

**Checks.** One-variable Weierstrass and Laurent presentations; denominator
one; the zero algebra. Without `(g,f)=A`, taking all entries zero does not
invert the denominator. Verify compatibility with restrictions and iterated
rational localisations, not just an abstract algebra equivalence.

### 1.5 Strictness of arbitrary positive polyradii

For `ρᵢ>0`, consume the weighted Tate algebra, its multiplicative norm and
the finite monomial extension of RestrictedPowerSeries §5.4. Prove

`T_{n,ρ} is strictly K-affinoid ↔ ∀ i, ρᵢ∈√|K×|`.

The forward construction uses powers of variables scaled to norm one; the
converse uses automatic continuity and the affinoid value-group theorem
of §2.2. In the strict case identify the weighted Gauss and supremum norms.
This is the interface for Part IV F1.1, not a replacement of the broader
non-strict affinoid terminology. Source: [BGR] 6.1.5.

**Checks.** Radius `p^(−1/2)` over `ℚ_p`, a positive radius outside
`p^ℚ`, and zero variables. A function on an open disc is not in general a
restricted series on its closed boundary; test `Σ T^n`.

## Layer 2: supremum seminorm, reduction and integral models

### 2.1 Pointwise and spectral descriptions

Construct evaluation norms using finite residue fields and prove boundedness,
ultrametricity, scalar compatibility and submultiplicativity of `|·|sup`.
Prove `|f^n|sup=|f|sup^n` for `n≥1`, including the zero algebra. Exponent
zero requires a nonzero algebra. Identify the kernel with the nilradical,
and the seminorm with the maximum of its values on the finitely many
minimal-prime quotients. It is unchanged by reduction.

Algebra homomorphisms contract these seminorms; integral injective ones
preserve them. For a monic equation
`f^d+Σ_{i<d} aᵢf^i=0`, `d>0`, prove the bound by
`max_{i<d}|aᵢ|sup^(1/(d−i))`. Retain the equality for a minimal monic
equation for an integral torsion-free algebra monomorphism from an
integrally closed domain, as in [BGR] 3.8.1/7, including a non-domain
target. For the general algebraic formulation use the finite-residue-field
maximal points and explicit boundedness hypotheses of that section.
For an integral affinoid map, construct an equation attaining the spectral
value as in [BGR] 6.2.2/4; its scope is not restricted to a chosen finite
presentation of the map.

### 2.2 Maximum modulus and Banach function algebras

For `A≠0`, every `|f|sup` is attained at a classical point. Prove the
value-group assertion uniformly: some `m≥1`, depending only on `A`,
satisfies `|f|sup^m∈|K|` for every `f`. In particular, if `|f|sup>0`
there is `c∈K×` with `|cf^m|sup=1`. Use normalisation and minimal primes,
without presupposing a geometric category.

Prove `A°={f:|f|sup≤1}`, `A°°={f:|f|sup<1}` and the pointwise version
of the latter. Prove the integral-equation criterion for a residue norm
and the spectral-radius identity
`|f|sup=inf_{n≥1}‖f^n‖^(1/n)`, agreeing with the shared smoothing API.
For every reduced affinoid and complete algebra norm prove
`|f|sup≤‖f‖≤C|f|sup`, for some `C>0`.
Construct the complete supremum-norm model and its continuous algebra
equivalence with the original model. Include [BGR] 3.8.3/7: if `B→A`
is finite, injective and torsion-free, `A` is a reduced Banach algebra,
and `B` is a valued integrally closed noetherian Banach algebra with
weakly stable fraction field, then `A` is a Banach function algebra.
Identify its supremum norm with the spectral norm on
`A⊗_B Frac(B)`, a finite product of fields. The domain special case alone
is insufficient. The field characteristic
is arbitrary, using §0.2. Deduce uniformity and automatic continuity from
an arbitrary Banach `K`-algebra into a reduced affinoid.

For nonzero `A`, the supremum seminorm is a multiplicative **norm** precisely
when `A` is reduced and `Ã` is a domain. A reduced domain by itself does
not suffice. Sources: [BGR] 3.8, 6.2.1–6.2.4; general spectral comparisons

Construct `φ̃:Ã→B̃`, with identity and composition laws. Prove the kernel

original presentation norms are equal. Include examples where a
surjective affinoid map does not induce a surjection on reductions.

For a presentation ring `A₀=π(Tₙ°)`, prove
`A°={a∈A : a is integral over A₀}` including nonreduced algebras.
No finiteness of `A°` as an `A₀`-module is asserted. A finite affinoid

finite-type `K̃`-algebra. Sources: [BGR] 6.3.1, 6.3.4–6.3.5.

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.6, *almost-noetherian-integral-affinoid-modules*.**
Identify its integral presentation with `A₀=π(Tₙ°)`, preserving the image of

`A₀`, `N⊆M` is any
submodule and `0<ε<1`, prove that a finitely generated `N'⊆N` exists

**Reduced quotient of a ring of definition.** For an open bounded subring `B⊆A`

An affinoid subdomain includes its representing algebra, map and universal

For a finite affinoid cover `Uᵢ`, `A→∏ᵢ𝒪(Uᵢ)` is faithfully flat.
Prove reducedness is local for a rational cover: `A` is reduced iff every

Sources: [BGR] Chapters 7–8; Part II consumes these subdomain interfaces.

## Layer 5: Čech comparison and acyclicity

Prove classical Tate acyclicity using the rational-localisation comparison
with foundational AdicSpaces and the affinoid-cover refinement of Layers 3–4.
Compare the finite-intersection algebras, restriction maps and augmented Čech
complexes. This supplies the classical acyclicity consumed by Parts II and III;
Part III's coherent-sheaf theorem is not a prerequisite. For the
two-piece Laurent cover use `d(u,v)=v|intersection−u|intersection`.
Transport Tate acyclicity and refinement through this chain map.

Retain augmented Čech exactness for **every algebraic `A`-module**, by
tensoring the bounded exact alternating Čech complex for `A` with the
module. Its terms are flat by affinoid-localisation flatness; bounded
exactness then makes this tensoring exact. Intersection algebras are
completed affinoid tensor products, not automatically ordinary algebraic
tensor products. For finite modules, supply the canonical Banach topologies
and strict exactness as a separate theorem. Construct the natural
Čech-to-derived-cohomology comparison for covers
whose finite intersections are acyclic, using native sheaf categories.
Apply it to Part III R3.1's finite-module sheaves. The general comparison
is independent of the quasi-Stein theorem which uses it. No arbitrary
module receives a fictitious Banach norm.

**Checks.** The Laurent sequence, a one-member identity cover, zero modules
and an infinitely generated direct sum of copies of `A`. Verify both the
augmentation and differential under the comparison. Exactness alone does
not certify closed images. Sources: [BGR] 8.2; [Kiehl-AB]; Part III R3.1.

## Layer 6: general G-topologies and rigid gluing

### 6.1 G-sites and sheaves

Develop admissible opens and covers with [BGR] 9.1's identity, restriction,
intersection and composition axioms, continuous maps, induced G-topologies,
bases and refinement. Construct their site on the preorder of admissible
opens and prove that the sheaf condition is precisely the admissible-cover
equaliser condition. Recover the ordinary open-set site of a topological
space. Prove the G0/G1/G2 completeness and enhancement results of §9.1.2,
including the universal property, and compatible pasting of §9.1.3.

Use Mathlib's sheaves and sheafification. Compare classical neighbourhood
stalks with site points, and BGR's plus construction with that sheafification.
Prove extension across a slightly finer G-topology by the dense-subsite
comparison, without constructing another category of sheaves.

### 6.2 The classical presentation of the common geometry

The weak affinoid basis uses finite affinoid covers; the strong topology is
detected by finite affinoid refinements after affinoid test maps. Prove
enhancement, restriction, admissibility of Zariski covers and the
idempotent/connectedness criterion. Construct the classical affinoid site
and structure sheaf used by Part II. General G-topology must be available below
both presentations, so this comparison does not define its own prerequisite.

Construct `RigidSpace K` as locally G-ringed spaces locally isomorphic to
these affinoids, with morphisms local on stalks. Prove the category laws,
the fully faithful contravariant affinoid-algebra embedding, admissible
restrictions, gluing and its universal property, and fibre products.
Construct affine and projective space, discs and annuli. Part II uses this
category and Layer 8's comparison; there is no second rigid carrier.
For quasi-separated rigid spaces, construct complete isometric field
extension using §1.3, compatibly with affinoid subdomains, gluing and
affinoid-coordinate faithful flatness. Carry the quasi-separated hypothesis
in these global base-extension statements.

**Checks.** The covering of the closed unit disc by its open disc and
unit circle is set-theoretic but not admissible. For `0<|ϖ|<1`, the
domains `|T|^n≤|ϖ|`, `n≥1`, give an admissible exhaustion of the open
disc: radii `|ϖ|^(1/n)` approach one even for discretely valued `K`.
Glue `ℙ¹` from two closed discs and identify the intersection annulus.

### 6.3 Relative compactness and properness

Define quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphisms by admissible affinoid
tests and finite covers, and separatedness by the diagonal closed immersion.
For an affinoid subdomain `U⊆Sp B` over `Sp A`, define `U⋐_A Sp B` by a
presentation `A⟨X₁,…,Xₙ⟩↠B` whose generator restrictions have supremum
norm `<1` on `U`. Prove equivalence with a single bound
`ε∈√|K×|`, `ε<1`, and the relative-polydisc closed-immersion criterion.
Establish restriction, separated-intersection, product and affinoid-base-change
laws. Finite affinoids are inner in themselves over the base.

Define Kiehl properness by separatedness and inner affinoid covers: over
each admissible affinoid of the base, the inverse image has two finite
affinoid covers `(Uᵢ)` and `(Vᵢ)` with `Vᵢ⋐Uᵢ`. Prove its local nature
on the base, composition and base-change laws, and properness of finite
morphisms. These classical predicates are supplied to Part II's properness
comparison and Part III's Kiehl theorems; adic properness is not their
definition. Sources: [Bosch] §6.3; [Kiehl-E] §2.

**Checks.** A smaller closed disc is inner in the unit disc, whereas the
unit disc is not inner in itself over `K`. A closed point is not an
affinoid open subdomain. For `ℙ¹`, the unit chart discs lie inside chart
discs of radius `|ϖ|⁻¹`; both pairs cover and exhibit properness. The pair
of unit discs used for gluing need not itself be an inner-cover pair.

## Layer 7: coherent sheaves and proper cohomology

### 7.1 Banach prerequisites for Kiehl's theorem

These are supplier contracts, not duplicate operator definitions. Banach
`A`-modules are also compatible Banach `K`-spaces; scalar towers and complete
ultrametric norms are explicit. For lattice statements choose a presentation
ring `A₀` and compatible norms/lattices. For Part III's closed-target and
restriction theorems, require the coefficient unit ball to be exactly the
image of the Gauss unit ball under that presentation and preserve this
condition in the norm comparisons. An arbitrary norm unit ball or `A°`
is not a substitute.

1. **PFA §§1.2 and 2.2; Part III R3.3 and R3.6:** use model-space
   quotients and bounded lifting; every Banach `A`-module is a continuous quotient
   of `c₀(I,A)` for some discrete index set, not necessarily countable.
   If `f:M→N` is surjective and continuous, there is `δ>0` such that
   `‖e‖<δ` implies `f−e` surjective. Deduce stability of a finite generating
   family under sufficiently small perturbations. This corollary is Part III
   R3.3's *surjection-small-perturbation*. Use bounded lifting and
   successive correction; an `A`-linear right inverse is not assumed.
2. **Part III R3.6, strict complete continuity:** for `u:M→N`, require a
   scalar `c`, `0<|c|≤1`, such that for every `ε>0` there is a continuous
   finite-image approximant `v`, `‖u−v‖<ε`, and finitely many vectors of
   the target unit ball whose `A₀`-span contains `c·v(M₀)`. The scalar is
   uniform; the finite family may change with `ε`. Prove independence under
   the allowed equivalent lattice models, implication to CompactOperators'
   complete continuity, and descent into a closed target submodule for
   source `c₀(I,A)`. No complemented-submodule hypothesis is added.
3. **Part III R3.6, Schwartz's theorem:** for affinoid `A`, surjective
   continuous `f` and completely continuous `g`, `f+g` has closed image
   and finite `A`-module cokernel. No finite-kernel conclusion is asserted.
4. **Part III R3.6, relatively compact restriction:** transport §6.3's
   classical inner relation through `rigidToAdic`. For finite `B`-module `M`, compose the
   actual restriction `M→𝒪(U)⊗_B M`, `m↦1⊗m`, with any continuous
   surjection `c₀(I,A)↠M`. This composite is strictly completely
   continuous over `A`. Use §2.3's almost noetherianity in the closed-target
   step; do not replace the restriction by an arbitrary map.

**Checks.** Zero, the identity on `K`, and the noncompact identity on
`c₀(ℕ,K)` distinguish the definitions. The map `h:Σa_nT^n↦Σa_nϖ^nT^n`
has truncation error at most `|ϖ|^N`, strict approximation with `c=1`,
and infinite-dimensional image; it fixes constants and has norm one.
`id−h` has image `T K⟨T⟩` and cokernel `K`. Descent to this closed
subspace is a required test. Taking `g=−id` violates Schwartz's compactness
hypothesis on an infinite model space. In `K²`, `(1,δ),(δ',1)` generate
when `|δ|,|δ'|<1`; for `f=e=id_K` the perturbation is not surjective,
so the permissible bound cannot exceed one. Sources: [Kiehl-E] §1,
Sätze 1.2 and 1.4, Lemma 1.3, §2; [Bosch] §§6.3–6.4.

### 7.2 Numerical slopes as a shared analysis interface

Supply `IsSlopeLE K r Q`, `IsSlopeDecomposition K U r M₁ M₂` and
`IsSlopeDecomposition.exists_projection`, the classical module-level
interfaces consumed by LAD §4.16. Use native polynomials, submodules,
continuous linear maps and finite projective modules. For `r>0`, the
affinoid root condition on `Q∈A[X]` is that every root
of `χ(Q)` has absolute value **at least** `r`, for every algebra map
`χ:A→L` with `L/K` algebraic, using the unique extended absolute value. Include
`r>0` in the predicate. For affinoid `A`, prove equivalence with testing
in finite extensions: include all finite residue fields and their finite
splitting extensions. A decomposition is continuously split and
operator-stable; its first summand is finite projective and annihilated
by a monic such `Q` with unit constant term. Every polynomial satisfying
the same conditions acts invertibly on the complementary summand. Its
continuous projector has the specified image and kernel and commutes with
the operator. Construct it from the continuous complementary-submodule
projection, independently of Fredholm theory. CompactOperators supplies
Riesz summands; LAD §4.16 proves the numerical comparison for a separated
Fredholm factor. Existence at every cutoff over an arbitrary affinoid
family is not asserted.

For `r=|p|^h` this means eigenvalue valuation `≤h`, including equality.
It concerns annihilator roots; the roots of `det(1−TU)` are reciprocals.
LAD §4.16 owns `slopeCriterion_classical_iff_geometric`, numerical
normalisation, functoriality and uniqueness, using §2's supremum theorem.
Its coefficient test for monic `Q=ΣaⱼXʲ` with unit `a₀` is
`|aⱼ/a₀|sup rʲ≤1` for every `j`; do not reprove that comparison here.
Sources: [Urban] §2.3; LAD §4.16; CompactOperators Layer 3.

**Checks.** For `c∈K×` and a finite projective Banach module, `c·id` with `|c|=r`
belongs wholly to the first summand; the zero operator has zero first
summand. For `0<|c|<1`, `X−c` fails the `r=1`
condition, whereas `1−cT` passes its root test. Actual polynomial
annihilation is required even over a nonreduced base; pointwise tests alone
cannot detect nilpotent endomorphisms.

### 7.3 Coherence, identity principle and quasi-Stein spaces

**Supplier contracts: Part III R3.2–R3.4.** Finite modules
and coherent sheaves on `Sp A` are equivalent via the associated-module
functor and global sections, compatibly with restriction, tensor products
and exact sequences. Include coherent ideals/closed subspaces, finite
algebras/finite morphisms and affinoid acyclicity.

**Classical identity principle (supplied to Part II R1.9).** On a connected
normal rigid space, any nonempty admissible open is
analytically Zariski dense. Restriction is injective for functions and
finite locally free sheaves. Do not assert this for arbitrary coherent
sheaves supported away from the open, or omit normality.

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.4.** A quasi-Stein exhaustion is countable,
increasing, admissible and affinoid,
with dense restrictions of coordinate rings. Prove density for coherent
sections, generation on each member by global sections and vanishing of
higher coherent cohomology. No relative-compactness condition or global
finite generating set is implicit. Include the relative version when
inverse images of affinoid opens are quasi-Stein. Sources: [Kiehl-AB];
[Conrad] §§1–2; Part III R3.4.

### 7.4 Proper mapping, strictness and base change

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.6.** For Kiehl-proper `f:X→Sp A` and
coherent `F`, prove `M^i=H^i(X,F)` finite over `A`, all higher direct
images coherent, and closed-range differentials for finite affinoid Čech
complexes computing this cohomology. Use the finite inner-cover definition
of properness, with its separatedness and base-change properties. Neither
smoothness nor reducedness is assumed.

For an affinoid subdomain `Sp B→Sp A` or a finite flat affinoid map,
prove the canonical base-change isomorphism
`B⊗_A M^i ≃ H^i(X_B,F_B)`. For every complete isometric `L/K`, prove
the same with `B=A_L`; compare its algebraic tensor with the completed
field tensor using §1.3. Maps are induced by pullback and scalar action
and commute with connecting homomorphisms. Arbitrary nonflat base change
does not follow. Source: [Kiehl-E] Satz 2.6, Satz 3.5 and §3;
Part III R3.6.

### 7.5 Principal filtrations and formal functions

For the same `f,F`, `a∈A`, and `i≥0`, let

`R_n=ker(M^i→H^i(X,F/a^nF))`, for `n≥0`.

Require `R_0=M^i`, decreasingness, `a^nM^i⊆R_n`,
`aR_n⊆R_(n+1)`, and equality in the last inclusion for all sufficiently
large `n`. Prove a uniform shift `d` with `R_(n+d)⊆a^nM^i` for every
`n`. Also prove a uniform shift `e` such that the transition

`H^i(X,F/a^(n+e)F)→H^i(X,F/a^nF)`

has image in the image of `M^i`. Thus both the kernel and cokernel systems
of `M^i/a^nM^i→H^i(X,F/a^nF)` are pro-zero; the two shifts need not
coincide. Include the transition maps, not just abstract isomorphic limits.
Source: [Kiehl-E] Theorem 3.4 and the argument preceding Theorem 3.7.

For every ideal `J⊆A`, prove the canonical formal-functions isomorphism
`(M^i)^∧_J ≃ lim_n H^i(X,F/J^nF)`, with naturality. The general-ideal
argument is required and uses the noetherian filtration/Artin–Rees inputs;
it is not obtained by merely relabelling `a` as `J`. This is ideal-adic
completion, not Banach completion. The proof and its classical/adic forms
share Part III's cohomology implementation.

**Checks.** For `a=0`, `R_0=M^i` and `R_n=0` for `n≥1`; for `a=1`,
`R_n=M^i` and quotient cohomology is zero. For the identity of `Sp A` in
degree zero, `R_n=a^nM`. On `ℙ¹`, compute `H⁰(𝒪)=K`, `H¹(𝒪)=0`
and compare the Čech, sheaf and base-change maps.

## Layer 8: analytification and rigid–adic comparison

### 8.1 Analytification, local rings and components

Construct the classical rigid analytification consumed by Part II R1.
Construct absolute
analytification and relative analytification over `Sp A` for schemes
locally of finite type over `Spec A`. The latter schemes need not be
locally of finite type over `K`. Include the universal property, points,
fibre products, immersions and finite maps, with their canonical comparison
maps. Build relative affine charts using completed presentations and glue
them. The flat local comparison gives exact pullback; the coherent-sheaf
and proper GAGA comparisons are Part III R3.7's targets.

For a classical analytic point `x` over a closed point `x₀`, identify
the completed local rings, compatibly with their local map. Prove that
`𝒪_{X,x₀}` is reduced, respectively normal, iff `𝒪_{X^an,x}` is.
Use §1.2 and Layers 3–4 for affinoid and analytic excellence, the shared
permanence theorems for finite-type schemes over affinoids, and the
completion criteria; normal here means an integrally closed local
domain. Deduce the global equivalences for reducedness and normality.
Also retain connectedness and irreducible-component comparisons, with
components carrying their reduced induced structures. Sources: [Conrad]
§1 and Appendix A; SchemeAndStackFoundations' excellence input.

**Checks.** The affine line at zero and the dual-number thickening. Over
a field of characteristic different from two, the origin on
`y²=x²(x+1)` has an algebraic local domain but an analytic germ with two
branches, using a convergent square root of `1+x` on a small disc.
Local integrality is therefore not an additional equivalence. Completion
isomorphisms do not alone justify a local-domain assertion.

### 8.2 Classical points and constructible density

Construct `Max A→Spa(A,A°)`, prove injectivity, and identify rational
traces and their coordinate rings. In `Spv A`, let `L_A` consist of the
valuations at most one on `A°` and strictly less than one on `A°°`.
Prove its equality with the constructible closure of the classical points;
deduce their constructible density in `Spa(A,A°)`. Constructible subsets
are determined by their classical traces. Prove the finite rational-cover
criterion through this comparison. Sources: [Huber-CV] Theorem 4.1,
Corollary 4.2; Part II R1.7's classical-point contract.

**Checks.** Classical points of the disc, the nonclassical Gauss point,
and `|T|≤|ϖ|`. A rank-two point just below the Gauss point can have
`v(T)<1` but `v(T)^n>|ϖ|` for every `n≥1`; it is outside the adic
open `⋃_n{|T|^n≤|ϖ|}` corresponding to the rigid open disc. Its
singleton is proconstructible, not constructible: density does not say
arbitrary subsets are determined by classical points.

### 8.3 The image of the rigid–adic functor

Construct the shared functor `r(Sp A)=Spa(A,A°)` and prove compatibility with
gluing, products, the structure sheaf and its ringed topos. It is fully
faithful on rigid spaces. Adic spaces locally of finite type over
`Spa(K,K°)` are locally images of affinoids. Restricted to quasi-separated
objects, `r` is an equivalence with quasi-separated adic spaces locally of
finite type. Prove `r(X)` affinoid iff `X` affinoid. Source: [Huber-FR]
Proposition 4.5; Part II R1.7.

**Checks.** Two rigid closed discs glued along the rigid open disc give
a non-quasi-separated example: in its adic image the two rank-two boundary
points from §8.2 remain distinct. Over algebraically closed `K`, also
construct the example of two adic discs glued along the complement
of the closure of the Gauss point; it is locally of finite type but is
not in the global image. These distinguish local image, full faithfulness
and essential surjectivity. Check the affinoid case and empty space.

Part II owns the further separatedness, properness and partial-properness
comparisons with its adic morphism classes, using §6.3's classical notions
and `r`. Consume its converses with their discrete-valuation hypotheses
and its separately stated locally quasi-finite exception; do not infer
an unqualified converse from the forward comparison.

### 8.4 Proper GAGA

**Supplier contract: Part III R3.7.** For a scheme proper over an
affinoid base, require the exact tensor-compatible equivalence of coherent
sheaves under analytification and the canonical `A`-linear cohomology
comparison in every degree. Include compatibility of higher direct images
with analytification for a proper morphism, even if the target is not
proper. Degree-zero maps are pullback/adjunction maps and the higher ones
extend them functorially.

**Checks.** `ℙ¹`, its line bundles and finite schemes including nilpotent
thickenings. Nonproper affine-line analytification has nonpolynomial global
functions and does not satisfy an unrestricted GAGA statement. Étale and
pro-étale comparisons are owned by Part IV and AdicEtaleGeometry; this
roadmap asserts no additional equivalence of those topoi.

## Dependency order and completion

1. Import the shared Tate and Banach foundations; prove characteristic-free
   weak stability and its Japanese application.
2. Prove affinoid normalisation and topology independently of geometry,
   then supremum and integral theory. The polyradius converse follows
   the value-group theorem; it is not needed to prove that theorem.
3. Compare the algebra with Part II's carriers, localisations, tensors
   and spectral data. General G-site theory is independent of this step.
4. Construct classical subdomains, Tate acyclicity, the G-site and rigid
   category, then rigid analytification and the rigid–adic functor. Use
   foundational adic results, not Part II's consumers of these classical
   constructions. Establish the classical properness predicates.
5. Transport Part III's coherent, quasi-Stein, proper-cohomology and GAGA
   results through the ringed-site equivalence. Prove the elementary
   numerical decomposition and projection of §7.2 independently; LAD then
   supplies the geometric and Fredholm-window comparisons.

Completion requires all stated generalities, all canonical-map compatibility
theorems and every check above. There must be one production definition of
each shared series, operator, tensor and geometric object. Compile the
actual modules and audit the transitive axioms of their capstone theorems;
only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound` are accepted. An
elaborating roadmap prototype is not a proof or an implementation milestone.

# Roadmap: scheme, stack, cohomology and intersection foundations

**Summary.** This roadmap is the general algebraic geometry that the arithmetic roadmaps stand on: relative Proj, henselian pairs and excellent rings; descent, algebraic spaces, torsors and algebraic stacks; cohomology on the Zariski, Nisnevich, étale, fppf and pro-étale sites with coherent duality and Brauer groups; curves, divisors and Picard functors; deformations, formal schemes, algebraization and de Jong's alterations; and Chow groups with Chern classes, Riemann–Roch and the Hodge index theorem. We want it because Mathlib provides schemes, their morphisms and much of the abstract categorical infrastructure, but the stacks, site cohomology, duality and alterations needed for Shimura varieties, moduli of curves and abelian varieties, Galois representations in étale cohomology and the comparison theorems of p-adic Hodge theory still require substantial shared development. Rather than let each arithmetic roadmap rebuild a private version, this roadmap fixes one set of carriers and statements that the others import and cite.

This roadmap builds the general algebraic geometry that the arithmetic roadmaps of Tau Ceti stand
on and that neither Mathlib nor another Tau Ceti roadmap owns. From Mathlib's `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme`,
its morphism classes and its big and small sites, and from the Tau Ceti library's quasi-coherent
algebras, line-bundle classes, divisors and models of curves, it builds six layers: the
scheme-theoretic base (relative Proj, extension of coherent sheaves, the local structure of morphisms
locally of finite type, henselization of pairs, excellent rings, perfect schemes, ideal sheaves);
descent, algebraic spaces, torsors, quotients and algebraic stacks; sheaf cohomology on sites with
the comparison of the Zariski, Nisnevich, étale, fppf and pro-étale topologies, coherent Grothendieck
duality, Brauer groups and equivariant cohomology; the curve, divisor and Picard theory that glues the
existing curve roadmaps together; infinitesimal deformations, formal schemes and algebraization,
modifications, the moduli stack of stable pointed curves and de Jong's alterations; and Chow groups
with Chern classes, intersection products, Riemann–Roch and the Hodge index theorem. Its end theorems
are the henselization of a pair with its universal property (Layer 0), Artin's bootstrap theorem and
the Keel–Mori theorem (Layer 1), coherent Grothendieck duality and the Brauer class of an Azumaya
algebra (Layer 2), the Picard torsors of a curve without a rational point (Layer 3), Schlessinger's
theorem, Grothendieck's existence theorem for coherent modules, algebraization of compatible
morphisms and de Jong's alteration theorems
(Layer 4), and Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch, the Hodge index theorem and the Weil bound for curves over
finite fields (Layer 5). Every object is defined on Mathlib's `Scheme`; every theorem names its
hypotheses.

| Layer | Title | What it delivers |

## Scope and ownership

The geometric Chow groups and all operations graded by absolute closure dimension
are restricted to schemes locally of finite type over a fixed field, with maps over
that field (§5). General bases, including DVRs, need a different grading and are
outside this API. Section 4.6 uses Mathlib's two-term cotangent complex for algebra
lift classes with an existing flat lift. The non-affine Brauer comparison of §2.22 includes
the construction of the gerbe of local splittings.


**This roadmap owns** the shared scheme-, space-, site- and coherent-sheaf foundations: the general
relative Proj and its comparison with the finitely generated case, extension of coherent modules,
henselization of pairs, the catenary, Cohen–Macaulay, Nagata and excellent packages, perfect schemes
and perfection, the universal-homeomorphism equivalence of small étale sites (§0.23a),
absolute, relative, iterated and finite-field scheme Frobenius with coherent twists (§0.29),
normal schemes, codimension-one points under finite dominant morphisms and ramification at a point (§0.30),
the ideal-sheaf comparison API, algebraic spaces with their small étale sites,
group algebraic spaces, groupoids, torsors and their classes, categorical and geometric quotient predicates,
projective quotients by finite groups, algebraic stacks, moduli spaces, Galois gerbs, the
functoriality of sheaf cohomology on sites, the comparison of the topologies of a scheme with the coefficient sheaves `𝔾_a`, `𝔾_m`, `μ_n`, the
Nisnevich site, the pro-étale site foundations (replete topoi, w-contractible covers,
left-completeness), coherent Grothendieck duality in the generality of the Stacks Project, the Brauer
group of a scheme, abelian-extension boundaries, equivariant sheaf cohomology, the curve and Picard theory that no curve roadmap
states, formal deformation theory with elementary obstruction theories, adic thickening systems, coherent existence and algebraization of compatible morphisms, modifications,
strict transforms and alterations, the moduli stack of stable pointed curves, Chow groups,
Chern classes, refined Gysin maps, intersection products, a K-theoretic pushforward for
Riemann–Roch, and surfaces. Formal geometry here uses chosen ideals and level-preserving adic thickening
systems. Comparison with the category of topologically locally ringed formal schemes and
independence from ideals of definition are outside this scope. Polarized algebraization of
formal schemes and a category equivalence for polarized systems are also outside this scope.

**Interfaces consumed by the arithmetic roadmaps.** The crystalline, prismatic, analytic and ℓ-adic
roadmaps consume this roadmap through comparison maps whose theorems they own; this roadmap fixes only
its side of each interface. (i) Cohomology is Mathlib's `Sheaf.H` on the named site; the pro-étale
ℓ-adic coefficient is `Scheme.ellAdicSheaf`, not a discrete constant sheaf; `Br′(X)` is the torsion of
`H²_ét(X, 𝔾_m)`, distinct from the Azumaya Brauer group until §2.22's comparison applies
(Bhatt–Scholze 2014, Def. 6.8.1, Lemma 6.8.2). (ii) Over `ℂ`, algebraic de Rham to Betti cohomology
(Grothendieck 1966, Thm. 1′) and finite-coefficient étale to Betti cohomology with its relative form
(SGA 4 XVI, Thm. 4.1) are taken on Layer 2's sites; over `ℝ` the Galois-equivariant Betti groups carry
the sign twist (Benoist–Wittenberg 2020, §1.1; Benoist 2019, (1.1) and (2.16)). (iii) Let `A` be an adic space, `S` a scheme and
`A → S` a morphism of locally ringed spaces. For schemes `X, Y` locally of finite type over `S`,
a proper `S`-morphism `f : X → Y`, a torsion ring `Λ` and `K ∈ D⁺(X_ét, Λ)`, form
`X^ad = X ×_S A`, `Y^ad = Y ×_S A` with site maps `φ_X, φ_Y`. The canonical map
`φ_Y^* Rf_* K → Rf^ad_* φ_X^* K` is an isomorphism (R. Huber, *Étale Cohomology of Rigid Analytic
Varieties and Adic Spaces*, setup 3.7.1, p. 225, Theorem 3.7.2, p. 226). This proper comparison
allows arbitrary torsion coefficients, including residue-characteristic torsion; the bounded-below
condition on `K` is part of the statement. The scheme–adic fibre products and site maps belong to
the analytic roadmap, so this is a README-only interface here. Comparisons with diamonds in
characteristic `p` are separate (Scholze 2017, §§26–27). (iv) `R lim_n RΓ_ét(X, ℤ/ℓⁿ)` with its Galois action is compared
with pro-étale `ℤ_ℓ`-cohomology by derived completeness, and `lim H^q` replaces `H^q R lim` only under a
stated `lim¹` vanishing (Bhatt–Scholze 2014, Def. 3.4.1, Prop. 3.4.2, Cor. 5.1.6). (v) Prismatic,
crystalline and `A_inf` specializations (Bhatt–Scholze 2022, Thm. 1.8; Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze 2018,
Thms. 14.3–14.5) and the `B_dR` comparison with its trace-normalized period line (Betts–Stix,
Props. 3.19–3.21) are consumed with derived tensor products and Frobenius twists written out.
(vi) Cycle classes `cl^r : CH^r(X) → H^{2r}_ét(X, Λ(r))`, `X` smooth over a perfect field and `n`
invertible, are defined by the ℓ-adic roadmaps on §5.1 and §5.6 (Milne LEC, §23, Thm. 23.4), compatible
with products, proper pushforward and Gysin maps.

## Conventions

1. Rings are commutative with identity; the zero ring is allowed unless a target excludes it.
   Schemes, morphisms and opens are Mathlib's `Scheme`, `Scheme.Hom`, `Scheme.Opens` in a fixed
   universe `u`; "Noetherian", "separated", "proper" and "smooth" are hypotheses written on the
   target that needs them, never folded into a definition.
2. Big sites are Mathlib's `zariskiTopology ≤ etaleTopology ≤ fppfTopology ≤ fpqcTopology` on the
   category of schemes (slices `Over S` for a base); small sites are `X.Etale` with
   `Scheme.smallEtaleTopology`, and `X.ProEt` with `Scheme.ProEt.topology`. Cohomology is Mathlib's
   `Sheaf.H`; for `O_X`-modules it is Tau Ceti's `Scheme.Modules.Cohomology`. Every cohomological
   statement says which coefficient regime it is in (`𝔾_m` and smooth groups, `p`-torsion in
   characteristic `p`, quasi-coherent, arbitrary abelian sheaves) and never transports a result across
   regimes without a named comparison. Finite and adic coefficient extensions are downstream
   consumers; their comparisons retain finite Tor amplitude and coherent derived reductions.
3. Stacks are pseudofunctors with Mathlib's `IsStack`; representability of a morphism of presheaves
   means by schemes, of stacks by algebraic spaces; torsors are fppf torsors; group actions are on the
   left; group objects are `GrpObj` in the cartesian monoidal categories `Over S` (schemes, the
   ModularCurves convention) and `Over h_S` (algebraic spaces).
4. The genus of a proper curve is `dim H¹(X, O_X)`; the degree of a locally free sheaf of rank `r` is
   `χ(E) − r·χ(O_X)`. Thickenings are closed immersions surjective on points; modifications are
   proper birational, alterations proper dominant and generically finite. Chow groups are graded by
   dimension, measured by `Order.height x` for the closure of a scheme point `x`;
   `Order.coheight x` measures codimension. Intersection products on smooth varieties are graded
   by codimension.
5. Names live under `TauCetiRoadmap.SchemeAndStackFoundations`, in namespaces named after the
   strand (`Henselization`, `Excellence`, `IdealPullback`, `Spaces`, `Groups`, `Torsor`,
   `Nisnevich`, `Coherent`, `Brauer`, `Curve`, `Picard`, `Formal`, `Deformation`, `IsAlteration`,
   `Chow`, among others); the names proposed for the library are the ones in the subsections
   below, under `AlgebraicGeometry` for direct extensions of Mathlib objects (relative Proj,
   thickenings, adic thickening systems, alterations) and under `TauCeti` for the ring-theoretic
   and curve strands. `Suggested.lean` contains the key definitions with real bodies and the
   headline theorems that are statable at the pins, with some Checks as `example`s; each
   subsection lists its declarations there on a *Lean:* line. This document names every API item
   and every test; every target or test named here and absent from `Suggested.lean` is specified
   in this README only and is equally required. Proposed names of such README-only items inside
   the strands of `Suggested.lean` are set in italics (for example *Torsor.hom_isIso*), so that
   they are not mistaken for declarations of that file.
6. Every definition subsection lists its unit tests under **Checks**: a genuine construction that
   satisfies the definition, a degenerate or edge case, a false positive obtained by dropping one
   essential clause of the definition, and, where a carrier is shared with a library or another
   roadmap, a compatibility test against that carrier. A wrong definition fails at least one of them.

## How to read the build

The layer numbers organize the subject; the prerequisite stages above and each `*Needs:*`
clause give the construction order. Layer 0 is scheme theory and commutative algebra on
Mathlib's carriers and supplies every later layer. Layer 1 builds algebraic spaces on the big
fppf site, then group spaces, torsors,
quotients and stacks; it needs Layer 0 only for the henselian and excellent packages used in its
examples. Layer 2 is the cohomology layer: its first half (§§2.1–2.17) is site-theoretic and needs
Layer 1 only through the torsor carrier, its second half (§§2.18–2.23) is coherent and needs Layer 0's
Cohen–Macaulay package. Layer 3 assembles the curve roadmaps and adds what they lack; it needs
Layer 2's Hilbert 90 and duality. Layer 4 needs Layer 0 (excellence, henselian pairs), Layer 1
(stacks, for the moduli of stable curves), Layer 2 (Ext groups and torsors of lifts) and Layer 3
(Picard schemes of curves). Layer 5 needs Layer 0's relative Proj, Layer 2's coherent duality,
Layer 3's degrees and Layer 4's blow-ups and deformation to the normal cone. Construction
prerequisites can have higher subsection numbers; comparison-only references are identified
as comparisons. In particular, construct groupoids before quotients, the Nisnevich site
before topology comparisons, and homotopy invariance before refined Gysin maps.

## Layer 0: schemes and morphisms

The scheme-theoretic base of the roadmap, following the Stacks Project's chapters on constructions,
morphisms and commutative algebra. Mathlib provides schemes, affine schemes, quasi-coherent modules,
gluing, fibre products and the named morphism classes with their base-change stability; Tau Ceti and
AlgebraicVectorBundles provide quasi-coherent algebras, the relative spectrum and graded algebras.
Layer 0 adds the sheaf comparison and direct-image algebras, the general relative Proj compared with
StableReduction's finitely generated case, extension of coherent sheaves and Hartogs statements, the
dimension theory and limit theory of morphisms locally of finite type, henselization of pairs as a
small colimit of étale neighbourhoods, the catenary, Cohen–Macaulay, Nagata and excellent packages,
perfect schemes and perfection, flat base change of annihilators and cokernels, and the ideal-sheaf
comparison API that closed immersions need.

**Conventions of this layer.** `S_aff` is Mathlib's small affine Zariski site `S.AffineZariskiSite`.
A quasi-coherent algebra is Tau Ceti's `TauCeti.AlgebraicGeometry.QuasicoherentAlgebra` (a commutative
monoid in `S.Modules` with quasi-coherent underlying module), a graded one is AlgebraicVectorBundles
L2A's `GradedQuasicoherentAlgebra`; gradings are indexed by `ℕ`, and the degree-zero part `A_0` is an
`O_S`-algebra through the unit `O_S → A_0`, which is an isomorphism only where a target says so. Henselian
pairs are Mathlib's `HenselianRing R I`; regular rings are `IsRegularRing`; regular sequences are
`RingTheory.Sequence.IsRegular`. Perfection of an `𝔽_p`-algebra is Mathlib's colimit-along-Frobenius
`PerfectClosure`, never the inverse-limit `Perfection`. Weil restriction is ModularCurves 0F; strict
henselization, miracle flatness and the openness of the regular locus are ModularCurves 4D; coherent
sheaves are JacobianChallenge Layer B's `FinitelyPresentedSheaf`.

### 0.1 Quasi-coherent algebras as sheaves of algebras, and direct-image algebras

Construct, for a quasi-coherent `O_S`-algebra `A`, the coequifibered presheaf of rings on `S_aff`
that Mathlib's relative gluing consumes, `U ↦ A(U)` with the localisation maps
`CommMon.isLocalization_basicOpen`, and prove the comparison `sectionsPresheaf_iso`: the sheaf of
algebras it generates is `A` itself as a sheaf of `O_S`-algebras, naturally in `A` (Stacks, Situation
27.3.1 (01LM), Lemma 27.3.2 (01LN)). Define `pushforwardAlgebra f`, the direct image `f_* O_X` for
`f : X → S` quasi-compact and quasi-separated, as a quasi-coherent `O_S`-algebra (the direct image of
a quasi-coherent module along such an `f` is quasi-coherent by Stacks, Lemma 26.24.1 (01LC)), and
prove `pushforwardAlgebra_affine`: for `f` affine it is AlgebraicVectorBundles L1A's
`affineFunctions`, and `pushforwardAlgebra_baseChange`: for a flat `g : S' → S` with base change
`f' : X' → S'`, the base change map `g^* f_* O_X → f'_* O_{X'}` is an isomorphism of
`O_{S'}`-algebras (Stacks, Lemma 30.5.2 (02KH), the case `i = 0`).
*Needs:* Tau Ceti `QuasicoherentAlgebra`, `CommMon.sectionsPresheaf`; AlgebraicVectorBundles L1A;
Mathlib `QuasiCompact`, `QuasiSeparated`.

**Checks.**
- `sectionsPresheaf_structureSheaf`: for `A = O_S` the presheaf is `U ↦ Γ(U, O_S)` and the
  comparison is the identity.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_id`: `(𝟙 S)_* O_S = O_S` as algebras.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_hartogs`: for the open immersion `𝔸² ∖ {0} → 𝔸²` over a field,
  the direct image is `O_{𝔸²}` by Hartogs and hence is quasi-coherent.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_reduced_points_isQuasicoherent`: over every field `k`, let
  `f : ⨿_{n≥0} Spec k → Spec k[t]` send `t` to `n`. Its direct image is quasi-coherent:
  the global module is `M = ∏_n k`, with `t` acting by `(n)_n`, and on each `D(g)` the
  canonical localization map `M_g → ∏_{g(n)≠0} k` is an isomorphism, compatible with
  restriction. Extend a tuple by zero to obtain surjectivity; a tuple supported on
  `g(n)=0` is killed by one multiplication by `g`, giving injectivity.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_unbounded_thickenings_not_quasicoherent`: over every field `k`,
  put `A = k[t]` and take `f : ⨿_{n≥1} Spec(A/(t^n)) → Spec A`. Its global module is
  `M = ∏_{n≥1} A/(t^n)`, whereas `f⁻¹D(t)` is empty and the sections there are zero.
  In `M_t` the unit tuple survives: for every `r`, the coordinate `n=r+1` of
  `t^r · (1)_n` is nonzero. Thus `M_t ≠ 0` and `f_*O` is not quasi-coherent.
- `pushforwardAlgebra_finite_thickenings_isQuasicoherent`: for the finite family
  `1 ≤ n ≤ N`, `f_*O` is quasi-coherent and `t^N` kills the whole global product,
  whose localization at `t` is zero, agreeing with the sections on `D(t)`.
  This includes the empty family `N=0`.

These localization comparisons use the affine quasi-coherence criterion
([Stacks, §26.7 (01I6)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01I6)); the qcqs
pushforward theorem is [Lemma 26.24.1 (01LC)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01LC).

### 0.2 Morphism properties of relative spectra and modules on them

Prove, for `p : Spec_S(A) → S` the relative spectrum of a quasi-coherent algebra: `p` is affine,
with `p_* O = A` (Stacks, Lemma 27.4.6 (01LX)); `p` is of finite type, of finite presentation,
finite, integral, a closed immersion, respectively, iff `A` is locally of finite type, of finite
presentation, finite, integral, a quotient of `O_S`, as an `O_S`-algebra
(`relativeSpec_finiteType_iff` and the four companions). Over an affine open `U ⊆ S` the preimage
is `Spec A(U)`, so each equivalence is the affine-local description of the morphism property:
Stacks, Lemma 29.15.2 (01T2) for finite type and Lemma 29.22.2 (01TQ) for finite presentation, each
with Lemma 29.11.2 (01S7) (an affine morphism is quasi-compact and separated); Lemma 29.45.2 (02K8)
for integral; Lemma 29.45.3 (01WI) for finite; Lemma 29.2.1 (01QO) for closed immersions. Prove `relativeSpec_modulesEquiv`: quasi-coherent `O_{Spec_S(A)}`-modules are equivalent to
quasi-coherent `O_S`-modules with an `A`-module structure, by `p_*`, with quasi-inverse
`G ↦ p^*G ⊗_{p^*A} O_{Spec_S A}` using the canonical algebra map `p^*A → O_{Spec_S A}` (Stacks, Lemma 29.11.7 (01SB)). *Needs:* §0.1; Tau Ceti `CommMon.relativeSpec`;
AlgebraicVectorBundles L1B.

**Checks.**
- `relativeSpec_tensor_counit`: for `S = Spec k`, `A = k[t]`, `F = O`, ordinary
  `p^*p_*F` has module `A ⊗_k A`; multiplication has nonzero kernel element

- `relativeSpec_identity`: for `A = O_S`, the inverse is the identity.
- `relativeSpec_zero_module`: the inverse sends the zero module to zero.

### 0.3 Proj, base change and the relative Proj

Prove `Proj.isPullback_baseChange`: for a graded `R`-algebra `A` and `R → R'`, Mathlib's
`Proj (A ⊗_R R')` is the base change of `Proj A` along `Spec R' → Spec R` (Stacks, Lemma 27.11.6
(01N2)). Construct `relativeProj A` for an arbitrary `ℕ`-graded quasi-coherent `O_S`-algebra `A`
(AlgebraicVectorBundles L2A's `GradedQuasicoherentAlgebra`), whose degree-zero part `A_0` is an
`O_S`-algebra through the unit `O_S → A_0` and need not be `O_S` (Stacks, Situation 27.15.1 (01NN)):
the scheme over `S` glued from `Proj A(U)` over the affine opens `U` of `S` (Stacks, Lemmas
27.15.2–27.15.4 (01NO, 01NP, 01NQ)). Its structure morphism `relativeProj.toBase` is glued from
the composites `Proj A(U) → Spec A(U)_0 → U` of Mathlib's `Proj.toSpecZero` with the map induced
by `O_S(U) → A_0(U)`, and is separated (Stacks, Lemma 27.16.9 (01O2)). Construct the quasi-coherent
twisting sheaves `O(n)`, `n ∈ ℤ`, with the graded map `A → ⊕_{n ≥ 0} (relativeProj.toBase)_* O(n)`
(Stacks, Lemma 27.15.5 (01NR)). *Generated in degree one* means generated by `A_1` as a graded
`A_0`-algebra; then `O(1)` is invertible and multiplication gives `O(n) ≅ O(1)^{⊗n}` (Stacks, Lemma
27.16.11 (01O4)). Generation by `A_1` as an `O_S`-algebra is a stronger condition, forcing
`O_S → A_0` to be surjective. Prove the affine comparison
`relativeProj_affine_iso : relativeProj A ≅ Proj A(S)` over `S` for affine `S`. Prove
`relativeProj_baseChange`: formation of `relativeProj` commutes with arbitrary base change
`g : S' → S`, with degree-zero part `g^* A_0`, compatibly with `O(n)` (Stacks, Lemma 27.16.10
(01O3)). Prove `relativeProj_veronese`: for `d ≥ 1` the Veronese subalgebra `A^{(d)} = ⊕_k A_{dk}`,
which has the same degree-zero part `A_0`, satisfies `relativeProj A^{(d)} ≅ relativeProj A` over
`S`, with `O(n)` corresponding to `O(dn)` (Stacks, Lemma 27.11.8 (0B5J), on affine charts). Prove
`relativeProj_closedImmersion`: if `A_1` is of finite type and `A` is generated in degree one, the
graded map `Sym_{O_S} A_1 → A` is surjective in every positive degree and induces a closed
immersion `relativeProj A → relativeProj (Sym_{O_S} A_1)` over `S` pulling `O(1)` back to `O(1)`
(Stacks, Lemmas 27.11.3 and 27.11.5 (01N0, 01N1), on affine charts), so `relativeProj A → S` is
projective. When the unit `O_S → A_0` is an isomorphism, as for symmetric algebras and §5.4's
projective bundles, these are the same constructions, not a second carrier. Prove the compatibility
`relativeProj_eq_stableReduction`: on a graded algebra that is finitely generated in the sense of
StableReduction Layer 2, whatever its degree-zero part, `relativeProj A` is StableReduction's
relative Proj, by an isomorphism over `S` compatible with `O(1)` and with base change; the finitely
generated construction is the special case, not a second carrier. *Needs:* AlgebraicVectorBundles
L2A; StableReduction Layer 2; Mathlib `Proj`, `Proj.toSpecZero`, `GradedAlgebra`, gluing.

**Checks.**
- `relativeProj_polynomial`: for `A = O_S[T_0, …, T_n]` (the symmetric algebra of `O_S^{n+1}`),
  `relativeProj A` is `ℙ^n_S`, that is `Proj ℤ[T_0..T_n] ×_ℤ S`.

for a finite-type quasi-coherent submodule `G' ⊆ G` (Lemma 28.23.2 (01PF)); a finite-type

subsheaf of `G` (Stacks, Lemma 28.23.2 (01PF)). Prove
`locallyFree_coherent_extension`: a finite locally free sheaf on an open `U` of a Noetherian scheme
extends to a coherent sheaf on `X` (Stacks, Lemma 28.23.5 (0G41)); it need not extend to a locally

### 0.5 Pseudo-coherent modules

Define `Module.IsPseudoCoherent A M` for a ring `A` and module `M`: `M` has a resolution
`⋯ → A^{a_2} → A^{a_1} → A^{a_0} → M → 0` by finite free modules, that is a chain complex of finite
free modules in degrees `≥ 0`, exact in positive degrees, with zeroth homology `M` (Stacks,

`⋯ → O_U^{a_2} → O_U^{a_1} → O_U^{a_0} → F|_U → 0`, with each `a_i` finite.

`PseudoCoherence.IsPseudoCoherentSheaf`. Prove *isPseudoCoherentSheaf_quasicoherent* and

alone is insufficient. These follow from the local resolutions and the affine comparison
([Stacks, Lemmas 36.10.1–36.10.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08E4)). API: `isPseudoCoherent_iff_finite`

`IsPseudoCoherent.of_shortExact` (two-out-of-three in a short exact sequence, from the two-out-of-three

`Scheme.Modules.IsPseudoCoherent.pullback` along flat morphisms. Hypotheses: `A` any commutative ring;
`X` any scheme. *Needs:* Mathlib `Module.FinitePresentation`, `Module.Finite`, `ChainComplex`; Tau

**Checks.**
- `test_free`: for every scheme `X` and `n`, `O_X^n` is pseudo-coherent (the constant resolution).
- `test_dual_numbers`: for `A = k[ε]/(ε²)` and `M = A/(ε) = k`, the periodic resolution
  `⋯ → A → A → A → k → 0` by multiplication by `ε` witnesses pseudo-coherence; the resolution never
  terminates, so `k` is pseudo-coherent of infinite projective dimension.
- `test_not_finitely_presented`: for `A = k[x_1, x_2, …]` in countably many variables and
  `M = A/(x_1, x_2, …)`, `M` is finite but not finitely presented, hence not pseudo-coherent.
- `test_noetherian_agrees`: over `ℤ`, a module is pseudo-coherent iff it is finitely generated.

**Checks for the resolution predicates.**
- *IsPseudoCoherentModule_free*: finite free modules have a resolution concentrated in degree zero.
- *IsPseudoCoherentModule_zero*: the zero module has the zero resolution.
- *IsPseudoCoherentModule_not_finitely_presented*: a module that is not finitely presented cannot
  have such a resolution; apply this to the infinitely generated-ideal quotient above.
- *IsPseudoCoherentSheaf_free*: `O_X^n` has a finite free resolution concentrated in degree zero.
- *IsPseudoCoherentSheaf_zero*: the zero sheaf satisfies the local resolution condition.
- *IsPseudoCoherentSheaf_extension_by_zero*: for a nonfield DVR `R`, fraction field `K`, and the
  generic open immersion `j`, the sheaf `j_!O` has zero global sections and restriction `O_{Spec K}`,
  and fails the predicate. These two restrictions determine
  the sheaf on the two-point space `Spec R`. Its affine section modules `0` and `K` are
  pseudo-coherent, so they do not detect this failure.

`PseudoCoherence.isPseudoCoherentSheaf_iff_affineOpens`, with the extension-by-zero Check as an

### 0.6 Reflexive sheaves, reflexive hulls and Hartogs

Define `Scheme.Modules.IsReflexive F` for a coherent `F` on a locally Noetherian `X`: the evaluation
map `ev_F : F → F^{∨∨}` of Tau Ceti's `SheafOfModules.dual` is an isomorphism (Stacks, Definition
31.13.1 (0AVU), stated there for integral `X`; here the same evaluation-map definition is made on
every locally Noetherian `X`). API: `isReflexive_iff_forall_affine` (affine-locally,
`Module.IsReflexive` of the sections; Lemma 31.13.2 (0AY0)), `isReflexive_iff_forall_stalk`
(reflexivity of every stalk, equivalently of the stalks at closed points; Lemma 31.13.5 (0AY3)),
`IsReflexive.locallyFree` (finite locally free sheaves are reflexive), `IsReflexive.dual` (the dual
of a coherent sheaf on a normal integral locally Noetherian scheme is reflexive; Lemma 31.13.8 (0AY4)
with target `O_X`), `reflexiveHull F := F^{∨∨}` for `X` normal integral with
`reflexiveHull_isReflexive` (Lemma 31.13.8 (0AY4) again), `reflexiveHull.unit : F → reflexiveHull F`
(injective exactly when `F` is torsion free, Lemma 31.13.4 (0AY2); an isomorphism on the open where
`F` is locally free, by `IsReflexive.locallyFree` on that open) and `reflexiveHull.lift` (its
universal property among maps to reflexive sheaves: the hull is left adjoint to the inclusion of
coherent reflexive sheaves into coherent sheaves; Remark 31.13.9 (0EBH)). Hypotheses: `X` locally
Noetherian; `F` coherent; the hull statements assume `X` normal integral. Prove `reflexive_extension_normal`:
on a normal locally Noetherian scheme `X`, a reflexive sheaf on an open `U` whose complement has
codimension `≥ 2` extends uniquely to a reflexive sheaf `j_* F` on `X` (Stacks, Lemma 31.13.12 (0EBJ):
for integral `X` with depth `≥ 2` at every point of the complement, `j^*` and `j_*` are inverse
equivalences between coherent reflexive sheaves on `X` and on `U`; on a normal `X` codimension `≥ 2`
gives that depth, and `X` is the disjoint union of its integral components), and for coherent
torsion-free `F` on a normal integral locally Noetherian `X`, `F^{∨∨} = j_* (F|_U)` when `F|_U` is
finite locally free and every point of `X ∖ U` has codimension at least two (Lemma 31.13.12 (0EBJ)
applied to `F^{∨∨}`, and Lemma 31.13.14 (0AY7), which decides whether a map on generic fibres extends
to a map into `F^{∨∨}` by a condition at the codimension-one points), with the `S_2` description of
reflexive sheaves: on a normal integral locally Noetherian `X`, `F` is reflexive iff it is torsion
free and `(S_2)`, iff `F = j_* j^* F` for some open `j : U → X` with complement of codimension `≥ 2`
on which `F` is finite locally free (Lemma 31.13.13 (0AY6)); and a reflexive sheaf has depth `≥ 2`
at every point where `O_X` does, so it is `(S_2)` when `X` is (Lemma 31.13.11 (0EBI)). Prove `coherent_hartogs`: for a coherent `F` on a locally Noetherian `X` and a closed `Z`
such that `depth F_x ≥ 2` at every point of `Z`, restriction `F(X) → F(X ∖ Z)` is an isomorphism
(Stacks, Lemma 31.5.11 (0E9I)).

Without integrality: prove `IsReflexive.two_le_depth_stalk`: for a coherent reflexive `F` on a
locally Noetherian `X` and a point `x` with `depth O_{X,x} ≥ 2`, `depth F_x ≥ 2` (Lemma 31.13.11
(0EBI), part (1), stated there for integral `X`; `F_x` is `Hom(Hom(F_x, O_{X,x}), O_{X,x})`, so
§0.17 `depth_hom_ge` applies, and the argument uses no integrality). Prove
`reflexive_extension_of_depth`: for a locally Noetherian `X` and an open `j : U → X` with
`depth O_{X,x} ≥ 2` at every `x ∉ U`, `j^*` and `j_*` are inverse equivalences between coherent
reflexive `O_X`-modules and coherent reflexive `O_U`-modules (Lemma 31.13.12 (0EBJ), stated there
for integral `X`; reflexive is `Scheme.Modules.IsReflexive` above). The proof is affine-local.
For a coherent reflexive `F` on `X`, `F → j_* j^* F` is an isomorphism by
`IsReflexive.two_le_depth_stalk` and `coherent_hartogs` applied on every open of `X` (the sheaf
form of 0E9I). For a coherent reflexive `G` on `U`,
extend it to a coherent `F` on `X` (§0.4 `coherent_extension`). Then `F^{∨∨}` restricts to
`G^{∨∨} = G` and has depth `≥ 2` at every point of `X ∖ U` (§0.17 `depth_hom_ge`), so
`F^{∨∨} = j_* G` by `coherent_hartogs` on every open of `X`, and `j_* G` is coherent. Its evaluation map
`F^{∨∨} → F^{∨∨∨∨}` is an isomorphism over `U`. At a point of `X ∖ U` both sides have depth
`≥ 2`, so the target has no associated prime there, and §0.17 `bijective_of_depth` makes the
map an isomorphism. On a normal `X` the codimension-two hypothesis of
`reflexive_extension_normal` gives this depth hypothesis. *Needs:* §0.4, §0.17 (depth,
`depth_hom_ge`, `bijective_of_depth`); Tau Ceti `SheafOfModules.dual`; Mathlib

- `test_unit`: for every locally Noetherian `X`, `O_X` is reflexive.
- `test_torsion`: on `X = Spec ℤ`, the tilde of `ℤ/2` has zero double dual, so it is not reflexive

`dim_x X` is the maximum of `trdeg_k κ(ξ)` over generic points of components through `x`,

### 0.8 Flatness over Dedekind bases, spreading out, étale coordinates and quasi-sections

Prove `flat_over_dedekind`: a morphism `X → S` to a Dedekind scheme with `X` reduced and every
irreducible component of `X` dominating `S` is flat. Here a Dedekind scheme is integral, locally Noetherian, normal and of dimension at most
one; equivalently its nonempty affine opens are spectra of Dedekind domains. The stalk modules
are torsion-free over the base stalks, hence flat
([Stacks, Lemma 15.22.11](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AUW)). Pure relative dimension is a
separate hypothesis in §5.2, including for finite-type morphisms. Prove
`generic_fibre_spreading`: for `f : X → S` of finite presentation with `S` integral and the generic
fibre `X_η` geometrically reduced (irreducible, integral, connected, normal, smooth), the same holds
for the fibres over a dense open of `S`; and `fibre_locus_constructible`: the locus of `s` where `X_s`
has a given one of these properties is constructible (Stacks, Lemmas 37.26.2 (0576), 37.26.4 (0578),
37.26.5 (0579)). Prove `flat_proper_fibre_loci`: for `f` proper and flat of finite presentation, the
loci where the fibre is geometrically reduced, respectively geometrically integral, are open (EGA
IV₃, Theorem 12.2.4 (v) and (viii), p. 183). Prove `fibre_power_irreducible`: for `f : X → S` flat of
finite presentation with geometrically irreducible fibres, every fibre power `X ×_S ⋯ ×_S X` has
geometrically irreducible fibres over `S` (its fibre over `s` is a fibre power of `X_s` over `κ(s)`,
and the projection from a product with a geometrically irreducible factor is a bijection on
irreducible components, Stacks, Lemma 33.8.4 (038F)) and is irreducible when `S` is (the fibre power is flat of
finite presentation over `S`, hence open by Lemma 29.26.10 (01UA), and a space with an open map onto
an irreducible space with irreducible fibres is irreducible, Topology, Lemma 5.8.14 (004Z)). Prove `etale_coordinates`: a morphism `f : X → S` smooth at `x` of relative dimension `d`
admits, on an open neighbourhood `U` of `x`, an étale morphism `U → 𝔸^d_S` over `S` (Stacks, Lemma
29.37.21 (054L)). Prove `rational_point_component`: a connected scheme smooth over a field with a
rational point is geometrically integral: it is geometrically connected because it is connected
with a rational point (Stacks, Lemma 33.7.14 (04KV)), geometrically normal and geometrically reduced
because it is smooth (Lemma 33.25.4 (056T)), so every `X_{k'}` is connected, normal and locally
Noetherian, hence integral (Properties, Lemma 28.7.7 (033N)). Prove `quasi_sections`: for
`f : X → S` smooth and surjective there is an étale surjective `S' → S` with a section of `X_{S'}`,
and for `f` smooth at `x`, with `x` closed in its fibre and
`κ(x)/κ(f(x))` separable, there is an étale map `S' → S` and a point `s'`
over `f(x)`, with `κ(s') ≅ κ(x)` over `κ(f(x))`, and a section whose value
at `s'` maps to `x` (Stacks, Lemmas 37.38.5 (057G), 37.38.6 (055U)). *Needs:* §0.7; Mathlib `Flat`,
`Smooth`, `SmoothOfRelativeDimension`, `Etale`, `AffineSpace`, `IsProper`, `Geometrically.Integral`.

### 0.9 Limits of schemes, Noetherian approximation and spreading out

Prove `affine_transition_limits`: a cofiltered diagram of schemes with affine transition maps has a
limit, computed affine-locally on any member, with `|lim X_i| = lim |X_i|` and the limit of

(01YX), 32.2.3 (01YZ); the underlying space of the limit is the limit of the underlying spaces by
Lemma 32.4.2 (0CUF), and since each projection to a member is affine, Lemma 32.2.2 (01YX), the limit

(01S7)). Prove `noetherian_approximation`: every quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme
is a cofiltered limit, with affine transition maps, of schemes of finite presentation over `ℤ`

`finite_presentation_limits`: for `S = lim S_i` as above with every `S_i` quasi-compact and

`IsGeometricallyUnibranch.baseChange_sepClosed` (invariance under separable field extension).

represent a finite locally constant étale sheaf. Every connected component `C` of `Y` is open
and closed, and the composite `C ↪ Y → X` is finite étale. Use the existing finite étale
morphism predicates for the representing map, by [Stacks, Lemma 59.64.4
(03RV)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RV); local Noetherianness makes `Y` locally

and finiteness and étaleness of `U.ι ≫ p`. Geometric unibranchness is not needed for this
finite-sheaf statement. The locally constant
Isom-schemes in Česnavičius 2020, Lemma 5.1 and its proof, can have infinite fibres and require
the stronger component result used there over a Noetherian semilocal base. Prove
`jacobian_etale_algebra`: for polynomials `f_1, …, f_r ∈ R[x_1, …, x_r]`, the localisation of
`R[x]/(f)` at the Jacobian determinant is an étale finitely presented `R`-algebra; it is finite

**Checks.**
- `unibranch_finite_components_eventual_sequences`: let `A ⊆ (ℕ → 𝔽₂)` be the subring of
  eventually constant sequences and `q : A → 𝔽₂` their eventual value. Its kernel `m∞`
  consists of the finitely supported sequences; it is not finitely generated, since any
  finite set of generators misses some coordinate idempotent `e_j`. Thus `q` is surjective
  and not finitely presented. All stalks of `X = Spec A` are `𝔽₂`, so `X` is geometrically
  unibranch, and `id_X` is a finite étale one-sheet cover. The actual quotient inclusion
  `i : Spec 𝔽₂ → X` is finite and closed, with image the connected component `{m∞}`;
  this image is not open and `i` is not étale. Every neighbourhood of `m∞` contains all but
  finitely many coordinate points. Affineness and field stalks therefore do not replace the
  local-Noetherian hypothesis.

  composite with `id_X` is finite étale. The family may be empty, in which case `X` is empty
  and there are no component inclusions.

- `IsLocalRing.not_isUnibranch_node`: for a field `k` of characteristic not `2`, the local ring of
  `k[x, y]/(y² − x²(x + 1))` at the origin is not unibranch (two branches).

  `ℝ[x, y]/(x² + y²)` at the origin is unibranch (its normalisation `ℂ[t]` is local above it) but
  not geometrically unibranch (residue extension `ℂ/ℝ` is separable of degree `2`).

### 0.19 CM- and `(S_n)`-quasi-excellence

For a Noetherian local ring `(A, m)` with completion `Â = AdicCompletion m A`, the formal fibres of
`A` are the rings `Â ⊗_A κ(p) = Ideal.Fiber p Â` over the primes `p` of `A` (taken at every prime,
not only at `m`). Define `Scheme.IsCMQuasiExcellent X` for a locally Noetherian `X`: every formal
fibre of every local ring `O_{X,x}` is Cohen–Macaulay, and every integral closed subscheme of `X`
has a nonempty Cohen–Macaulay open subscheme; `Scheme.IsCMExcellent X`: moreover `X` is universally
catenary; `Scheme.IsSnQuasiExcellent n X`: the same with `(S_n)` in place of Cohen–Macaulay
(Česnavičius 2021, Definition 1.2 and the sentence after it, p. 2; §2.8, pp. 6–7). API:
`isLocallyNoetherian`, `isCohenMacaulay_formalFibre`, `exists_isCohenMacaulay_open`,
`isSnQuasiExcellent_of_isCMQuasiExcellent`, `isCMQuasiExcellent_iff_of_openCover`,
`IsCMQuasiExcellent.of_finiteType`. Prove `quasiExcellent_cm_sn`: quasi-excellent schemes (§0.21)
are CM- and `(S_n)`-quasi-excellent for every `n` (Česnavičius 2021, Example 1.3 (p. 2), §2.10 (p.

  finite type over `E`, the same generators make it finite type over `𝔽₂`. It is therefore

  sequences is not finitely generated, as in §0.10, which proves the non-Noetherian claim.

  The map `P → R` taking `x_{2i}` to `t_i²` and `x_{2i+1}` to `t_i³` is surjective, so
  `R` is a finite-type domain algebra over `P`. Its normalisation is `T`, which is not
  finite over `R`; thus `R` is not N-1 or Japanese, and `P` is not universally Japanese
  ([Stacks, Definitions 10.161.1 (032F)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032F)
  and [10.162.1 (032R)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032R)). To identify the
  normalisation, use `t_i = t_i³/t_i²` to identify the fraction fields and the monic
  equation `Z² − t_i²` to see that each `t_i` is integral over `R`. The ring `T` is
  integrally closed: a fraction and an integral equation over `T` involve finitely many
  variables, where the polynomial ring over `k` is integrally closed. Hence the elements
  of the common fraction field integral over `R` are exactly `T`. If finitely many
  polynomials generated `T` as an `R`-module, choose `j` outside all their variable
  supports and set every `t_i` with `i ≠ j` to zero. Their images would be scalars and
  the image of `R` would be `k[t_j², t_j³]`, forcing `t_j` into that subring. Its elements
  have zero coefficient of degree one, a contradiction. The quotient map is finite type
  regardless of whether its kernel is finitely generated. Writing `P` as a union of
  finite-variable polynomial rings therefore does not establish universal Japanese-ness:
  [Stacks, Lemma 10.162.4 (032S)](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/032S) gives stability
  under finite-type algebras, not arbitrary filtered unions.
- `IsN1.test_finite_cusps`: for a field `k` and `r ∈ ℕ`, let
  `R_r = k[t_1², t_1³, …, t_r², t_r³] ⊆ T_r = k[t_1, …, t_r]`. The same fraction-field
  and integrality calculation identifies `T_r` as the normalisation of `R_r`. It is
  generated over `R_r` by the `2^r` monomials `∏_{i=1}^r t_i^{ε_i}`, with each
  `ε_i ∈ {0, 1}`: remove even powers from each exponent into the coefficient ring.
  At `r = 0` both rings are `k` and the generating family is `{1}`; at `r = 1` it is
  `{1, t_1}`. Thus `R_r` is N-1, and it is also Japanese since it is finite type over
  `k` (Stacks, Proposition 10.162.16 (0335)). The countable case fails because no single
  finite family generates its normalisation.
